items.title: 白皮书称指数及指数化投资步入高质量发展新阶段
items.summary: 中新网上海11月12日电 (高志苗)2026年上海证券交易所国际投资者大会12日在上海举行。《指数与指数化投资发展白皮书》(以下简称《白皮书》)同期发布，这是中国境内市场首部从指数及指数产品视角出发的行业研究报告。《白皮书》指出，中国境内多方政策引领，指数及指数化投资步入高质量发展新阶段。截至2025年底，境内指数产品规模达7.23万亿元，同比增长44.32%；全球ETF(交易型开放式指数基金)规模迈向20万亿美元。

items.title: UK Commandos to get AI-enabled edge from British scale-up Arondite, as company expands to NATO's northern flank
items.summary: British commandos will see operational effectiveness and warfighting readiness boosted with deployment of UK start-up Arondite’s advanced AI software. Multi-million pound deal comes as Arondite bring their cutting-edge British tech to Norwa
items.bodyHtml:
• British commandos will see operational effectiveness and warfighting readiness boosted with deployment of UK start-up Arondite’s advanced AI software.
  • Multi-million pound deal comes as Arondite bring their cutting-edge British tech to Norway, strengthening collective Euro-Atlantic security.
  • Announcement made at Atlantic Future Forum, the UK’s flagship international security conference and a unique demonstration of British convening power and strong partnerships across NATO.

UK Royal Marine commandos will get an AI-enabled edge on the battlefield, as the Royal Navy agrees a multi-million pound deal with British defence scale-up Arondite to deploy their cutting-edge software onto UK Commando Force (UKCF) systems.

Under the deal, the Navy will deploy Arondite’s software across commando units, using AI capabilities to help commandos make decisions much faster in complex and contested environments, and deploy autonomy, data at an unprecedented scale.

The software integrates all UKCF sensors, autonomous platforms and data feeds into a unified fighting system, helping to enhance readiness, planning speed and operational effectiveness.  

The project comes as Arondite announce a £35 million expansion into Norway, bringing their advanced technology to NATO’s northern flank and enhancing collective security in the High North.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP, said:

British defence tech is in demand. Arondite’s work with the Royal Navy will put cutting-edge software in the hands of our commandos, and their expansion into Norway shows the appetite for British technology among our closest allies.

This is a statement of intent from a British scale-up whose work with UK defence will see its workforce double to 150 employees by next summer. That means highly skilled, well-paid jobs here in the UK, and a sharper edge for our forces and allies in the High North.

The UK and Norway stand shoulder to shoulder on NATO’s northern flank, and this expansion will only strengthen that collective security.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said:

Defending Britain and our allies in the age of AI means harnessing the very best of British technology.

Arondite is at the cutting edge of that effort, putting AI to work strengthening our collective security. Its expansion into Norway shows how British innovation can help our closest allies meet the security challenges of today and tomorrow.

The partnership comes as UKCF receives a £100 million uplift in capability investment through the UK Defence Investment Plan. This will let the force develop future warfighting capabilities for special maritime and amphibious operations across the High North as part of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF).

The Chief of the Defence Staff, Sir Richard Knighton, announced the partnership between the Navy and Arondite aboard HMS Prince of Wales during the Atlantic Future Forum, the UK’s flagship international security conference and a unique demonstration of British convening power.

Chief of Defence Staff, Sir Richard Knighton KCB ADC FREng, said:

UK Commando Force is our foremost amphibious strike force, and it must be ready to fight and win in the most contested environments.

Cobalt will give our commandos a decisive edge, bringing their sensors, autonomous platforms and data together so that they can make decisions faster than any adversary.

The Cobalt mission orchestration software will enable seamless co-ordination between UKCF, UK defence units and partner forces across the JEF coalition. It will also allow future hardware and AI capabilities to be deployed rapidly. UKCF and Arondite will make the platform available to Norwegian units for joint testing during upcoming deployments, in line with the JEF’s new Northern Navies Initiative announced by the First Sea Lord on the first day of Atlantic Future Forum.

Alongside the UKCF contract, Arondite today announced it is expanding to Norway, opening its first international office in Oslo. The company will invest £35 million over the next five years to scale its work with Norwegian Armed Forces, Norwegian industry and NATO allies.

Building on its work with Defence, Arondite is on track to double its headcount to 150 employees by summer 2027, creating highly skilled jobs and careers in the UK.

Will Blyth, Co-founder and CEO of Arondite, said:

UK Commando Force remain ready to defend the High North at a moment’s notice. As the threats we face become more complex and unpredictable, commando units are employing the latest technologies to reach further and adapt faster than our adversaries. It is a real privilege to support teams who are adopting technology at the speed modern deterrence demands.

Our allies in Norway are working side-by-side with UK Commandos every day on the frontline of European security. They have some of the most complex missions in the world and they rightly demand technology that works from day one, which is why I am proud to announce Arondite’s first office outside of the UK will be in Oslo, as part of our long-term commitment to Norway.

From the Lunna House agreement to the combined Type 26 anti-submarine frigate fleet, the UK-Norway relationship is one of deep defence integration. Norway sits on NATO’s northern flank, and the two nations have worked closely together for decades to strengthen security in the Atlantic High North.

The Type 26 frigate deal supports 4,000 jobs across the UK supply chain, including more than 2,000 in Scotland.

The Royal Navy’s investment into the capability of UK Commando Force is backed by the Defence Investment Plan, which sets out £298 billion of defence investment over the next four years.

items.title: UK hosts global summit to combat financial crime
items.summary: The Global Financial Industry Partnership (GFIP) Summit 2026, hosted by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) on behalf of the Joint Chiefs of Global Tax Enforcement (J5), brought together international experts to strengthen cooperation against tax
items.bodyHtml:
The Global Financial Industry Partnership (GFIP) Summit 2026, hosted by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) on behalf of the Joint Chiefs of Global Tax Enforcement (J5), brought together international experts to strengthen cooperation against tax crime, money laundering and wider financial crime. 

Financial crime increasingly operates across borders, sectors and technologies. Criminal networks exploit those connections to move illicit funds and conceal their activities. 

The summit focused on three priorities: strengthening operational coordination across the financial system, improving cross-border information sharing and ensuring public-private partnerships deliver measurable results. 

JP Marks, HMRC Chief Executive and First Permanent Secretary, said: 

Financial crime is constantly evolving and our response has to evolve with it. Strong global partnerships are essential to stay ahead of the threats we face. 

By bringing together the different strengths of government, law enforcement and industry, we can see more, connect more and deliver greater disruption than any of us can alone. 

GFIP has already shown what can be achieved through international collaboration and I’m grateful for the leadership and commitment of everyone involved. Together we can build on that progress, continue to innovate and deliver even more in the years ahead. 

GFIP brings together government, law enforcement, financial institutions, fintechs and financial intelligence units to turn shared insight into coordinated action against financial crime. 

Since its launch in 2022, partners have developed joint assessments of emerging threats, including identity crime, fintech-enabled financial crime and trade-based money laundering, while testing new ways to improve information sharing and operational cooperation. 

Further information 

The J5 consists of HMRC, the Australian Taxation Office, the Canada Revenue Agency, the Dutch Fiscal Intelligence and Investigation Service and IRS Criminal Investigation in the U.S. By sharing intelligence, coordinating operations, and leveraging advanced technology, the J5 has uncovered schemes that would be difficult for any one country to dismantle alone. For more information about the J5, visit www.j5alliance.global

items.title: Scottish cooking-products innovator Ooni fires up global growth with government-backed finance
items.summary: The Scottish firm employs over 160 people across the UK and is currently recruiting for a further 8 UK-based roles Announcement made alongside UK Export Finance’s first Scotland Business Forum, bringing together Scottish businesses, lenders
items.bodyHtml:
• The Scottish firm employs over 160 people across the UK and is currently recruiting for a further 8 UK-based roles
  • Announcement made alongside UK Export Finance’s first Scotland Business Forum, bringing together Scottish businesses, lenders and government to unlock more export-led growth

Ooni, an Edinburgh-based cooking-products company, is building on its international success with £10 million of financing provided by HSBC UK and guaranteed by UK Export Finance (UKEF), the government’s export credit agency. The financing provides Ooni with a flexible working capital buffer to underpin continued expansion across key markets in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand.

Founded in 2012, Ooni has grown from a Kickstarter-funded start-up into a global consumer brand. The company currently employs over 230 people globally, with 167 roles based in the UK. Following recent growth, Ooni is now hiring 8 additional UK-based roles.

The announcement comes alongside UKEF’s first Scotland Business Forum in Edinburgh on 12 November, part of International Trade Week. The Forum will bring Scottish exporters together with banks, government and trade specialists to discuss how businesses can access the finance and support they need to expand internationally.

Minister for Trade Anas Sarwar said:

Ooni is the perfect example of how Government and business can work together to take British products to customers around the world.

As we celebrate International Trade Week, UKEF continues to help ambitious firms secure the finance they need to grow exports, create jobs and drive growth in every postcode.

Founded by Edinburgh-born Darina Garland and her husband Kristian Tapaninaho, Ooni has operations in several international markets while retaining a significant presence in Scotland, including its product development operation at Ooni Park in Broxburn and offices at Edinburgh Park.

Carol Harvey, Export Finance Manager for UKEF, said:

Ooni’s journey from start-up to world-leading brand is a brilliant example of Scottish innovation and ambition.

We’re proud to work with HSBC UK to help Ooni invest in growth and jobs in Scotland while taking its products to even more customers around the world.

Andrew Brown, Chief Financial Officer at Ooni, said:

Our 2025 profit growth gave our partners a clear vote of confidence in the strength of the Ooni brand and our strategic direction, despite persistent global market headwinds. That underlying balance sheet resilience led HSBC to extend our credit facility from £6 million to £10 million, supporting Ooni on its next phase of growth.

Stephanie Betant, Managing Director and Head of Global Trade Solutions at HSBC UK, said:

Ooni is a great example of the ambition we see among UK businesses looking beyond their home market for growth.

As companies expand internationally, having the right trade, working capital and banking solutions in place makes all the difference – helping them manage complexity, strengthen resilience and seize opportunities in new markets.

At HSBC UK, we’re proud to collaborate with UKEF so businesses like Ooni can turn international ambition into sustainable growth.

The Scotland Business Forum forms part of UKEF’s wider work with lending partners to expand access to export finance across the UK, supporting the government’s ambition to drive growth in every region and nation.

Over the last financial year, UKEF provided over £11 billion in loans, guarantees and insurance to help UK companies export and grow, supporting up to 85,000 jobs and contributing up to £6.4 billion to the economy.
items.bodyText:
The Scottish firm employs over 160 people across the UK and is currently recruiting for a further 8 UK-based roles
  Announcement made alongside UK Export Finance’s first Scotland Business Forum, bringing together Scottish businesses, lenders and government to unlock more export-led growth


Ooni, an Edinburgh-based cooking-products company, is building on its international success with £10 million of financing provided by HSBC UK and guaranteed by UK Export Finance (UKEF), the government’s export credit agency. The financing provides Ooni with a flexible working capital buffer to underpin continued expansion across key markets in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand.

Founded in 2012, Ooni has grown from a Kickstarter-funded start-up into a global consumer brand. The company currently employs over 230 people globally, with 167 roles based in the UK. Following recent growth, Ooni is now hiring 8 additional UK-based roles.

The announcement comes alongside UKEF’s first Scotland Business Forum in Edinburgh on 12 November, part of International Trade Week. The Forum will bring Scottish exporters together with banks, government and trade specialists to discuss how businesses can access the finance and support they need to expand internationally.

Minister for Trade Anas Sarwar said:


  Ooni is the perfect example of how Government and business can work together to take British products to customers around the world.

  As we celebrate International Trade Week, UKEF continues to help ambitious firms secure the finance they need to grow exports, create jobs and drive growth in every postcode.


Founded by Edinburgh-born Darina Garland and her husband Kristian Tapaninaho, Ooni has operations in several international markets while retaining a significant presence in Scotland, including its product development operation at Ooni Park in Broxburn and offices at Edinburgh Park.

Carol Harvey, Export Finance Manager for UKEF, said:


  Ooni’s journey from start-up to world-leading brand is a brilliant example of Scottish innovation and ambition.

  We’re proud to work with HSBC UK to help Ooni invest in growth and jobs in Scotland while taking its products to even more customers around the world.


Andrew Brown, Chief Financial Officer at Ooni, said:


  Our 2025 profit growth gave our partners a clear vote of confidence in the strength of the Ooni brand and our strategic direction, despite persistent global market headwinds. That underlying balance sheet resilience led HSBC to extend our credit facility from £6 million to £10 million, supporting Ooni on its next phase of growth.


Stephanie Betant, Managing Director and Head of Global Trade Solutions at HSBC UK, said:


  Ooni is a great example of the ambition we see among UK businesses looking beyond their home market for growth.

  As companies expand internationally, having the right trade, working capital and banking solutions in place makes all the difference – helping them manage complexity, strengthen resilience and seize opportunities in new markets.

  At HSBC UK, we’re proud to collaborate with UKEF so businesses like Ooni can turn international ambition into sustainable growth.


The Scotland Business Forum forms part of UKEF’s wider work with lending partners to expand access to export finance across the UK, supporting the government’s ambition to drive growth in every region and nation.

Over the last financial year, UKEF provided over £11 billion in loans, guarantees and insurance to help UK companies export and grow, supporting up to 85,000 jobs and contributing up to £6.4 billion to the economy.

items.bodyHtml:
The Prime Minister spoke to the Emir of Qatar, His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani this morning. 

The Prime Minister began by thanking the Emir for Qatar’s efforts to support de-escalation in the Middle East.

The two leaders noted that a return to conflict would have profound consequences and help no one. They agreed to work closely together with the US and regional partners to help find a diplomatic solution and work to re-open the Strait of Hormuz. 

They agreed to keep each other updated and to speak again soon.
items.bodyText:
The Prime Minister spoke to the Emir of Qatar, His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani this morning. 

The Prime Minister began by thanking the Emir for Qatar’s efforts to support de-escalation in the Middle East.

The two leaders noted that a return to conflict would have profound consequences and help no one. They agreed to work closely together with the US and regional partners to help find a diplomatic solution and work to re-open the Strait of Hormuz. 

They agreed to keep each other updated and to speak again soon.

items.title: Water bosses must not be rewarded for failure by another name, says Environment Secretary
items.summary: Water bosses must not be allowed to dodge the government’s bonus ban by disguising bonuses as other forms of pay, the Environment Secretary has warned today (12 November). A review of the bonus ban rule begins today, which Dame Angela Eagle
items.bodyHtml:
Water bosses must not be allowed to dodge the government’s bonus ban by disguising bonuses as other forms of pay, the Environment Secretary has warned today (12 November).

A review of the bonus ban rule begins today, which Dame Angela Eagle has asked must be wide-ranging as she moves to close the loopholes that reward failure.

The government’s ban has already stopped over £10 million going to water bosses since it was introduced. With nine water companies triggering the ban in the last financial year alone, and more than £6.5 million of potential bonuses blocked.

Yet, some executives have seen their total pay rise over 2025-26 despite continued poor performance. Ofwat has warned that retention payments and large, unexplained increases in base pay risk undermining the spirit of the bonus ban and eroding public trust.

The public can have their say in Ofwat’s four-week call for evidence, closing on 10 December. The findings will inform the government’s work to strengthen accountability in the water sector, including through the strengthened Water Bill.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said:

People are sick of seeing water bosses profit while rivers are polluted and customers are repeatedly let down.

A wide-ranging review launching today will ensure that failure doesn’t pay, whatever name the payment goes by.

The bonus ban was the first step. Where there are loopholes, I want them closed.

The action follows the first ever joint report from the regulators which leaves nowhere for underperforming companies to hide. By pooling their data, the regulators are closing the gaps that let failing firms point to a good score from one regulator while falling short with another.

It is published alongside the Environment Agency’s Environmental Performance Assessment Report, which shows that pollution incidents remain far too high, with only one company achieving the top four-star rating.

One-star ratings automatically mean that bonuses will be blocked for executives at Southern Water, Thames Water, South West Water and Yorkshire Water. The same applies to any company with a Category 1 pollution incident, which has a major, serious, persistent or extensive impact on the environment, people or property.

The Environment Secretary will also set out clear improvement actions for each water company, including tackling leakage, delivering sustained reductions in pollution incidents and improving customer satisfaction.

This is part of the government’s plan to put the public back in control of water. The Environment Secretary has already set clear expectations for the next Price Review, warning companies they must deliver better value for money for struggling households. Eight new regional water councils will give local people a say, and a strengthened Water Bill will give the public stronger control and accountability.

items.title: New report shows progress in cutting levels of ‘forever chemicals’ in England’s rivers
items.summary: Levels of two ‘forever chemicals’, PFOS and PFOA, in England’s rivers and freshwater fish have fallen significantly over the past 10 years, according to a new Environment Agency report, which says restrictions and targeted action from gover
items.bodyHtml:
Levels of two ‘forever chemicals’, PFOS and PFOA, in England’s rivers and freshwater fish have fallen significantly over the past 10 years, according to a new Environment Agency report, which says restrictions and targeted action from government have helped.

PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in a wide range of products and industrial processes. They are often called ‘forever chemicals’ because many break down very slowly over hundreds of years and can build up in the environment over time.  

The new PFAS sources, pathways & environmental data report published today (Thursday 12 November) updates the Environment Agency’s 2021 assessment, providing an updated picture of these persistent substances in the environment. It also draws on a much larger body of environmental data and advances in monitoring and analysis.

It found that, between 2016 and 2025, levels of PFOS in English rivers fell by around 30% and PFOA by 29%. Meanwhile PFOS concentrations in freshwater fish declined by approximately 49%.

These significant reductions in the environment show that regulatory action including by the government, such as the controls and restrictions on the chemicals PFOS and PFOA, can lead to measurable reductions of key legacy PFAS. However, the report found the presence of PFAS continues to be widespread, reflecting decades of historic use and continued releases from some sources.

The findings will support delivery of the UK’s first ever PFAS Plan, which the Government published earlier this year to better protect the nation and environment from these persistent chemicals.

Tackling one of the most pressing environmental challenges of our time, the Plan sets out future direction to better understand where these chemicals are coming from, how they spread and how to reduce exposure to them.

The Environment Agency’s Chief Scientist, Dr Robert Bradburne said:

Our understanding of PFAS has advanced significantly since 2021. We can now monitor a much wider range of these chemicals with greater accuracy, giving us a clearer picture of where they are found and how they behave in the environment.

Environment Minister Emma Hardy said: 

We are acting to crack down on forever chemicals through tougher rules on their use, updated guidance, widespread monitoring, and support for safer alternatives.

The Environment Agency will continue to expand its evidence base on PFAS and similar chemicals through research into airborne monitoring, water thresholds and potential PFAS replacements, helping inform future policy, regulation, and targeted intervention to help drive action where it can make the greatest difference.

Levels of two ‘forever chemicals’, PFOS and PFOA, in England’s rivers and freshwater fish have fallen significantly over the past 10 years, according to a new Environment Agency report, which says restrictions and targeted action from government have helped.

PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in a wide range of products and industrial processes. They are often called ‘forever chemicals’ because many break down very slowly over hundreds of years and can build up in the environment over time.  

The new PFAS sources, pathways & environmental data report published today (Thursday 12 November) updates the Environment Agency’s 2021 assessment, providing an updated picture of these persistent substances in the environment. It also draws on a much larger body of environmental data and advances in monitoring and analysis.

It found that, between 2016 and 2025, levels of PFOS in English rivers fell by around 30% and PFOA by 29%. Meanwhile PFOS concentrations in freshwater fish declined by approximately 49%.

The findings will support delivery of the UK’s first ever PFAS Plan, which the Government published earlier this year to better protect the nation and environment from these persistent chemicals.

items.title: Major changes to Blue Plaque schemes will see more of England’s ‘hidden heroes’ celebrated
items.summary: Changes driven by the Culture Secretary will open up the scheme to a wider range of people, places and stories across England Nominations for a National Blue Plaque are now open on Historic England’s website The National and Greater London
items.bodyHtml:
• Changes driven by the Culture Secretary will open up the scheme to a wider range of people, places and stories across England  
  • Nominations for a National Blue Plaque are now open on Historic England’s website

The National and Greater London Blue Plaques schemes are being expanded to celebrate more inspirational people from across Britain, with nominations now open to the public, the Government has announced. 

New criteria will allow blue plaques to be placed on buildings that have been substantially altered or replaced since a historical person or group was connected to them, including homes, shops, workplaces, community buildings and streets.  

Previously, the criteria required a person or group to be associated with a building that was still in existence and not altered beyond all recognition. However, many brilliant people or groups throughout history have been connected to buildings that have since been redeveloped or demolished, including terraced houses and industrial factories. The changes will remove this barrier, opening the scheme up to a wider range of people, places and stories, helping to ensure more of Britain’s diverse history is represented. These include people connected to lost music and performance venues, former residents of demolished homes, and workers and innovators connected to former factories and workshops.  

To be honoured with a blue plaque, a person or group must have significantly contributed to human welfare or happiness and/or made an exceptional contribution to their field. Sites for a blue plaque must have a strong connection to a historical person who must have been dead for at least 20 years, or to a group which was formed at least 20 years ago and is no longer functioning.  

This year, £100,000 has been given to Historic England to support the programme and provide grants for community groups and grassroots organisations researching and developing nominations that address historic underrepresentation and improve geographical reach. Current projects include a partnership between charity Creative Lives and local archives across the East of England to uncover and share overlooked stories.   

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: 

Throughout our history, it has been ordinary, extraordinary people who have built our country and created lasting change.   

From millworkers who fought for fair wages, safe working conditions and the rights of women to the Windrush generation who helped shape our NHS, transport, manufacturing industries and more - too often their contributions have been airbrushed from our national story. Until now, it was difficult to commemorate their achievements with a blue plaque. These rules were outdated, unfair, and do not reflect who we are as a nation. 

That’s why we have changed the rules so that we can properly commemorate the heroes who shaped our communities and changed our country for the better. I hope people across the country will come forward and nominate the people whose contributions are a vital part of our national story, and deserve to be told and remembered.

Professor David Olusoga Hon FBA: 

English history has been shaped by women as well as men, by the poor as well as the wealthy and by people across England and not just those who lived in London.  

These welcome changes will liberate Historic England and English Heritage to celebrate the stories of England’s hidden heroes with their beloved blue plaques.

Ellie Djerir, Historic England’s Head of Participation Programmes, said:  

Every community has people whose stories deserve to be remembered, but some of the buildings connected to them no longer stand. By widening the criteria of the National Blue Plaque Scheme, we can now celebrate more of the people who have shaped our history, wherever they lived and worked.  

With the opening of this year’s nomination window, we’re looking forward to seeing the people that the public put forward for a plaque, and working with community groups across the country to help bring those stories to light.

 Matt Thompson, English Heritage’s Conservation, Curatorial and Learning Director, said:  

English Heritage feels this change will offer greater flexibility to recognise a wider range of individuals whose achievements deserve to be celebrated.  

Our charity has long been committed to addressing the historic under-representation within the scheme and we have made significant progress. This work will continue and this change will bring more opportunities to further enrich the scheme and the streets of London.

Run by Historic England on behalf of DCMS, the National Blue Plaque Scheme builds on the success of the London blue plaque scheme and local schemes across the country. Launched in 2023, the scheme extends across the country, with twelve plaques now placed from Plymouth to Liverpool. The London scheme, run by the English Heritage, will also adopt the updated criteria from this round of nominations. 

Recent people honoured by the National Blue Plaque Scheme include Daphne Steel, the first Black matron in the NHS; George Harrison, the lead guitarist of The Beatles; and Reverend Wilbert Awdry, creator of Thomas the Tank Engine. 

Applications are now open for both schemes until 13th January 2027. Blue plaques from these nominations will be unveiled in 2027. 

ENDS 

Notes to editors

  1. Updated criteria can be found on Historic England’s and English Heritage’s websites.  

  2. Nominations for Historic England’s National scheme can be here.  

  3. Nominations for English Heritage’s London scheme can be made here.  

Full list of blue plaques erected under the National scheme: 

  • Daphne Steele; first Black matron in NHS - Ilkley, West Yorkshire 

  • Clarice Cliff; ceramic designer - Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire 

  • George Harrison; The Beatles’ lead guitarist - Wavertree, Liverpool 

  • Cary Grant; Hollywood actor - Bishopston, Bristol 

  • Jack Leslie; pioneering Black footballer - Plymouth, Devon 

  • Esmé Church; actress and director - Bradford, West Yorkshire 

  • Reverend Wilbert Awdry; creator of Thomas the Tank Engine - Stroud, Gloucestershire 

  • Judy Fryd; founder of Mencap - Harpenden, Hertfordshire 

  • Mary Beale; pioneering female artist - Eastleigh, Hampshire 

  • Mary Cartwright; celebrated mathematician - Cambridge, Cambridgeshire 

  • Frank Soo; England footballer of East Asian descent, Buxton, Derbyshire 

  • Dorothea Bate; palaeontologist and archaeozoologist, Tring, Hertfordshire  

Full list of English Heritage’s 2026 plaques in London: 

  • Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin; the astronomer who discovered what stars are made of. 

  • Duse Mohamed Ali; pioneering Pan-Africanist and influential journalist. 

  • Julia Margaret Cameron; groundbreaking Victorian photographer  

  • Jill Craigie; film pioneer, feminist and writer 

  • Kamal Chunchie; early advocate for Black and Asian communities in the East End. 

  • Amy Gentry; pioneer of women’s rowing. 

  • Stefan Zweig; acclaimed Austrian writer who was one of the most widely read authors of the inter-war period. 

  • Sir Laurence Olivier; one of the greatest actors of the 20th century 

  • Asquith Xavier; the railway worker who challenged racial discrimination and fought against a workplace ‘colour bar’ 

  • Dr Annie McCall; who transformed maternity care and midwifery training 

  • Gertrude Tuckwell; who campaigned for better conditions for working women and helped shape some of the earliest legislation protecting them. 

  • Dudley Clarke; master of military deception

items.title: More familiar carers and less travel under new social care plans
items.summary: People will see the same carer more regularly so they can get to know their needs and spot changes sooner under new neighbourhood commissioning for social care Local councils will be tasked with arranging social care in people’s home in a s
items.bodyHtml:
• People will see the same carer more regularly so they can get to know their needs and spot changes sooner under new neighbourhood commissioning for social care
  • Local councils will be tasked with arranging social care in people’s home in a smaller geographical area or ‘neighbourhood’
  • Care workers will spend less time travelling between visits, with more predictable rounds closer to home

Thousands of people receiving care at home will see more familiar faces while care workers spend less time travelling between visits, under new plans to organise social care around local neighbourhoods.

Councils will be encouraged to commission home care across smaller geographical areas, with one or two main providers serving each neighbourhood.

New guidance and toolkits will be published in the spring to support local councils move to neighbourhood-based models of home care commissioning. The government will work with local councils over the coming months to track and support their progress.

For care workers, that means they can spend their working day in a much smaller area, rather than travelling long distances between visits.

For people receiving care, it means a better chance of seeing the same carers regularly and building relationships with people who know them, their needs and their families.

Familiarity can also help care workers notice changes in someone’s health or wellbeing sooner, helping people get the right support before problems escalate.

Currently, councils can commission individual visits from multiple providers spread across large areas. People may see different carers across multiple days, while workers can spend significant parts of their day travelling between appointments.

Research by the Health Innovation Network South West into care rounds across 6 providers in Bristol found that reorganising existing visits into geographical zones could potentially deliver the same care with 35% less staff time and 65% less driving.

Minister of State for Social Care and Mental Health, Alison McGovern, said:

We have a growing, ageing population and an NHS facing significant pressures. We are turning it around, but our NHS is at risk of being overburdened. Our national care service is the answer, and neighbourhood commissioning is a step towards this. 

Commissioning social care by neighbourhoods will help people stay well, independent and at home for longer. Home care will be more personalised, and people will see familiar carers who understand their needs and priorities. Carers won’t travel as far, saving time instead of rushing from visit to visit and carrying out set tasks in an impersonal way.

Under our plans, social care will work in lockstep with our NHS; better care at home means fewer unnecessary trips to hospital. We will work with councils and our NHS to deliver more care in our community, care that is proactive, planned and preventative, as we continue to lay the foundations for our national care service.

The government is shifting more care into the community, as part of its 10 Year Health Plan. Neighbourhood commissioning of social care parallels the ongoing work to build neighbourhood health across the country, which will bring together GPs, local councils, social care providers and voluntary, community and social enterprise to deliver more health and care services in the community.

This follows the Secretary of State’s announcement that the government will provide £40 million for GPs to provide extra support to around 300,000 vulnerable patients, to reduce avoidable hospital admissions and prevent serious illness. GPs will identify patients in their community who may require additional care targeted at the most at risk.

In September, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that a fully funded national care service will be established in the next Parliament, providing free personal care for older people, based on need rather than their ability to pay. The national care service will be founded on the same principles as the NHS and will be funded by changes to the triple lock pension.

In the short term, the government is:

  • making an additional £4.6 billion funding available for local councils in 2028 to 2029 compared with 2025 to 2026
  • establishing the first ever fair pay agreement for care workers
  • developing an adult social care workforce plan

Baroness Casey’s review of adult social care has been brought forward a full year, which will deliver recommendations for building a national care service.

Acting upon Baroness Casey’s recommendations, the government has also established a safeguarding board, is developing fast-track care for people with motor neurone disease and will appoint a dementia tsar.

Dr Jane Townson OBE, Chief Executive of the Homecare Association, said: 

We welcome the move to neighbourhood commissioning, which reflects what the Homecare Association has long argued: commissioning is the key to quality, fair work and better outcomes. 

To succeed, it must come with fees that cover the cost of care, predictable work and payment for whole rounds rather than contact minutes. People must also keep a real choice over who supports them. 

Done well, neighbourhood commissioning can mean familiar care workers who know the people they support, less time on the road and more secure jobs. These relationships help care workers spot changes early and keep people well at home. We look forward to working with government, councils and the NHS to develop guidance that puts these principles into practice.

Caroline Abrahams CBE, Emily Holzhausen CBE and Jackie O’Sullivan, co-chairs of the Care and Support Alliance, said: 

Commissioning home care at a neighbourhood level makes a lot of sense, and we hope it will help to promote more joined-up health and care for those older and disabled people who need it.

Just as importantly, it should lead to care professionals being able to spend more time on the job, and fewer hours travelling, thereby supporting greater continuity in their relationships with people in receipt of care and their families. Since strong relationships are central to good quality care, this really matters.

Phil Holmes, President of the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services (ADASS), said: 

We support efforts to improve continuity of care because relationships matter to carers and those who draw on care and support. Most councils are already moving towards models that give people more consistency, while placing a strong emphasis on the quality of care and regularly reviewing arrangements to make sure they are working. 

The starting point must always be people’s experiences and the outcomes that matter most to them. By making the best use of neighbourhoods and local communities, we can help more people see familiar carers who understand their needs and can spot any changes early. 

This is about moving away from a system defined by time and task, where too many people see a succession of strangers at the door, and towards one built on trust and personalised support.

Most councils are already moving towards models that give people more consistency, while placing a strong emphasis on the quality of care and regularly reviewing arrangements to make sure they are working. 

  The starting point must always be people’s experiences and the outcomes that matter most to them. By making the best use of neighbourhoods and local communities, we can help more people see familiar carers who understand their needs and can spot any changes early. 

  This is about moving away from a system defined by time and task, where too many people see a succession of strangers at the door, and towards one built on trust and personalised support.

items.title: Flat owners handed massive boost to fight rip-off service charges
items.summary: Millions of leaseholders to get stronger rights to know exactly what they are paying for and challenge unfair or unexplained service charges New protections will stop leaseholders being saddled with landlords’ legal bills for challenging co
items.bodyHtml:
• Millions of leaseholders to get stronger rights to know exactly what they are paying for and challenge unfair or unexplained service charges
  • New protections will stop leaseholders being saddled with landlords’ legal bills for challenging costs
  • Further changes will make information on charges standardised, clearer and upfront

Over three million leaseholders will have more control of their cash and stronger rights to tackle unfair service charges, as the government delivers another everyday fix to stop homeowners being left out of pocket by unfair costs.

From 1 April 2027, leaseholders will gain strong powers to demand information about their service charges, making it easier to see what they are paying for and why.

This will give people a clearer picture of how their building is managed, maintained, repaired and insured. Leaseholders will be able to ask for information from previous years and landlords will need a good reason to refuse to provide it.

From the same date, leaseholders will also get stronger protection from having to pay their landlord’s legal costs when they challenge a charge. This will end a huge barrier to fighting costs, by stopping landlords from charging leaseholders whether they win or lose, as a power to put them off.

Landlords will need court or tribunal approval to pass on any legal costs to leaseholders and to balance the scales of justice, leaseholders will get the new right to claw back their own legal expenses too.

Together, these changes will make it easier for leaseholders to understand and challenge unfair costs - another everyday fix tackling a real cost of living concern for homeowners, families and aspiring first-time buyers.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

It is simply wrong that millions of leaseholders can be hit with unfair charges, then face another bill just for challenging them. That isn’t right, and where we can act quickly to change it, we will.

Today’s changes are only the beginning. We’re giving leaseholders stronger rights now, while we press ahead with the bigger reforms needed to put power back in homeowners’ hands and end the feudal leasehold system for good.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said:

Rapidly escalating and frequently opaque service charges are placing huge financial strain on hard-pressed leaseholders across the country.

Today, we’re acting to protect them by introducing regulations that will improve the fairness and transparency of service charges so that unreasonable increases can be more easily challenged.

As we work to dismantle the feudal leasehold system in this Parliament, we won’t leave existing leaseholders behind.

Even stronger rules from 1 November 2027

From 1 November 2027, leaseholders will automatically get clearer information about the charges they are being asked to pay – whether their building is owned by a private landlord, council or housing association.

This includes detailed information about the building insurance they help pay for, along with stronger protections against excessive or unreasonable fees for arranging and managing that insurance. Leaseholders will also receive clearly set out information on admin fees they could face.

Private landlords will have extra requirements. They will have to use simpler, standardised service charge demand forms and provide financial accounts and annual reports - giving leaseholders clearer information about what they are being charged and how their money is being spent.

Clearer service charge reporting extended to social housing from 1 November 2028

From 1 November 2028, councils and housing associations will also have to provide their leaseholders with the new standardised service charge demand forms, financial accounts and annual reports.

Plans form part of a wider leasehold shake-up

These changes bring in key protections from the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024, giving leaseholders more information and greater power over the costs they are asked to pay.

Further reforms are also planned through the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, which is due to be introduced in Parliament before Christmas 2026.

Chief Executive of the Leasehold Advisory Service, Kion Ahadi said:

Service charges are the most common issue leaseholders contact us about. We welcome these changes as an important step forward in helping people understand what they are paying for and challenge costs they believe are unfair.

Leaseholders need clear information about how their money is being spent and a fair opportunity to raise concerns.

Better access to that information and stronger protection from landlords’ legal bills will give them more confidence to hold their landlord to account.

Further information

Following consultations in 2024 and 2025, five sets of regulations are being laid in Parliament on 12 November 2026 to bring these new leaseholder protections into force. Together they put in place the detailed rules for the new service charge, information, building insurance and landlord legal cost protections. Subject to Parliamentary approval, different parts of those regulations then come into force at different points: 1 April 2027, 1 November 2027 and 1 November 2028.

One additional set of regulations will be laid in Parliament before the end of 2026, to set out further detail on how the litigation cost reforms will work. The regulations will commence on 1 April 2027.

The reforms are being phased in to get protections to leaseholders as quickly as possible while giving landlords time to make the necessary changes to their billing, accounting and service charge systems. Responses to the government’s consultation made clear that organisations would need sufficient time to prepare for the new requirements.

Councils and housing associations have an additional 12 months to introduce the new standardised service charge demands, accounts and annual reports because of the complexity of their accounting and service charge systems. The government has gathered evidence from social landlords to inform this timetable.

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will overhaul the way flats are owned and managed. This includes making a revised commonhold model – a stronger form of ownership – the default for most new flats. It will also make it easier for existing leaseholders to move to commonhold, will cap existing ground rents at £250 and replace the current forfeiture system with a fairer enforcement regime.

Commonhold gives flat owners outright ownership of their home and a greater say over how their building is run, rather than having a third-party freeholder controlling the building. While commonhold already exists, the Bill will overhaul the current model to make it work better for homeowners and become a realistic alternative to leasehold.

items.title: Government steps in to reduce packaging costs for British businesses and pubs
items.summary: New action has been announced by the Government to ensure restaurants, pubs and hospitality businesses get a fairer deal in disposing of packaging and waste. Changes will cut double charging for recycling the same packaging, saving business
items.bodyHtml:
New action has been announced by the Government to ensure restaurants, pubs and hospitality businesses get a fairer deal in disposing of packaging and waste.

Changes will cut double charging for recycling the same packaging, saving businesses up to 6p per beer bottle and 10p per wine bottle. For a pub selling 10,000 beer bottles and 3,700 wine bottles, this would save them up to £870 a year. 

Glass drinks containers being sold directly from producers to pubs, restaurants, and other licensed hospitality venues will no longer be liable for Extended Producer Responsibility fees from April 2027.

The measures are part of the government’s commitment to back the British glass industry.

Businesses will also be consulted on fees they pay for packaging waste, so that easy-to-recycle packaging like glass and paper cost less and hard-to-recycle packaging such as some plastics costs more. This could help reduce fees for the most recyclable packaging by up to 40% per year. 

Extended Producer Responsibility was introduced to incentivise businesses to switch to more sustainable packaging, as part of the government’s drive to reduce waste. The changes announced today will make it fairer and better targeted.

Separately, the independent Trade Remedies Authority is undertaking two investigations on imports of glass containers. This includes a dumping investigation on Chinese-origin imports and a subsidy investigation on Turkish-origin imports. 

Following a recommendation made by the Trade Remedies Authority, a provisional anti-dumping measure on Chinese imports was imposed on 9 September. Both investigations remain ongoing. 

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: 

We’ve listened to industry and hospitality businesses and are stepping in to reduce the fees for the most recyclable packaging – including tackling double charging on glass bought by pubs.  

This government is committed to supporting British business and these changes back the glass industry and pubs while making sure we’re all doing our bit to reduce waste.

Nick Kirk, Executive Director of British Glass, said:

We welcome today’s announcement, which recognises both the importance of the UK glass industry and the need for a fairer approach to packaging fees, giving confidence to UK manufacturers. The measures outlined are a positive step towards ensuring that highly recyclable materials such as glass are properly recognised within the system, while also benefiting other recyclable materials including metal and paper.

We look forward to working with Government on the next phase of reforms to create a packaging framework that rewards circularity, supports British manufacturing and gives businesses the confidence to invest.

British Soft Drinks Association Director General, Andy Bagnall, said:

Tackling double-charging for drinks containers supplied directly to hospitality is a significant first step towards addressing the unfair packaging costs our industry has faced for several years under Extended Producer Responsibility.

Soft drinks businesses take the responsibility for recycling the packaging they place on the market seriously, and a successful EPR scheme can increase recycling rates and reduce waste, but unfair allocation of costs undermines its effectiveness. We look forward to working closely with Defra on a solution for indirect supply that builds on the ratio-based approach announced today.

Emma McClarkin, Chief Executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, said:

Across the beer and pub sector there will be much relief that the Government will reduce the costs of glass packaging fees and is also seeking to end the pernicious double charging that has been unfairly affecting Britain’s cherished pubs. 

The direction of travel will be warmly welcomed, but it is essential that the long-term cumulative impact of the UK’s packaging policies are taken into consideration if we are to have a prosperous beer and pub sector in every post code. 

These measures could reduce cost pressures on Britain’s brewers by tens of millions.  However, it is vital that the 12,000 publicans that run leased and tenanted pubs as SMEs are also be included, as otherwise over a quarter of Britain’s pubs will not equally benefit from this important change. 

We look forward to working closely with government in building on these important changes which are clear signal of intent to reduce the costs of doing business for brewers and pubs which sit at the heart of local communities throughout the country.

The Government remains committed to the principle that producers should contribute towards the costs of managing packaging waste and help reduce it, with £1.4 billion already provided to councils through the scheme to improve recycling services.  

At the same time, it recognised that pEPR must operate fairly and not disproportionately impact some industries and hospitality businesses. 

Further measures to support businesses are in the pipeline 

  • Next month, a call for evidence will be launched to explore ways more businesses can reuse packaging on greater scales - helping reduce waste and plastic.  

  • In early 2027, PackUK will also launch a call-for-evidence on fees manufacturers pay for packaging waste - to ensure easy-to-recycle packaging costs less.

Notes to editors:

  • The measures relating to dual-use glass will cover England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. 

  • The figures are based on current fees and industry estimates (10,000 beer bottles and 3,700 wine bottles) on consumption.

  • Estimated savings for beer bottles varies from 4p to 6p, dependent on size. 

  • Any savings would be realised by the businesses that is responsible for the EPR fees, such as drinks manufacturers, rather than by pubs directly.

  • The call for evidence on reusable packaging will cover England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.  

  • The plans to consult on stronger fee modulation will cover England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

items.title: Sovereign AI and British Business Bank invest in British firm developing the next generation of AI hardware
items.summary: UK Government’s Sovereign AI and the British Business Bank back Fractile - a Bristol and London based frontier AI hardware firm developing advanced chips, as part of a funding round worth more than £500 million Investment supports the gover
items.bodyHtml:
• UK Government’s Sovereign AI and the British Business Bank back Fractile - a Bristol and London based frontier AI hardware firm developing advanced chips, as part of a funding round worth more than £500 million
  • Investment supports the government’s ambition to make Britain a world leader in developing the technology that powers artificial intelligence
  • Backing British companies will strengthen sovereign capabilities, reduce reliance on overseas technology and support highly skilled jobs and industrial renewal across the country

Fractile, a startup based across London and Bristol developing advanced chips - the physical hardware that powers artificial intelligence - has secured backing from the UK Government’s Sovereign AI Venture Fund and the British Business Bank as part of a round worth over £500 million.

The investment, announced today [Wednesday 11 November], is another step in the government’s ambition to make Britain a world leader in the technologies that will shape the future of AI, ensuring that British scientific excellence translates into British companies, highly skilled jobs and industrial strength.

It will also help strengthen Britain’s sovereign capabilities in critical technologies, reducing dependence on fragile overseas supply chains and ensuring the UK has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy 

Fractile is re-inventing the hardware that AI runs on, so that it is faster, more energy efficient, and less costly. It is taking a unique approach, looking at the full stack of technologies that AI rests upon: from chips, to software and fundamental research into machine learning (the mathematical algorithms that underpin AI). Today’s funding round values the company at over £5 billion. Besides Sovereign AI and the British Business Bank, it is also being backed through this Series C round by investors including CapitalG, Lightspeed and Redpoint.

From Alan Turing’s pioneering work to the creation of Arm in Cambridge, Britain has a proud history of laying the foundations for modern computing. Yet too often, the industrial and commercial rewards of British breakthroughs have been realised elsewhere.

The government is determined to change that, backing ambitious homegrown companies to grow into global technology leaders while keeping more of the jobs, expertise and economic value they create here in Britain.

Through Sovereign AI, the government is backing British chip designers, advanced hardware companies and AI entrepreneurs. By anchoring these critical capabilities on home soil, the government is safeguarding the UK’s critical infrastructure, keeping British data secure and ensuring the economic returns of technological breakthroughs directly benefit British workers. 

The British Business Bank is the UK’s economic development bank, helping innovative businesses access the finance they need to start up, scale up and stay in the UK. Their support will help the company access the long-term capital needed to scale its breakthrough AI hardware technology in the UK.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said:

For too long, Britain has produced some of the world’s best scientific ideas, only to see too much of the technology, industry and wealth they create built elsewhere.

We are determined to change that. If AI is going to serve the British people, strengthen our public services and create good jobs across the country, Britain needs to build more of the technology that powers it.

Fractile represents the very best of British ambition, bringing together world-class chip design, engineering and AI expertise to develop faster, cheaper and more energy-efficient hardware.

By backing brilliant British companies like Fractile, we’re making sure Britain has the industrial strength and sovereign capability to shape the future of AI, with the jobs and economic rewards coming home to communities across our country.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said:

Fractile is a fantastic British success story. This fundraising news, backed by the British Business Bank and Sovereign AI, will boost our ability to make the chips and cutting-edge tech powering AI here at home.

With plans to expand their presence in Bristol, Fractile are helping to put our plans for reindustrialisation into action – delivering the good jobs and growth that will benefit communities across the country and drive our economy forward.

Sovereign AI Investment Partner Joséphine Kant said:

Walter and the team at Fractile are taking on an ambitious challenge, with the potential to make a significant contribution to the global future of AI hardware. Their approach brings together deep expertise across chip design, software, and machine learning, and we believe it has the potential to compete with the very best globally.

Leandros Kalisperas, Chief Investment Officer of the British Business Bank, said:

Fractile is pushing the frontier of AI forward by rearchitecting the hardware stack. Walter and his team are building chips designed to work faster and at greater capacity, allowing AI to reach new potential, scaling faster and more cost effectively. This is British innovation at its best - exceptional technical minds focused on building technology that can compete and win on a global stage. We’re proud to be backing them at this critical stage of growth.

This news comes a fortnight after the Budget, where the Chancellor confirmed a further £140 million backing for Sovereign AI, with an additional £60 million to support the Fund’s investments, plus £80 million for Sovereign AI’s R&D Procurement Scheme. The Chancellor also announced that Sovereign AI would expand into a new focus area of Physical and Industrial AI, building on the UK’s leading research base and growing strengths in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing. Meanwhile the UK is also pushing with plans to build and deploy the compute infrastructure it needs for the AI era, and ensuring that Britain is home to next wave of leading AI and compute companies, with up to £2 billion of investment over the coming years, under the AI Compute Roadmap.

Sovereign AI is the government’s big bet on promising early-stage AI companies to help them grow, scale and succeed from Britain, offering a range of backing to high-potential AI businesses that are starting out on British shores.  

Combining the pace and ambition of venture capital with the weight of the state behind it, Sovereign AI is moving fast, backing ambition and cutting through the red tape that so often holds brilliant ideas back, so they can go on to succeed globally.

All of the startups Sovereign AI supports have a meaningful presence here in the UK, and create well paid jobs right across the country - supporting the Government’s ambition for good growth in every postcode. These startups are all firmly anchored in the UK with either their founders, leadership, operating headquarters or a large proportion of their talent based here in Britain.

The Chancellor also expanded the British Business Bank’s investment capacity by £5 billion to £30.6 billion, giving it more firepower to back innovative British firms as they grow. The package unveiled at the Budget will back growing businesses across every part of the UK and is expected to support more than 24,600 existing jobs and create more than 15,800 new jobs over the lifetime of the finance.

Notes to editors: 

  • The Sovereign AI Fund will invest directly in promising UK AI companies to help them scale in the UK. Our investments will be focused on companies at the early and growth-stage.
  • Typical equity investments will be worth around £1-10 million, though every company’s circumstances will be different. 
  • Like most venture capital funds we do not comment on specific investment figures as they are commercially sensitive- The British Business Bank creates deeper pools of scale up capital for UK companies by backing venture capital funds. It has backed over 150 venture capital and growth funds to date, most recently investing £180m across six AI and deeptech funds
  • Alongside this, it invests directly in fast-growing technology businesses and is the UK’s most active late-stage investor in deeptech. Recent AI investments include Wayve, Kraken Technologies, PhysicsX, PolyAI, Salience Labs and Ineffable Intelligence.

ENDS

items.title: Colleges put at heart of drive to get young people learning
items.summary: Today’s 16- to 18-year-olds who have fallen out of education will be given more chances to get back into learning, as colleges are put at the heart of an urgent national drive to tackle the NEETs crisis. In a major call to action to the fur
items.bodyHtml:
Today’s 16- to 18-year-olds who have fallen out of education will be given more chances to get back into learning, as colleges are put at the heart of an urgent national drive to tackle the NEETs crisis.

In a major call to action to the further education sector today ahead of Alan Milburn’s final report on the NEET crisis, the Education Secretary urged colleges across the country to get young people who aren’t in education back through their doors to give them a chance to succeed.

Milburn’s work has been a clarion call for the whole of government and society, shining a light on the lack of responsibility and incentives across the system for getting young people back into learning or work.

That’s why the Education Secretary has called on colleges to connect with employers and provide young people with meaningful work experience that can create a route into a job - rather than waiting for long-term reform to ensure no child is left behind.

She asked for them to bring forward ideas and plans to urgently make this vision a reality across the country, proving to young people that change can happen.

In return, the Education Secretary pledged to work with the sector to break down the barriers that can make it harder or riskier for colleges to take those young people on. This includes:

  • Providing significantly more flexibility on the number of hours of English and maths required of young people who are NEET and returning to education and allowing for remaining hours to be delivered through one-to-one and small group support. 

  • Changing how schools, colleges and others are measured, recognised, and rewarded, including better recognising progress in English and Maths and disincentivising premature exam entries.  
  • Providing funding certainty for enrolling young NEETs, so colleges are not disincentivised from giving students a second chance.

She said at the Association of Colleges conference:

Frankly, I think it’s unforgivable that there are almost 150,000 16-18-year-olds who right now are NEET.

Instead of sitting at home, we need to get them into college or doing an apprenticeship.

I want us to reach them with an exciting, new, and engaging offer.

Every single one of us is the room have the power and ability to give today’s 16-, 17- and 18-year-olds new hope.

Because there are hundreds of thousands out there who need a second chance. Some of them need a third or fourth chance.

Let’s take action today together to give it to them. I’ll break your barriers down for you but in return I need your help.

Let’s set ourselves the mission to get these young people back into college. And that’s what you do best – engage, support, train, educate - and most of all give hope and give purpose.

And my promise to you is to put colleges not at the back of the queue but at the heart of that new mission. And in return I ask you to meet this moment and make hope real for the next generation.

Warning that too many of the young people struggling today are part of a generation whose education was hit by Covid, she argues that supporting 150,000 16- to 18-year-old NEETs will be key to helping to solve the crisis. 

The Education Secretary said:

Practically a whole generation completely let down. And let’s not forget, this is the generation whose education was harmed by covid, and who didn’t get the catch up they were promised.

This is the generation whose Sure Start was cancelled…whose youth services were cut…whose futures were sold short.

And they were educated in a one-size-fits-all system. It’s worked for some, but it’s left far too many behind.

The government is taking long-term action to tackle the problem at its roots, including creating a more engaging national curriculum, stopping the endless cycle of repeated English and maths GCSE resits through new Level 1 qualifications, reforming SEND, expanding vocational education through new V Levels and vocational GCSEs and giving local leaders a greater role in shaping 16 to 19 provision.
