items.title: Minister intervenes to keep iconic bust of Edward the Black Prince in the UK
items.summary: The export bar allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire this national treasure The UK Government has intervened to ensure a bust of Prince Edward of Woodstock (1330–1376), known as The Black Prince, is kept in the country in t
items.bodyHtml:
• The export bar allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire this national treasure

The UK Government has intervened to ensure a bust of Prince Edward of Woodstock (1330–1376), known as The Black Prince, is kept in the country in the hope that a UK gallery or institution can save it for the nation.

Renowned as an extraordinary medieval military commander during The Hundred Years War, Edward was the son of King Edward III of England. He won major victories, including the Battle of Poitiers (1356), and supposedly became known as The Black Prince because of the colour of his armour.

The bust was part of a series of eighteenth century depictions of Edward the Black Prince, which came to define how the image of him was subsequently presented. Since this bust was created nearly three hundred years ago, its iconic representation has been copied countless times and has become the accepted image of this important historical figure.

The government has placed a temporary export ban on the sculpture in the hope of keeping it accessible to the UK public. The deferral period gives time for museums and galleries to raise the funds needed to acquire the bust, for example through philanthropic support, or for a private individual to purchase it and donate it to the nation.

Created around 1735, the bust is the work of leading Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack. Rysbrack did much of his most famous work in England, where he was renowned for portrait busts and architectural decorations.

Heritage Minister Baroness Twycross said:

This striking sculpture of Edward the Black Prince still defines how we imagine this legendary figure in British history.

For nearly three hundred years it has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.

RCEWA committee member, Stuart Lochhead, said: 

Michael Rysbrack was one of the most important sculptors of eighteenth-century Britain, developing a classicising style that established a new taste for portraiture, monuments and statuary. This handsome marble bust of Edward, the Black Prince, served a particular purpose for Georgian patrons and the royal court, who used such portraits for dynastic and patriotic self-fashioning, aligning themselves with a lineage of English kingship and chivalric virtue that would define imagery for generations. It is one of the finest and earliest known busts of this genre, and its export from the United Kingdom would be a great loss to scholarship and our understanding of Georgian society.

The Minister’s decision follows the advice of the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest (RCEWA).

The Committee made its recommendation on the basis that the bust met the first and third Waverley criteria for its outstanding connection with our history and national life and its outstanding significance to the study of 18th-century British sculpture and its use in political propaganda, royal patronage and positioning.

The decision on the export licence application for the painting will be deferred for an initial period ending on 5 February 2027 inclusive in which we welcome expressions of interest from an appropriate purchaser to try and acquire the object. At the end of the first deferral period owners will have a consideration period of 15 Business Days to consider any offer(s) to purchase the painting at the recommended price of £496,044.51 (plus VAT of £9,920.89). The second deferral period will commence following the signing of an Option Agreement and will last for four months.

Notes to editors:

  1. Organisations or individuals interested in purchasing the bust should contact the RCEWA on 02072680534 or rcewa@artscouncil.org.uk.
  2. Details of the ITEM are as follows: The Black Prince, c.1735, Michael Rysbrack (1694-1770); Marble; 84 cm high
  3. Provenance: (Probably) commissioned by Frederick Prince of Wales (1707-1751), for the Octagon Temple, Carlton House, Pall Mall, London. (Probably) passed to Lady Archibald Hamilton (c.1704-1753), (presumably) by descent to her daughter Elizabeth (1720-1800; née Hamilton), who had married Francis Greville, 1st Earl of Warwick; recorded in the State Bedroom, Warwick Castle in the inventory of 1806; by descent; sold Sotheby’s, 9 December 2005 (lot 134); Private Collection; by descent.
  4. The Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest is an independent body, serviced by Arts Council England (ACE), which advises the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport on whether a cultural object, intended for export, is of national importance under specified criteria.

items.title: 新书《郁达夫的朋友圈》在京首发
items.summary: 中新网北京11月6日电 (冯艺璇)今年是郁达夫诞辰130周年。11月5日，报刊史研究学者、作家、红色报刊史料研学中心馆长谢华的新著《郁达夫的朋友圈》首发式在北京举行。该书由河南文艺出版社出版，郁达夫之女郁美兰作序，依据日记、书信、回忆录等一手史料，梳理郁达夫与鲁迅、郭沫若、沈从文、林语堂、徐志摩等人的交往、观念碰撞及离合，呈现郁达夫鲜为人知的红色关联，打破“颓废文人”的刻板印象。

items.summary: 新华社重庆11月6日电(记者周闻韬)6日，重庆市应急管理局向社会公布了重庆万州恩广高速万州至开江段A2合同段“3·30”较大瓦斯爆炸事故调查报告。事故调查组认定，该起事故是一起因施工单位长期关停风机设备，导致铁峰山隧道进口端左洞瓦斯大量积聚，随后在未经审批、瓦斯浓度超限的情况下冒险组织复工，致使隧道内通电的非防爆电缆产生火花引发瓦斯爆炸的较大生产安全责任事故。

items.title: Statement on the sentencing of Joshua Wong
items.summary: Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment following a further charge under the National Security Law (NSL). This comes just months after leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance were convicted under the same legislation. These are furthe
items.bodyHtml: Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment following a further charge under the National Security Law (NSL). This comes just months after leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance were convicted under the same legislation. These are further examples of how the NSL is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation. We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the NSL and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to uphold their international commitments and honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British Joint Declaration (1984).

items.title: Landmark agreement between National Housing Bank and Greater Manchester Combined Authority unlocks up to £500m for new homes and regeneration
items.summary: A boost of up to £500m for new homes and mixed-use regeneration projects across Greater Manchester has been unlocked through a landmark agreement between the Combined Authority and Homes England’s public financial institution, the National
items.bodyHtml:
A boost of up to £500m for new homes and mixed-use regeneration projects across Greater Manchester has been unlocked through a landmark agreement between the Combined Authority and Homes England’s public financial institution, the National Housing Bank.  

The agreement is the first of its kind in England, building on a strong track record of trail-blazing collaboration that has supported transformative projects including Victoria North and in Stockport MDC.  

Previously, Greater Manchester was also the first combined authority to sign a Strategic Place Partnership with Homes England, the government’s housing and regeneration agency.  

This new agreement opens the door for investment of up to £500m into projects alongside the Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund, which launched one year ago.  

To be considered for funding, all projects will need to align with the National Housing Bank’s mandate, with each proposed investment being subject to the Bank’s standard due diligence, governance and approval processes.

Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig said:

Over the past decade Greater Manchester has grown faster than anywhere else in the UK. But not every resident or place has yet felt the benefit. We set up the Good Growth Fund to spread that growth to all of our places, so that no community is left behind.  

The progress we have made in its first year shows that we are delivering on that ambition. People can see new homes being built, town centres being transformed, new businesses opening up and new jobs being created – all made possible by the Good Growth Fund. But we can do more.  

Our Social Contract takes our commitment further – if you get public money you should contribute to our communities, to make Greater Manchester better for everyone. Through creating new apprenticeships and work placements and creating opportunities for local businesses, the impact of our investment will be felt locally for generations to come.  

Good jobs, opportunities for our young people, a home you can afford in an area and community you are proud of. These are all ingredients of good growth and the Greater Manchester I’m determined we can build.

National Housing Bank Chief Executive Simon Century said:

This agreement is supported by national and local expertise, backed with purpose-driven finance, and powered by regionally led ambition.    

It builds from strong foundations of successful collaboration with the Mayor, regional leaders, partners and local people who best know their region and what it needs to thrive.   

Together we will aim to further accelerate the delivery of the new homes and mixed-use regeneration schemes across Greater Manchester that best work for communities now and in the future across the region.

Paul Dennett, Deputy Mayor of Greater Manchester and City Mayor of Salford, said:

The Good Growth Fund is an important way that Greater Manchester is responding to the housing crisis, using the city region’s growth to help build more social and affordable homes, so that more of our residents can have a safe and healthy place to call home.   

By using public investment, we’re unlocking complex sites so that Greater Manchester can build more affordable, energy-efficient and accessible homes, quicker. And we’re ensuring that this is done alongside the transport, services and infrastructure needed to create sustainable, well-connected and safe communities.  

Our Good Growth Fund approach links the investment given to social value expectations, pushing developments to not only create good jobs but create early-career opportunities, including apprenticeships, too – and to support our environmental goals and accessibility needs.   

This is what good growth looks like in practice: bold development that puts our places and residents first; uses the levers at our disposal to make development happen quicker; and uses the city region’s growth for the greater public good.

The National Housing Bank, a Homes England company, delivers purpose-led finance for housing delivery. It aims to break down barriers to investment at scale and accelerate the delivery and regeneration of places across England.   

ENDS

Media enquiries

Email HomesEnglandNews@communities.gov.uk

Telephone 020 7874 8262

The National Housing Bank press office is contactable between 9am and 5:30pm, Monday to Friday.

items.title: New ‘say what you pay’ law to help young people into work
items.summary: Jobseekers will see salaries before applying under new laws requiring job adverts to “say what you pay” Siemens Mobility to give 10,000 young people work experience in engineering and technology PM rallies more businesses to back the Govern
items.bodyHtml:
• Jobseekers will see salaries before applying under new laws requiring job adverts to “say what you pay”
  • Siemens Mobility to give 10,000 young people work experience in engineering and technology
  • PM rallies more businesses to back the Government’s target of delivering 200,000 work experience opportunities

Jobseekers will no longer have to apply for jobs without knowing what they pay, under new plans announced by the Prime Minister to legally require employers to publish salaries in job adverts.

Too many jobseekers are still expected to apply for roles without knowing what they pay. It is estimated that less than half (41%) of employers always publish salary ranges and only 1 in 5 (18%) always publish specific salaries.

The Government will mandate job adverts to ‘say what you pay’ by making publishing salaries a legal requirement, backing employers already doing the right thing and making openness about pay the minimum standard. 

The change will tackle a common frustration for jobseekers, particularly young people applying for their first job, who can still be asked to apply without knowing what they will earn while also helping to address pay inequalities that can disadvantage women.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:  

Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it. That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.

But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.

It’s fantastic to see Siemens Mobility doing exactly that, creating 10,000 opportunities in engineering and technology and inspiring thousands more children through its national science lesson.

There is overwhelming support for greater pay transparency, with early analysis showing 94% of respondents to the government consultation backing the requirement, including 93% of businesses. Publishing salaries upfront can help expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes.

Applying for a first job can be daunting, particularly after time out of work or education. For young people taking their first steps into work, knowing the salary upfront helps young people focus on the right opportunities and apply with greater confidence. Hiding pay details also disadvantages women by forcing them to negotiate blind, leaving them more vulnerable to lower pay offers.

The Government will bring forward legislation as soon as possible. In the meantime, the Prime Minister is calling on all businesses to say what they pay on job ads now, rather than wait for the law to change.

The changes are part of the Government’s wider drive to get more young people earning or learning, break down barriers to work and open up more opportunities to help young people get a foot in the door. Further reforms will follow the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, due in the coming weeks.

Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson said:

What a job pays is rightly at the forefront of people’s minds when looking for work - it shouldn’t be a guessing game.

It’s more important than ever today for people to know if a role will pay the bills or if you’re qualified enough for it. Mandatory salary information on job adverts will help young people make informed choices, help close the gender pay gap, and tackle an everyday annoyance that can stand in the way of applying for a job.

Whether it’s a young person looking for their first job or a mum getting back into work, no-one should have to enter an already daunting process salary blind.

Penny East, Chief Executive of the Fawcett Society said:

For too long, salary secrecy has put women at a disadvantage, leaving them negotiating in the dark and making it much harder to challenge unfair and unequal pay. Requiring employers to publish salaries in job adverts is a significant step towards making work fairer for women and tackling the gender pay gap.

Fawcett has long campaigned for greater pay transparency. The decision taken by government today is real progress. Women will no longer have to make decisions about their financial futures based on vague promises or unclear terms.

Nishi Mayor, Director of Employer Engagement & Partnerships, Youth Futures Foundation said:

With one in eight 16-24 year olds currently not in education, employment, or training, it is right and important that Government is consulting with employers to help make the path into work smoother for young people by removing barriers to entering the workplace.

We know from our work trialling real-world practices around recruiting and retaining young people with trailblazing employers that too many young people struggle to access opportunities when they are looking for jobs.   

Providing clear information about pay can help young people make informed decisions about employment opportunities, which for employers could mean more applications from more suitable candidates, ensuring they have the talent pipeline they need.

The Government is also joining forces with a growing movement of businesses creating more work experience opportunities, helping to deliver its ambition of 200,000 additional placements for 14–16-year-olds.

Siemens Mobility is the latest major employer to step up, with its new work experience programme creating more than 3,300 opportunities every year and reaching 10,000 young people over three years. Combining digital learning with hands-on experience, young people will meet engineers, tackle real-world challenges and see how advanced manufacturing, AI and digital technology are transforming Britain’s railways.

To mark the launch, the Prime Minister will join children for a national science lesson with thousands more taking part online. Through practical challenges and demonstrations, pupils will meet Siemens Mobility apprentices and engineers and discover where studying science and technical subjects could take them.

The programme aims to spark interest in engineering from an early age and challenge stereotypes about who those careers are for. University College London research shows engineering aspirations diverge by age 10, with just 11% of girls aspiring to engineering careers compared with 44% of boys.

The Prime Minister welcomed Siemens Mobility’s commitment and called on more businesses to step up, building on commitments from the retail and hospitality sectors to create hundreds of thousands of opportunities for young people.

The Government is also developing new vocational and technical routes to turn that early inspiration into a clearer path from classroom to career, giving young people the skills and experience employers need.

Aglaja Schneider, Managing Director of Siemens Mobility UK & Ireland, said:

I started my own career as a graduate at Siemens Mobility, so I know first-hand how important those early opportunities can be. I particularly hope today’s lesson inspires more girls to see the possibilities that engineering and technology can offer.

That’s what our Tech Experience Launchpad is about. With up to 70,000 workers potentially leaving Britain’s rail industry by 2030, investing in future talent has never been more important.

As a key partner to the railway, we’re investing in Britain’s future through our people, technology and manufacturing capabilities. From the Rail Technology Centre in Wiltshire, to our Goole Rail Village in Yorkshire, our £360 million investment in the UK is a powerful example of that commitment, creating opportunities in advanced engineering and manufacturing, while helping to develop the next generation of skilled talent who will build and shape Britain’s future railways.

Rob Morris, Managing Director, Siemens Mobility UK & Ireland, said:

Britain’s railways are changing fast. From AI and digital technology to advanced manufacturing, we need a new generation of engineers and innovators to shape their future.

Our £360 million investment in Britain is about more than building world-class rail facilities. It’s about creating skilled jobs, developing talent and strengthening the industrial capabilities Britain needs for the future.

Becky Worsey, Assistant Chief Engineer at Siemens Mobility, who is taking part in the STEM lesson, said:

As an engineer and a mum to a ten-year-old daughter that wants to have a job like mine, I want young people to see that engineering is for them. There are so many different routes into the industry and career options behind the railways people use every day.

If children get the opportunity to meet an engineer, walk into a place like our new state-of-the-art Rail Technology Centre and understand that the science they are learning at school is being used to solve real problems, those careers suddenly become much easier to imagine.

Additional information:

  • The Government will bring forward legislation to require employers to include salary information on job adverts as soon as possible, with further details on scope, required information, implementation, and enforcement to be set out in due course.
  • The estimate that less than half (41%) of employers always publish salary ranges and only 1 in 5 (18%) always publish specific salaries, is from the CIPD’s Pay, performance and transparency report (2024), page 30.
  • The finding that 11% of girls aged 10 aspire to engineering careers, compared with 44% of boys, is from UCL Institute of Education’s ASPIRES 2: Young people’s science and career aspirations, age 10–19 (2020). discovery.ucl.ac.uk – Employers can help bridge the 200,000 work experience opportunities gap for 14-16 year olds by making a pledge to open their doors via the Careers and Enterprise Company: National Mission Work Experience | CEC Corporate Web

items.title: UK citizen returned from DRC for specialist Ebola care
items.summary: A UK medical doctor who was working on the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has returned to the UK for specialist treatment after testing positive for the disease. The UK government worked with the DRC government
items.bodyHtml:
A UK medical doctor who was working on the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has returned to the UK for specialist treatment after testing positive for the disease.

The UK government worked with the DRC government and international health partners to bring the patient home safely on a medical evacuation flight. The journey followed established infection prevention and control procedures, which also apply to everyone involved in the individual’s care.

They are now being cared for in a high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free Hospital, London. This unit is highly specialised and specifically designed for this purpose, staffed by expert clinical teams.

Dr Renu Bindra, Deputy Director, All Hazards Public Health Response at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said:

UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.

Ebola does not spread through the air. It is passed on through direct contact with the bodily fluids of a person who has symptoms.

The Royal Free Hospital isolation unit has strict isolation protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission.

items.title: Man who murdered Henry Nowak has sentence increased
items.summary: Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed Henry Nowak to death, had the minimum term of his life sentence increased by 4 years to 25 years, after Attorney General Ellie Reeves KC referred the case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence s
items.bodyHtml:
Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed Henry Nowak to death, had the minimum term of his life sentence increased by 4 years to 25 years, after Attorney General Ellie Reeves KC referred the case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme.  

The court heard that on the evening of 3 December 2025, Vickrum Digwa, 23, of St Denys, Southampton, was carrying a large Sikh dagger in a sheath over the outside of his clothing, when he encountered Henry Nowak, an 18-year-old first year student at Southampton University who was walking home.  

Digwa and Nowak were entirely unknown to each other. Following a brief interaction, Digwa stabbed Nowak in the chest with the dagger, as well as several times to his legs and abdomen.   

After the attack, Digwa then filmed the victim as he tried to get away from him and continued to film him as he lay dying. Digwa was also found to have instructed his mother to remove the murder weapon and repeatedly lied to attending police officers about what had happened.  

In a Victim Impact Statement, Henry’s father described the devastating impact of his son’s death and the deep grief experienced by the family at losing him at such a young age.  

The Attorney General Ellie Reeves KC MP said:  

The brutality and cruelty of this case horrified me, and I know that feeling is shared by the British public. I welcome the Court of Appeal’s decision to increase the minimum term of Digwa’s life sentence.  

My thoughts remain with Henry’s family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time. No sentence can ever fill the void left by his loss, and I hope this outcome goes some way towards bringing them the justice they deserve.

On 1 June 2026, at Southampton Crown Court, Digwa was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 21 years for one count of murder and one count of having a bladed article.   

On 5 November 2026, at the Court of Appeal, Digwa’s sentence was increased to a minimum term of 25 years.

items.title: Investigation over risk to multi-million pound charity property
items.summary: The House of St Barnabas was set up in 1862 to provide temporary relief and support to people experiencing homelessness and it entered liquidation in January 2024. Linked to this charity was The House of St Barnabas in Soho. As a result of
items.bodyHtml:
The House of St Barnabas was set up in 1862 to provide temporary relief and support to people experiencing homelessness and it entered liquidation in January 2024. Linked to this charity was The House of St Barnabas in Soho. As a result of the liquidation a new corporate trustee, The Explorers Club (Soho), was appointed to the charity, in place of The House of St Barnabas.  

The Explorers Club (Soho) then entered into a licence in early 2026 with the private company The Explorers Club (London) Ltd (‘TEC(London)’) allowing TEC(London) to use the charity’s property located at 1 Greek Street, to run a private members club and collect members’ fees. The licence fee would generate income for the charity and allow it to continue operating.  

Last month, the regulator received a serious incident report informing it that the charity has been a victim of fraud as it disputes a loan that has been secured against its property at 1 Greek Street. The loan appears not to have been repaid and, as a result, the creditor is taking steps to recover its loan. The Commission has concerns that the charity’s main asset – the 1 Greek Street property – is at serious risk. 

The regulator is launching this inquiry to establish the facts leading up to this point, to examine the financial arrangements and decision-making involving the charity. 

Scope of the inquiry

The inquiry will examine the administration, governance and management of the charity and in particular:  

  • whether charitable property is at risk  

  • whether the governance arrangements are fit for purpose including the management and oversight of the licence agreement with The Explorer Club (London). 

  • the decision making around the charity’s financial arrangements including loans. 

The  scope of the inquiry can be extended if additional regulatory issues emerge.  

It is the Commission’s policy, after it has concluded an inquiry, to publish a report detailing the issues examined, any action taken, and the inquiry’s outcomes.  

ENDS 

Notes to editors:

  • The Charity Commission is the independent, non-ministerial government department that registers and regulates charities in England and Wales. Its ambition is to be an expert regulator that is fair, balanced, and independent so that charity can thrive. This ambition will help to create and sustain an environment where charities further build public trust and ultimately fulfil their essential role in enhancing lives and strengthening society. Read further information about what the Commission does.  

  • On 29 October 2026 the Charity Commission (‘the Commission’) opened a statutory inquiry (‘the inquiry’) into the Charity under section 46 of the Charities Act 2011 as a result of its regulatory concerns that there is a significant risk to the charity’s assets. 

  • A statutory inquiry is a legal power enabling the Commission to formally investigate matters of regulatory concern within a charity and to use protective powers for the benefit of the charity and its beneficiaries, assets, or reputation. Reports of previous inquiries are available on GOV.UK.  

  • We also provide charities with guidance on what happens when the Commission opens an inquiry.

Press office

Email pressenquiries@charitycommission.gov.uk

Out of hours press office contact number: 07785 748787

items.title: MHRA sets out approach to strengthen patient and public involvement and engagement in medicines and medical device regulation
items.summary: Patients and the public will have a greater role in shaping medicines and medical device regulation under a new plan published today by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). The Patient and Public Involvement and E
items.bodyHtml:
Patients and the public will have a greater role in shaping medicines and medical device regulation under a new plan published today by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). 

The Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement Plan 2026–2030 (PPIE), a key tenet of the MHRA’s Strategy 2030, sets out how the agency will involve and engage people earlier, hear from a wider range of patient groups and communities and explain openly and clearly how patients’ experiences shape its work. 

Patients’ lived experience will help inform decisions at the MHRA, including the assessment of medicine benefits and risks, safety reviews, regulatory policy, patient information and the development of regulatory approaches for rare diseases, medical devices, future regulatory pathways, artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies. 

The plan supports the MHRA’s newly-published Strategy to 2030, builds on its Patient Involvement Strategy 2021–2025 and responds to feedback calling for more inclusive participation and information on how patient involvement shapes regulatory decisions. 

Under the plan, the MHRA will: 

  • Strengthen feedback, monitoring and reporting so people can see how their contributions have influenced the MHRA’s work. 

  • Expand membership of its Patient and Public Community to better reflect the diversity of the UK population. 

  • Use deliberative engagement to ensure patient and public perspectives shape how the benefits and risks of medicines are assessed. 

  • Involve patients and the public in work to make medicines information clearer and more accessible. 

  • Work with the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to reduce duplication in patient involvement evidence used for regulatory and health technology assessments. 

Professor Anthony Harnden, Chair of the MHRA, said: 

Our Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement Plan is a vital evolution in the way we connect and listen to patients and the public at a time when the dynamic landscape of medicines and medical devices regulation is changing rapidly.  

Bringing those who matter most into the heart of our regulatory and decision-making processes, patients and the public can tell us how treatments affect their everyday lives, what benefits they value most and where information needs to be clearer. That insight helps us ask better questions and make better-informed regulatory decisions. 

Through this plan, we will involve people earlier, hear from a broader range of communities and patient demographics and explain how their contributions have influenced our work.

Patient involvement has already helped shape the MHRA’s work on rare diseases. A dedicated advisory group of 23 patient representatives has contributed to the MHRA’s Rare Disease Consortium, helping identify priorities, informing draft guidance and spearheading medicines repurposing. 

Mercy Jeyasingham MBE, MHRA Non-Executive Director and Chair of the People and Public Engagement Committee, said:

This plan combines ambition with practical and achievable commitments to strengthen how we involve patients and the public in our work. 

A consistent approach across the agency will help ensure that people’s experiences inform our work and that those contributing understand how their input has been used. The People and Public Engagement Committee will oversee progress, helping turn these commitments into meaningful and lasting improvements.

Professor Henrietta Hughes OBE, Patient Safety Commissioner for England, said:  

I welcome this plan and its commitment to putting patients’ voices at the heart of regulation. Patient experience should be central to regulatory decisions. 

Listening to a diverse range of voices, particularly those that are under-represented, provides early insight into risks and inequalities. This insight is what strengthens patient safety and helps ensure regulation reflects what matters most to the people it serves.

Karen Titchener, Patient Safety Commissioner for Scotland, said: 

People across Scotland have repeatedly told us how important it is that their experiences of healthcare are listened to and acted upon. Patients and families are experts in their own experiences, and their insights can help shape safer medicines, medical devices and healthcare systems. 

I welcome the MHRA’s commitment to broadening participation and involving patients earlier in decision-making. Meaningful engagement helps ensure that regulatory decisions are informed not only by clinical evidence, but also by the realities of people’s lives.

Notes to editors

  1. The MHRA regulates medicines, medical devices and blood components for transfusion in the UK. 

  2. Read the Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement Plan 2026–2030

  3. The MHRA’s People and Public Engagement Committee will review progress in delivering the plan.  

  4. The Patient and Public Community was established in October 2024. It brings together patients, patient organisations and charities to inform the MHRA’s work and policy development. 

  5. For media enquiries, please contact newscentre@mhra.gov.uk or call 020 3080 7651.  

ENDS

items.title: New veteran support centre confirmed for Scotland
items.summary: The funding comes as UK Government Scotland Office Minister Melanie Ward hosted a Remembrance Reception in Edinburgh on Thursday evening to celebrate Scotland’s Armed Forces community, including veterans. An estimated one million veterans a
items.bodyHtml:
The funding comes as UK Government Scotland Office Minister Melanie Ward hosted a Remembrance Reception in Edinburgh on Thursday evening to celebrate Scotland’s Armed Forces community, including veterans.

An estimated one million veterans and their families in the UK will benefit from easier access to local services, thanks to the VALOUR network expanding. 

Earlier this year, 14 organisations were awarded over £13m to launch the first wave of VALOUR-recognised centres, including SSAFA Scotland’s drop-in centre in Glasgow which was awarded up to £1 million. 

Now the Defence Medical Welfare Service (DMWS) charity in Dumfries and Galloway is receiving £859,281 as a further 21 organisations share more than £13.2m of funding to launch the second wave of VALOUR-recognised centres by the beginning of 2027.

DMWS helps those who have and continue to serve on the frontline and their families with medical welfare and associated assistance. It is embedded within NHS Boards across Scotland, providing critical support at the bedside for Armed Forces patients (serving, reservists, veterans and their families).

VALOUR has been designed to help the UK’s estimated two million veterans get the support they need through VALOUR-recognised centres, a helpline service or on GOV.UK.  

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

It is a privilege to be able to honour our veterans, not just as we mark Remembrance Day, but year-round as we remember the service and the sacrifice of those who fought for the lives we live today.

I’m incredibly proud to see the VALOUR network grow to provide support to more veterans and their families - those who have given so much to protect communities across the country.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said:

Our veterans and serving troops have made huge sacrifices to keep us safe, and I’m immensely proud of each and every one of them. But our gratitude can’t stop at words, or end when they leave the forces. 

This £859,000 UK Government funding will help the Defence Medical Welfare Service in Dumfries and Galloway be there for them and their families when they need it most. It’s a vital boost for our Armed Forces community in Scotland, and exactly what they deserve.

Minister for Veterans and People Calvin Bailey MBE MP said:

Ahead of Remembrance Sunday, I’m pleased that we can pay tribute to the service and sacrifice of our armed forces community by giving veterans easier access to the support they need, regardless of where they are in the UK. 

I’ve heard wonderful stories of how centres like Citizens Advice are making a real difference to people’s lives. Joining the VALOUR system will help them support even more veterans and their families.

DMWS CEO Abby Dryden said:

DMWS is proud to be part of the VALOUR system and to help deliver a more joined-up approach to support for veterans, serving personnel and their families across South Scotland. By bringing organisations together and strengthening pathways into support, VALOUR will make it easier for people to access the right help at the right time, wherever they live.

This partnership reflects our shared commitment to ensuring that no member of the Armed Forces community has to face challenges alone. We are incredibly proud to work alongside our partners to build a stronger, more connected system of support for the Armed Forces Community and families and carers across South Scotland.

VALOUR is overseen by a headquarters in the Office for Veterans’ Affairs (OVA) within the Ministry of Defence. It will bring together national oversight, regional coordination and local delivery to improve how services work together. 

VALOUR field officers are also working regionally to strengthen collaboration between partners such as councils, local public services and charities. 

The continued rollout of VALOUR demonstrates the UK Government’s delivery of the 10-year Veterans Strategy, which aims to celebrate, contribute to, and support those who serve and have served. Funding for VALOUR is included in the Defence Investment Plan. 

There are approximately 176,000 veterans living in Scotland.

Scotland now has two VALOUR-recognised centres:

  • DMWS; and
  • SSAFA Connect in Glasgow, which supports veterans and Forces families navigating housing, health, and employment challenges in Glasgow, Inverclyde, Edinburgh, Renfrewshire, North and South Lanarkshire, West Dunbartonshire, and West Lothian.

On Thursday Minister Ward hosted a Remembrance Reception at the UK Government’s Queen Elizabeth House HQ in Edinburgh, bringing together Scotland’s Armed Forces community, including veteran organisations and military representatives, as well as Scottish MPs and other guests.

ENDS

 Background

  • Over £26m of development funding for VALOUR-recognised centres has been allocated in two rounds of funding. 

  • 21 lead organisations are receiving £13,260,580 of development funding in round 2, with £26,516,357 million granted in total. They will join the first round of 14 organisations announced in March 2026, and are: 

  • Defence Medical Welfare Service charity 
  • The Poppy Factory 
  • Sir Oswald Stoll Foundation 
  • Age UK Waltham Forest 
  • Mid Suffolk Citizens Advice Bureau   
  • Stevenage Borough Council 
  • Veterans Support Northern Ireland 
  • Adferiad 
  • Monmouthshire County Council 
  • City of York Council 
  • Leeds City Council 
  • Herefordshire Veterans Support Centre   
  • The Veterans Contact Point 
  • Loughborough Wellbeing Centre 
  • CVS Lincolnshire 
  • Citizens Advice Rushmoor 
  • The Lantern Trust (Weymouth) 
  • Wiltshire Council 
  • Westmorland & Furness Council 
  • Dover District Council 

  • East Durham Veterans Trust – will receive additional funding in round 2 

  • Further information on VALOUR - and how to access support - can be found at www.gov.uk/valour

Now the Defence Medical Welfare Service (DMWS) charity in Dumfries and Galloway is receiving £859,281 as a further 21 organisations share more than £13.2m of funding to launch the second wave of VALOUR-recognised centres by the beginning of 2027.

DMWS helps those who have and continue to serve on the frontline and their families with medical welfare and associated assistance. It is embedded within NHS Boards across Scotland, providing critical support at the bedside for Armed Forces patients (serving, reservists, veterans and their families).

VALOUR has been designed to help the UK’s estimated two million veterans get the support they need through VALOUR-recognised centres, a helpline service or on GOV.UK.  

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:


  It is a privilege to be able to honour our veterans, not just as we mark Remembrance Day, but year-round as we remember the service and the sacrifice of those who fought for the lives we live today.

  I’m incredibly proud to see the VALOUR network grow to provide support to more veterans and their families - those who have given so much to protect communities across the country.


Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said:


  Our veterans and serving troops have made huge sacrifices to keep us safe, and I’m immensely proud of each and every one of them. But our gratitude can’t stop at words, or end when they leave the forces. 

  This £859,000 UK Government funding will help the Defence Medical Welfare Service in Dumfries and Galloway be there for them and their families when they need it most. It’s a vital boost for our Armed Forces community in Scotland, and exactly what they deserve.


Minister for Veterans and People Calvin Bailey MBE MP said:


  Ahead of Remembrance Sunday, I’m pleased that we can pay tribute to the service and sacrifice of our armed forces community by giving veterans easier access to the support they need, regardless of where they are in the UK. 

  I’ve heard wonderful stories of how centres like Citizens Advice are making a real difference to people’s lives. Joining the VALOUR system will help them support even more veterans and their families.


DMWS CEO Abby Dryden said:


  DMWS is proud to be part of the VALOUR system and to help deliver a more joined-up approach to support for veterans, serving personnel and their families across South Scotland. By bringing organisations together and strengthening pathways into support, VALOUR will make it easier for people to access the right help at the right time, wherever they live.

  This partnership reflects our shared commitment to ensuring that no member of the Armed Forces community has to face challenges alone. We are incredibly proud to work alongside our partners to build a stronger, more connected system of support for the Armed Forces Community and families and carers across South Scotland.


VALOUR is overseen by a headquarters in the Office for Veterans’ Affairs (OVA) within the Ministry of Defence. It will bring together national oversight, regional coordination and local delivery to improve how services work together. 

VALOUR field officers are also working regionally to strengthen collaboration between partners such as councils, local public services and charities. 

The continued rollout of VALOUR demonstrates the UK Government’s delivery of the 10-year Veterans Strategy, which aims to celebrate, contribute to, and support those who serve and have served. Funding for VALOUR is included in the Defence Investment Plan. 

There are approximately 176,000 veterans living in Scotland.

Scotland now has two VALOUR-recognised centres:


  DMWS; and
  SSAFA Connect in Glasgow, which supports veterans and Forces families navigating housing, health, and employment challenges in Glasgow, Inverclyde, Edinburgh, Renfrewshire, North and South Lanarkshire, West Dunbartonshire, and West Lothian.


On Thursday Minister Ward hosted a Remembrance Reception at the UK Government’s Queen Elizabeth House HQ in Edinburgh, bringing together Scotland’s Armed Forces community, including veteran organisations and military representatives, as well as Scottish MPs and other guests.

ENDS

 Background


  Over £26m of development funding for VALOUR-recognised centres has been allocated in two rounds of funding. 
  
    21 lead organisations are receiving £13,260,580 of development funding in round 2, with £26,516,357 million granted in total. They will join the first round of 14 organisations announced in March 2026, and are:

items.title: PM meetings with world leaders at CHOGM
items.summary: The Prime Minister met a series of world leaders during the retreat at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua yesterday. That included meeting the Indian Minister of External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. The Prime Mini
items.bodyHtml:
The Prime Minister met a series of world leaders during the retreat at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua yesterday.

That included meeting the Indian Minister of External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. The Prime Minister underscored his commitment to the close friendship between the UK and India, and both reiterated their desire to end the bloodshed in Ukraine.

He also met the Prime Minister of Mauritius, Navin Ramgoolam. During the discussion, the Prime Minister underlined his commitment to working with Mauritius and the United States on a way forward that secured the operation of the Diego Garcia base and protected national security for all three countries. They agreed to work on a shared plan to make further progress by the end of the year.

Ahead of the retreat the Prime Minister spoke to the President of the World Bank Ajay Banga.

They discussed the Prime Minister’s reset on debt and his focus on ensuring accessible, sustainable finance for small and developing nations through both the Commonwealth and the UK’s Presidency of G20.

The Prime Minister returned to the United Kingdom this morning.

items.title: Sovereign AI puts cash and compute behind UK startup using AI to redefine chemistry
items.summary: UK Government’s Sovereign AI backing Potential Sciences - a British startup whose new approach to using AI in science could make the design of new medicines faster, cheaper and more reliable than current methods Sovereign AI is the governme
items.bodyHtml:
• UK Government’s Sovereign AI backing Potential Sciences - a British startup whose new approach to using AI in science could make the design of new medicines faster, cheaper and more reliable than current methods
  • Sovereign AI is the government’s big bet on promising AI companies to help them grow, scale and succeed from Britain, driving the modern reindustrialisation of Britain 
  • Package of support includes investment and compute as the company announces an eight-figure funding round today

Potential Sciences, a British startup aiming to unlock the next big advance in how we use AI to design new medicines, has secured backing from the UK Government’s Sovereign AI venture fund as part of an eight-figure fundraise announced today (Thursday 5 November).

The investment and access to compute - the processing power needed to run and train AI models - being made available reflects the UK’s ambition to back homegrown companies developing the critical technologies that will drive the modern reindustrialisation of Britain, and the next wave of AI innovation.

Using AI for the design of new chemicals - and discovering new medicines in particular - is opening up new possibilities for tackling diseases like cancer and Parkinson’s, which could offer hope to patients and families across the country. However progress has been held back because AI usually relies on data from slow, costly real world lab experiments.

Potential Sciences are taking a new approach, with an AI model focused on the fundamental laws of physics, rather than previous experimental data. This could make the AI calculations needed to design chemicals 100 times cheaper than at present - unlocking a wave of new discoveries in fields that are currently uneconomical to focus on.

Sovereign AI is the government’s big bet on promising early-stage AI companies to help them grow, scale and succeed from Britain, offering a range of backing to high-potential AI businesses that are starting out on British shores.  

Combining the pace and ambition of venture capital with the weight of the state behind it, Sovereign AI is moving fast, backing ambition so that Britain’s AI innovators and entrepreneurs can go on to succeed globally.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said:

Potential Sciences is a startup that’s grasping an opportunity Britain is uniquely well-placed to capitalise on: using our deep expertise in data, fundamental science and computing to potentially unleash the next great wave of medical discovery.

Solving chemistry’s ‘data bottleneck’ could allow researchers to explore new treatments for diseases that are currently deemed too rare or expensive to focus on. This is AI at its best – pushing the boundaries of innovation, ultimately to improve people’s lives.

Science Minister Chris McDonald said:

As a former chemical engineer, I know firsthand how the field can make a real difference; whether that’s discovering new medicines to treat and beat disease, or finding cheaper and more efficient ways to bring innovations to life.

This investment plays into everything that’s good about British innovation, and shows what could be possible when we bring scientific research together with AI. Backing homegrown success stories like Potential Sciences, we’re giving companies the support they need to realise their ambitions, and backing science and innovation to deliver the medical breakthroughs that people all over the country will benefit from.

Hatem Helal, founder and CEO of Potential Sciences, said

AI for drug discovery has learned almost everything the existing experimental record can teach it. The next leap needs new data, and the laws of physics can supply it, as long as your software can use modern hardware.

We rebuilt quantum chemistry for GPUs so that gold-standard accuracy is affordable at the scale AI needs. When your code is 100 times more efficient, a seed round buys what used to take a dedicated datacenter.

Sovereign AI is backing Potential Sciences as an investor in today’s funding round. Other backers include Twin Path Ventures, Odyssey, Portfolio Ventures, Blue Wire Capital, rule30, Nauta Capital and Lightfield Equity, as well as angel investment from the likes of Patrick Collison (co-founder of Stripe) and Chris Gibson (co-founder and former CEO of Recursion). While AI engineer Andrew Fitzgibbon and entrepreneur James Hawkins will support the company as advisors.

Sovereign AI is also making compute available to the company through the AI Research Resource, the UK’s national suite of advanced supercomputers, including the Isambard-AI supercomputer in Bristol.

Chair of the Prime Minister’s AI Taskforce, Lord Vallance, said:

Drug discovery is an expensive and uncertain business and we still don’t have effective treatments and cures for many diseases. Potential Sciences has proposed an elegant solution: turning to the fundamentals of quantum science and AI. That could be a gamechanger and speaks to the ingenuity and inspiration that Sovereign AI seeks to foster into new businesses and products.

Sovereign AI Investment Partner Joséphine Kant said: 

I first met Hatem in Cambridge, and he immediately struck me as a formidable founder. He combines technical excellence with low ego and unapologetic ambition. He knows the science in extraordinary detail, but he’s also deliberate about bringing in people who are exceptional in areas different from his own.

Potential Sciences have the ambition to become a true frontier lab for chemistry, with the potential to fundamentally change how the field works.

This news comes a week after the Budget, where the Chancellor confirmed a further £140 million backing for Sovereign AI, with an additional £60 million to support the Fund’s investments, plus £80 million for Sovereign AI’s R&D Procurement Scheme. The Chancellor also announced that Sovereign AI would expand into a new focus area of Physical and Industrial AI, building on the UK’s leading research base and growing strengths in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

All of the startups Sovereign AI supports have a meaningful presence here in the UK, and create well paid jobs right across the country - supporting the Government’s ambition for good growth in every postcode. These startups are all firmly anchored in the UK with either their founders, leadership, operating headquarters or a large proportion of their talent based here in Britain.

Notes to editors: 

  • The Fund will invest directly in promising UK AI companies to help them scale in the UK. Our investments will be focused on companies at the early and growth-stage. 
  • Typical equity investments will be worth around £1-10 million, though every company’s circumstances will be different.  
  • Like most venture capital funds we do not comment on specific investment figures as they are commercially sensitive.

ENDS

items.title: Law Officers mark 25 years of Pro Bono Week
items.summary: The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP, and Solicitor General, Andy Slaughter KC MP, have marked the 25th anniversary of Pro Bono Week by joining lawyers, charities, students and parliamentarians at events celebrating voluntary legal work
items.bodyHtml:
The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP, and Solicitor General, Andy Slaughter KC MP, have marked the 25th anniversary of Pro Bono Week by joining lawyers, charities, students and parliamentarians at events celebrating voluntary legal work. 

On 26 October, the Solicitor General launched the new History of Pro Bono Exhibition in Parliament. It charts the tradition of lawyers providing free legal help, from ancient Greece and Rome to the present day, with photographs, videos and articles from more than 50 law firms, charities, universities and individuals. 

Opening Pro Bono Week on Monday 2 November, the Attorney General paid tribute to the lawyers, charities, universities and other organisations that have sustained the movement over the past 25 years. She also reflected on volunteering at her law school’s legal clinic while studying for the Bar, which reinforced why she wanted to become a lawyer.  

The Attorney General at the opening of Pro Bono Week on Monday 2 November.

The Attorney General at the opening of Pro Bono Week on Monday 2 November.

The Attorney General Ellie Reeves KC MP said: 

For 25 years, Pro Bono Week has celebrated the legal profession at its very best, with lawyers giving their time and expertise to help people who may otherwise have nowhere to turn. 

Pro bono can provide a lifeline when an everyday problem becomes a legal crisis. It also gives lawyers experiences that challenge and inspire them, connecting them with people whose lives will stay with them long afterwards. 

As we celebrate everything that has been achieved over the past 25 years, I hope we also look ahead and ensure this tradition of legal volunteering continues to grow and change lives.

On Tuesday 3 November, the Solicitor General spoke at two events. The first marked the 10th anniversary of the Law Society’s Pro Bono Charter. He recognised the Charter’s role in building a culture of pro bono across the profession and encouraged legal organisations to maintain and expand their commitments.  

The Solicitor General at the Pro Bono Week Young Lawyers Event for early-career and aspiring legal professionals.

He later addressed the Pro Bono Week Young Lawyers Event for early-career and aspiring legal professionals. He encouraged them to participate in pro bono as part of their careers. 

The Solicitor General Andy Slaughter KC MP said: 

Pro bono work makes a valuable contribution to access to justice. Over the past 25 years, thousands of lawyers have volunteered their skills to support people through some of the most difficult and distressing days of their lives. 

Pro bono is a vital part of our legal system. I want to thank everyone who gives their time and expertise, and encourage the next generation of lawyers to carry that tradition forward.

items.title: Government to end 'wild west' e-bike parking with new powers for local leaders
items.summary: new national standards to improve shared e-bike schemes, with clear rules for operators, riders and councils crack down on nuisance parking and antisocial behaviour to keep pavements clear and make journeys safer latest measure in Prime Min
items.bodyHtml:
• new national standards to improve shared e-bike schemes, with clear rules for operators, riders and councils 
  • crack down on nuisance parking and antisocial behaviour to keep pavements clear and make journeys safer 
  • latest measure in Prime Minister’s series of everyday fixes to make life easier while putting more power in local hands

People across the country will benefit from safer and easier journeys, as Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander is set to give local leaders the powers to stop ‘wild west’ e-bike parking and tackle antisocial behaviour.

Shared e-bikes, such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt, are an increasingly popular way to get around, making short journeys quick and convenient. New rules proposed by the government today (5 November 2026) would help make these schemes work better for everyone.

Local leaders will be able to licence schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.

The shared cycle scheme consultation, launched today, sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

Measures include:

  • a parking plan – so they aren’t inconveniencing the public
  • a plan for antisocial and illegal behaviour – to prevent users riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements, and setting out clear consequences such as fines for this behaviour 
  • fleet management plans, defined fleet sizes and operating areas – so bikes aren’t overcrowding streets
  • a fleet maintenance plan – so that cycles are always safe to use
  • potential insurance requirements for operators so people can claim compensation if they’re hit by someone on a shared cycle

The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning. This will mean people can be confident their bike will work when they need it and that bikes will be available in the right places without cluttering up streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

E-bikes can make getting around that bit easier, but when they block pavements or are used irresponsibly, they can be a real frustration.

I want to sort that by giving communities more control over where they are parked and making sure companies and riders play by the rules.

While making the big, long-term changes to make transport better and more affordable for people across the country, this is a small but important everyday fix to make our streets safer.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said:

Shared e-bike schemes have revolutionised the way people travel around our towns and cities. They are easy to use, get us active and help reduce emissions, but we need to make sure they work with the communities where they operate.

That’s why we are taking decisive action to give local leaders the power to stop nuisance parking, tackle antisocial behaviour and make journeys safer.

Operators have been calling for more regulation on shared cycle schemes, so they have greater certainty on where and how they run, putting an end to the patchwork of rules for operating in different areas.

This will give local authorities the tools they need to shape their streets to work best for the communities they serve, as part of a wider government move to put more powers in local hands, ensuring decisions are made by those who know local areas best.

In London, the Transport Secretary is working with the Mayor and Transport for London (TfL) on devolving new powers to TfL to ensure the rules are implemented and enforced across London, ending the postcode lottery of different standards being implemented and enforced in different boroughs.

The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said:

The ‘wild west’ approach to dockless e-bikes cannot continue. While these services are helping thousands more Londoners to cycle, their rapid growth has also brought challenges around safety, inconsiderate parking and the lack of data needed to properly manage them.

I’ve been calling for powers to better manage dockless e-bike schemes since 2017, when the first schemes arrived in London, so I welcome the government’s plans to give cities the powers they need to do this. For too long, cities have been left without the tools needed to properly manage these services, despite clear evidence that the current approach is not working.

I’m pleased to see the Department for Transport setting clear standards and empowering local leaders to better support vital growth in sustainable travel so we can keep building a safer, fairer, greener London for everyone.

The consultation continues the government’s commitment to helping make active travel a viable option for more people. £4.5 billion will be invested over the next 5 years, including a recent £104 million invested in the UK’s 12,000 miles worth of cycling routes – helping reach ambitious targets of getting over half of people to walk or cycle for short journeys in towns and cities.

Agustin Guilisasti, Founder and CEO of Forest, said:

When I founded Forest, it was with the hope of a greener London, built around the people who live and work here. To see London becoming a cycling city is something to celebrate. But to achieve this, we need national standards and a coherent, well-regulated, London-wide system – better for riders and, importantly, better for pedestrians and the city.

With around 350,000 shared e-bike trips taken every day in London, this is a real opportunity to work with government and local leaders to make cycling an easy, everyday choice. That means enough bikes in the right places and enough parking, so people can arrive easily and park responsibly – for calmer streets, cleaner air and a city that moves.

Wayne Ting, Chief Executive Officer at Lime, said:

As the UK’s largest shared e-bike operator, we’re proud to have helped hundreds of thousands of people in the UK become regular cyclists – to the point that ‘Liming’ has become a verb. Millions of people now choose Lime to get to work, meet friends, run errands and more – making travel in cities across the UK easier, more affordable and less dependent on cars.

Lime’s unmatched experience in working with cities to build and grow UK e-bike schemes means we know what it takes to make shared cycling work at scale. It’s why we recognise the current patchwork approach is confusing for riders, councils and operators, all of whom deserve greater clarity and certainty.

Today’s consultation is an important step forward. We look forward to working with government and local authorities to help deliver schemes that work for riders, operators, and everyone in the communities we serve, all for a greener and more connected UK.

Eleanor Briggs, Head of Policy, Public Affairs and Campaigns at Guide Dogs, said:

We welcome the government’s consultation on introducing national standards for shared e-bike schemes, giving local authorities much-needed powers to tackle dangerous parking and unsafe use. For people with sight loss, badly parked rental e-bikes are a barrier to independent travel, blocking pavements, creating unexpected obstacles and making it harder to navigate safely.

Guide Dogs frequently hears from people with a vision impairment about irresponsible and antisocial use of e-bikes on pavements, putting pedestrians at risk. We look forward to engaging with the consultation and working with government, local authorities and operators to ensure rental schemes are safe, accessible and work for everyone, including people with sight loss.

Mike Wordingham, RNIB’s Head of Policy, said:

Dockless e-bikes are heavy, fast, silent and unpredictable. An astonishing 92% of blind and partially sighted people tell us they have had to walk into the road due to street obstacles such as e-bikes.

We are glad the government is recognising this issue and putting forward plans to tackle it. But tackling rider behaviour will be difficult, and it’s vital the desire for local flexibility doesn’t lead to a patchwork of regulations and inconsistency in implementing them. Everyone deserves to feel safe.

We urge the government to listen to blind and partially sighted people and work closely with operators and local authorities to make sure regulations successfully reduce the risk these bikes pose to people with sight loss.

National Active Travel Commissioner, Chris Boardman, said:

That’s why I’m delighted the government is stepping in to give local leaders the powers they need to tackle the problem and make sure these schemes work for everyone.

But we shouldn’t lose sight of the bigger picture. Shared bike use is booming, and that’s exactly what we want to see – affordable, healthy, low-carbon transport, available when you need it. Whether it’s a short hop across town, the daily commute or an unplanned journey, shared bikes offer predictable journey times and another option when other transport is disrupted.

The demand is clearly there. Now we need to manage that success properly, keeping pavements clear while enabling even more people to enjoy the benefits.

Christina Moe Gjerde, VP for Northern Europe at Voi, said:

We welcome the government’s proposals to raise standards for shared e-bikes across the country. Voi operates thousands of shared bikes countrywide, and consistent national standards, backed by local licensing, will let responsible operators work with councils to keep pavements clear.

Georgia Heathman, Bolt’s Public Policy Manager for UK and Ireland, said:

We welcome the government’s consultation on national standards for shared e-bikes and the opportunity to work with ministers, local authorities and the wider sector to shape them.     crack down on nuisance parking and antisocial behaviour to keep pavements clear and make journeys safer 
    latest measure in Prime Minister’s series of everyday fixes to make life easier while putting more power in local hands
  


People across the country will benefit from safer and easier journeys, as Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander is set to give local leaders the powers to stop ‘wild west’ e-bike parking and tackle antisocial behaviour.

Shared e-bikes, such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt, are an increasingly popular way to get around, making short journeys quick and convenient. New rules proposed by the government today (5 November 2026) would help make these schemes work better for everyone.

Local leaders will be able to licence schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.

The shared cycle scheme consultation, launched today, sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

Measures include:


  a parking plan – so they aren’t inconveniencing the public
  a plan for antisocial and illegal behaviour – to prevent users riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements, and setting out clear consequences such as fines for this behaviour 
  fleet management plans, defined fleet sizes and operating areas – so bikes aren’t overcrowding streets
  a fleet maintenance plan – so that cycles are always safe to use
  potential insurance requirements for operators so people can claim compensation if they’re hit by someone on a shared cycle


The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning. This will mean people can be confident their bike will work when they need it and that bikes will be available in the right places without cluttering up streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:


  E-bikes can make getting around that bit easier, but when they block pavements or are used irresponsibly, they can be a real frustration.

  I want to sort that by giving communities more control over where they are parked and making sure companies and riders play by the rules.

  While making the big, long-term changes to make transport better and more affordable for people across the country, this is a small but important everyday fix to make our streets safer.


Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said:


  Shared e-bike schemes have revolutionised the way people travel around our towns and cities. They are easy to use, get us active and help reduce emissions, but we need to make sure they work with the communities where they operate.

  That’s why we are taking decisive action to give local leaders the power to stop nuisance parking, tackle antisocial behaviour and make journeys safer.


Operators have been calling for more regulation on shared cycle schemes, so they have greater certainty on where and how they run, putting an end to the patchwork of rules for operating in different areas.

This will give local authorities the tools they need to shape their streets to work best for the communities they serve, as part of a wider government move to put more powers in local hands, ensuring decisions are made by those who know local areas best.

In London, the Transport Secretary is working with the Mayor and Transport for London (TfL) on devolving new powers to TfL to ensure the rules are implemented and enforced across London, ending the postcode lottery of different standards being implemented and enforced in different boroughs.

  I’m pleased to see the Department for Transport setting clear standards and empowering local leaders to better support vital growth in sustainable travel so we can keep building a safer, fairer, greener London for everyone.

items.title: RSH data indicates increase in social housing tenant satisfaction
items.summary: Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSM) results released today by the Regulator of Social Housing saw an average increase from 72% last year to 74% for 2025/26 for tenants living in low-cost rental accommodation (LCRA). Telephone surveys remain
items.bodyHtml:
Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSM) results released today by the Regulator of Social Housing saw an average increase from 72% last year to 74% for 2025/26 for tenants living in low-cost rental accommodation (LCRA).

Telephone surveys remain the most widely used collection method. Overall satisfaction has increased in every collection method, including by telephone where the proportion of tenants reporting they are satisfied overall has increased from 71% to 73%.

The TSMs are collected from all large social landlords – those with 1,000 homes or more.

They allow tenants to scrutinise their landlord’s performance, give insights to landlords on where they might improve their services, and provide a source of intelligence for regulation.

The 2025/26 data also shows that landlords have reported improvements in their repairs and maintenance services, with 83% of non-emergency repairs completed on time in 2025/26, compared to 77% in 2023/24.

Average (median) satisfaction with the timeliness of repairs has risen from 67% in 2023/24 to 73% in 2025/26, the largest increase across the tenant perception TSMs.

Satisfaction with the maintenance of the home has increased from 71% to 74% over the same period.

The vast majority of homes owned by large landlords, as at 31 March 2026, had required gas (99.7%), fire (98.9%), asbestos (98.7%), water (98.2%) and lift safety checks (98.0%) completed. These have each increased since TSMs began in 2023/24, with asbestos, water and lift safety having the comparatively largest increases.

And 86% of over 319,000 stage one complaints made during 2025/26 were responded to within the Housing Ombudsman’s Complaint Handling Code timescales. This has increased from 73% in the first year of collection (2023/24).

The TSMs also provide landlords with valuable information as to how services might be further improved. Around one in six (16%) of LCRA tenants surveyed are dissatisfied with the overall service from their landlord.

Overall average (landlord median) satisfaction for low-cost home ownership (LCHO) remains lower (50%) than LCRA, showing that landlords have work to do to improve services and satisfaction for shared owners. 

Kate Dodsworth, RSH Deputy Chief Executive, said: “The TSM results are based on feedback from almost half a million tenants, providing the most comprehensive view of tenant satisfaction across large social landlords in England.

“The increased level of tenant satisfaction reported by landlords underlines the value of landlords listening to tenants, understanding the issues that matter most to them and using those insights to improve services.

“Tenant feedback is one of the most important tools landlords have for assessing performance. The challenge now is to continue turning that insight into tangible improvements for residents.”

ENDS

Notes for editors

  1. Landlords owning 1,000 homes or more need to submit their results to RSH annually. This is a requirement of RSH’s Transparency, Influence and Accountability standard. RSH’s analysis of the TSM results is based on the returns from these large landlords. Small providers with less than 1,000 homes must also collect the information and make it available to their tenants.
  2. TSMs are collected and reported by landlords according to detailed requirements set by RSH. This includes, for example, the questions landlords must use in their surveys of tenants. There are 22 TSMs reported in 2025/26. 12 are ‘tenant perception’ questions that landlords must ask tenants. 10 are ‘management information’ questions that landlords complete themselves, relating to repairs, complaints and anti-social behaviour. A new TSM covering electrical safety checks will be reported for the first time covering the 2025/26 reporting year.
  3. In 2025/26 landlords surveyed almost half a million tenants. This is a rich and important source of feedback about individual landlords and the social housing sector as a whole. The full suite of TSM information is published on RSH’s website.
  4. TSMs are intended to be interpreted in the round and with other relevant information to inform a view of landlord performance. The published landlord data includes key contextual information including on survey collection method(s) and the profile of each landlord. RSH has also published for each landlord their overall satisfaction by collection method. These are useful for reasonably comparing performance between landlords. The TSMs are one source of regulatory intelligence, and no regulatory judgement is based solely on TSM results.
  5. As set out in RSH’s regulatory casework review, it is important for landlords to use insights from data to properly understand issues and drive improvements. This TSM publication can help inform how TSMs can be used to understand performance and improve service delivery.
  6. RSH promotes a viable, efficient and well-governed social housing sector able to deliver more and better social homes. It does this by setting standards and carrying out robust regulation focusing on driving improvement in social landlords, including local authorities, and ensuring that housing associations are well-governed, financially viable and offer value for money. It takes appropriate action if the outcomes of the standards are not being delivered.
  7. For media enquiries please contact vicky.moore@rsh.gov.uk or christian.cosby@rsh.gov.uk. For general enquiries, please contact enquiries@rsh.gov.uk.
