items.title: Government announces up to £15 million to bring the joy of reading to 300,000 more young children
items.summary: Move that will support up to 300,000 more pre-school children, builds on the work of book-giving charities, such as Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library UK and BookTrust New investment will increase access to books for young children and help
items.bodyHtml:
• Move that will support up to 300,000 more pre-school children, builds on the work of book-giving charities, such as Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library UK and BookTrust 
  • New investment will increase access to books for young children and help improve children’s readiness for school  

A new programme announced in the Budget will give up to 300,000 children across England greater access to books in the run up to starting school, regardless of their background or circumstances.  

The £15 million investment will focus on pre-school children to help build confidence, communication and a lasting love of learning. As well as supporting children it will give parents some breathing space with costs. 

Getting books into children’s hands early helps build the skills they need to thrive at school. Last year a record 72.3% of children reached a good level of development by the end of Reception, so the government is on track to beat its 75% school readiness target by 2028. Around 1,000 Best Start Family Hubs are also being rolled out across the country, working with the National Literacy Trust and BookTrust as part of their wider support for families to encourage more shared reading at home. 

It builds on the government’s work to build a lifelong love of reading. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport has committed £12.5 million of dormant assets funding from the Every Child Can Programme to ensure every primary school in England has a library by the end of this Parliament. On top of this a further £5 million is being provided to secondary schools to buy books and reading materials that encourage more young people to read for enjoyment. 

Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy said: 

A good book in your hands can be truly transformative. Children’s books are where curiosity takes root and a lifelong love of reading begins. We believe that every child, regardless of their background or postcode, should have access to the things that bring joy, learning and creativity to their lives, and this programme will help make that a reality. 

Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said: 

Sharing a book with a child is about so much more than learning to read. It’s precious time together that can build their imagination, curiosity and excitement about stories. 

Getting more books into the hands of young children is an important first step, and we want to build on that throughout childhood. Through our curriculum reforms and the National Year of Reading, we’re helping make reading a part of children’s lives from their earliest years right through school. 

Alongside this, our Best Start Family Hubs are supporting families to foster a love of reading at home and helping ensure children develop the skills and confidence that will benefit them throughout their lives.

The move follows the success of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library UK, which works with local partners to deliver books to the homes of families monthly, and BookTrust, which provides free books at key points in the early years. 

Since launching in 2007, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library UK has gifted almost 8 million free, age-appropriate books directly to children under five, with nearly 100,000 children receiving a free book every month, helping to boost early literacy, shared family reading and school readiness across the country. BookTrust has helped transform the lives of over 1.4 million children annually by providing free books and early years resources, successfully engaging around 93% of newborns and inspiring 84% of low income parents to read more with their families. 

Darren Henley, Chief Executive, Arts Council England, said: 

We know the many benefits that reading brings to our children: it is a gift that opens minds, sparks imagination and changes lives. We’re thrilled to support this initiative to put more books in the hands of children across England, helping more young people to learn, dream and thrive.

Steve Korris, Executive Director of The Dollywood Foundation UK, home of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library said: 

Dolly’s dream was for every child to grow up with books of their own, regardless of their family’s circumstances. We’re delighted that the Government is backing that ambition through this investment in early years book gifting. 

Through the Imagination Library, we see the excitement a book arriving monthly through the letterbox brings, and how sharing stories helps families build bonds, children develop language and confidence, and a love of reading take root. This funding is a welcome opportunity to bring those benefits to many more children across England, giving them the strongest possible start, well before their first day at school.

Diana Gerald MBE and Annie Crombie, Co-CEOs of BookTrust, said: 

Every child deserves the chance to experience the joy of books and reading, whatever their background or postcode. Shared reading is often a child’s first experience of culture, creativity and storytelling, laying the foundations for a lifelong love of books. Through our Bookstart programme and with the work of more than 7,000 partner organisations in villages, towns and communities across the UK, we see every day the difference that access to books and support makes to the 1.4 million children and families we reach. We welcome this investment, which will help more children discover the joy of reading and the opportunities it can create.

Funding will be delivered by Arts Council England. Further details on the design of the programme will be published in due course. 

The government is also investing in opportunities for children and young people beyond the classroom, including £22.5 million for youth-led cultural activities in England’s most deprived areas and £132.5 million to support disadvantaged young people, including £12.5 million for music in libraries and £10 million for creative mentoring for care-experienced young people. This sits alongside wider support for careers education, traineeships and pathways into the creative industries.

  We know the many benefits that reading brings to our children: it is a gift that opens minds, sparks imagination and changes lives. We’re thrilled to support this initiative to put more books in the hands of children across England, helping more young people to learn, dream and thrive.


Steve Korris, Executive Director of The Dollywood Foundation UK, home of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library said: 


  Dolly’s dream was for every child to grow up with books of their own, regardless of their family’s circumstances. We’re delighted that the Government is backing that ambition through this investment in early years book gifting. 

  Through the Imagination Library, we see the excitement a book arriving monthly through the letterbox brings, and how sharing stories helps families build bonds, children develop language and confidence, and a love of reading take root. This funding is a welcome opportunity to bring those benefits to many more children across England, giving them the strongest possible start, well before their first day at school.


Diana Gerald MBE and Annie Crombie, Co-CEOs of BookTrust, said: 


  Every child deserves the chance to experience the joy of books and reading, whatever their background or postcode. Shared reading is often a child’s first experience of culture, creativity and storytelling, laying the foundations for a lifelong love of books. Through our Bookstart programme and with the work of more than 7,000 partner organisations in villages, towns and communities across the UK, we see every day the difference that access to books and support makes to the 1.4 million children and families we reach. We welcome this investment, which will help more children discover the joy of reading and the opportunities it can create.


Funding will be delivered by Arts Council England. Further details on the design of the programme will be published in due course. 

The government is also investing in opportunities for children and young people beyond the classroom, including £22.5 million for youth-led cultural activities in England’s most deprived areas and £132.5 million to support disadvantaged young people, including £12.5 million for music in libraries and £10 million for creative mentoring for care-experienced young people. This sits alongside wider support for careers education, traineeships and pathways into the creative industries.

items.title: Government bid to make England TB-free by 2038, with vaccines for cattle and badgers
items.summary: The Government is winning its battle against bovine TB – with the number of new TB herd breakdowns in England down by a fifth compared to the previous 12 months and no badgers culled for the first time in over a decade. Progress in the figh
items.bodyHtml:
The Government is winning its battle against bovine TB – with the number of new TB herd breakdowns in England down by a fifth compared to the previous 12 months and no badgers culled for the first time in over a decade.

Progress in the fight back against the devastating disease comes as the Government (Thursday 5th November) formally adopts a long-term strategy, aimed at eradicating TB from England altogether by 2038.

The multi-faceted approach includes the development of vaccines for cattle and badgers, mandatory blood tests, more robust wildlife surveillance and more test choice.

Developed in partnership with experts and stakeholders, including farmers, vets and scientists, the strategy sets out a clear direction of travel as its long-term plan to tackle bovine TB in England. It was originally published in June and will now be formally taken forward by government.

Bovine TB remains one of the most significant animal health challenges we face. The disease continues to impose a heavy emotional and financial burden on farming families, disrupt rural businesses and leads to the loss of thousands of cattle every year.  

The announcement comes as encouraging progress is being made in tackling bovine TB, with herds losing TB free status in England falling by a fifth over the past year and 2026 marking the first year in more than a decade in which no badgers were culled as part of efforts to control the disease – delivering on a manifesto pledge to end the cull.

Biosecurity Minister Baroness Hayman said: 

Bovine TB has devasted our farming communities, causing heartbreaking losses, uncertainty and financial hardship. No farmer should have to accept this disease as an unavoidable part of their livelihood. 

Our comprehensive strategy will ensure the continuation of the end to badger culling, and prevent the spread of this horrific disease.

Work is already underway on several key measures set out in the strategy, including: 

  • Cattle vaccination: Continuing the development of a deployable cattle vaccine alongside a new skin test to detect infected animals from vaccinated animals, (DIVA), with an ambition to deploy cattle vaccination by 2030 
  • Improved disease testing: Expanding the government-funded mandatory blood testing and piloting additional privately funded testing to help detect infection. 
  • Badger vaccination: Rolling out vaccination in priority areas through the newly contracted Badger Vaccination Field Force. 
  • Wildlife surveillance: Introducing a new government-funded scheme to collect and test found dead badgers to improve understanding of the disease. 

The government will also establish a new industry-government board to replace the existing Bovine TB Partnership for England, bringing together government and industry to oversee delivery of the strategy. The board, expected to be established in 2027, will consider and endorse the first delivery plan, setting out the priority actions needed to tackle the disease and how they will be implemented

The government will continue working with farmers, veterinary professionals and other partners to deliver a coordinated approach to tackling bovine TB, helping to protect animal health and reduce the impact of the disease on rural communities. 

ENDS

Notes to editors 

  • Read the government’s response to the recommended strategy. 

  • The percentage of herds under restriction due to a TB incident at the end of June 2026 was lower in England than at the end of June 2025, 3.4% compared with 4.2%. It has been on a declining trajectory in the Hish Risk Area and England as a whole since 2017 and has sharply declined in the Edge Area since 2024. Bovine TB statistics - GOV.UK 
  • The 12-monthly total number of cattle slaughtered for TB control reasons in England (test reactors and direct contacts) reached a historical maximum of 34,518 in 12 months ending April 2018. The latest statistics show 20,244 animals removed in the latest 12-month reporting period ending June 2026, a 4% decrease from the 21,126 animals removed in the 12 months ending June 2025

items.title: Plan to drive down homelessness for young people leaving care
items.summary: Young people who have been in care will be better protected from falling into homelessness with new duties on councils to support young people as they step out of care and towards independent living. The Care Leaver Homelessness Reduction A
items.bodyHtml:
Young people who have been in care will be better protected from falling into homelessness with new duties on councils to support young people as they step out of care and towards independent living.

The Care Leaver Homelessness Reduction Action Plan, launched at the start of Care Leavers Month 2026, declares that no young person should become homeless when they leave care. It also gives clear new duties to local authorities to prevent that from happening.

Currently, too many young people lose their support overnight when they leave care. Without family to fall back on, they can face poor mental health, money worries, a lack of jobs or education, and too few suitable homes.

Under new rules, local authorities are required to publish their plans for care leavers’ accommodation needs, work with housing partners, and support those at risk of homelessness in their local offer for care leavers. Additionally, certain care leavers under 25 can no longer be found intentionally homeless, which is currently a barrier to getting much-needed assistance that fails to reflect their particular circumstances.

The Plan also encourages local authorities to publish local targets and what support is available for young people at risk of homelessness and commits targeted support and advice to areas of higher risk, overseen by MHCLG youth homelessness advisers.

It follows the Prime Minister setting out his confidence last week that everyone sleeping rough will be offered a route off the streets before Christmas, as he brought businesses, charities and local leaders together for the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street to drive further action from across society. At the Budget, the government also announced new funding to sustain this support through the rest of this Parliament.

Children’s Minister Josh MacAlister said:

Supporting young people who have been in care is a vital part of our national mission to end rough sleeping.

Too many care leavers step into adulthood without a strong support network around them, and homelessness can be one of the tragic consequences.

We’re changing children’s social care from top to bottom, making enduring relationships the focus of the system and expanding support for care leavers to help ensure they have a place to call home.

Minister for Homelessness, Florence Eshalomi, said:

Our commitment to tackling homelessness is about so much more than offering a bed to sleep in, or a roof over someone’s head: it’s about preventing people from ever reaching that point in the first place.

That’s why we’re launching this plan to make sure young people leaving care don’t face a cliff edge just when they need support most.

These measures will give care leavers the support and opportunities they need as they move out of care and start their adult lives.

The number of care leavers aged 18 to 24 in England has risen to 86,890, up almost 10% in two years, and they remain over-represented in the homelessness system. The plan aims to halve the proportion of care experienced people who are homeless.

The government’s Action Plan:

  • builds on rules introduced in the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act this year, under which local authorities are required to publish their plans to support care leavers at risk of homelessness in their local offer, and certain care leavers under 25 can no longer be found intentionally homeless. Wider rules mean they also no longer have to meet local connection tests to get social housing.

  • expects councils to publish clearly what housing and support they offer care leavers, to plan ahead for their accommodation needs and to work with local housing teams.

  • brings together the guidance, tools, resources and support available to local authorities and their partners to help strengthen local prevention activity, including a new guide for councils entitled Planning Housing Pathways for Care Leavers, updated guidance on joint working between housing and children’s services, guidance on young people who stay with their foster carers after 18, a new youth homelessness prevention toolkit, and a new Homelessness Code of Guidance youth chapter. In 2027, there will be updated guidance on social housing allocations;

  • introduces a new £3m Test, Learn, Grow programme focussed on youth homelessness prevention

The plan builds on the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026. Staying Close, which helps care leavers find and keep a safe home and access health, education and work up to the age of 25, is already running in 50 areas and will become a national duty on councils for care leavers up to 25 from 2029.

From autumn 2027, government departments and public bodies will also become corporate parents, with a duty to work together with councils to support care leavers.

The new Plan also follows the government’s Review of early deaths of care leavers, published on 25 August, which highlighted the isolation many young people face when they leave care.

Seyi Obakin, Chief Executive Officer at Centrepoint said:

We warmly welcome the Government’s spotlight on care leavers as they continue to face a greater risk of experiencing homelessness.

We know that the number of care leavers aged 18–20 assessed as facing homelessness in England increased by 37% over the past five years. These young people often leave care without the safety net of a family or supportive network around them and need help to transition into adulthood.

Roughly 48% of the young people we support have been in care. They often have no choice but to deal with the challenges and responsibilities of living independently at a young age, so the launch of this new action plan will help focus efforts and provide an important opportunity to strengthen the support available to them.

We stand ready to play our part and work collectively with Government and our partners to make sure it’s implemented.  For us, this means ensuring young people have access to safe, stable and genuinely affordable housing, alongside the financial, practical and emotional support they need to sustain a home and build an independent life. 

Every young person deserves the solid foundations of a home from which to thrive and build a future.

Louise Mumcular, Policy Officer at Coram said: 

We welcome publication of the government’s Care Leaver Homelessness Reduction Action Plan. For too long, care experienced young people have faced disproportionately high risks of homelessness, often at a time when they are navigating the challenges of adulthood without the support networks many of their peers rely on. Every year our Coram Voice advocacy service provides support to hundreds of care leavers every year across the country, and housing is the most common issue for which young people seek support.

The commitments announced today are important steps in the right direction. We particularly welcome the government’s recognition that no young person should become homeless as a result of leaving care.

Ambitious national targets will only be achieved if they are backed by sufficient investment, consistent implementation across local areas, access to suitable and affordable housing, and meaningful support that helps young people sustain tenancies and thrive. It will be particularly important to strengthen support at key transition points and moments of vulnerability, such as when young people move home, leave education or training, or experience a breakdown in living arrangements. Every care-experienced young person must have not just a roof over their head, but a safe, stable and supportive home.

items.title: Communities to get a stronger say over billions of pounds of water investment
items.summary: Communities across England will get a bigger say over how water companies invest in their area under plans to put more power in local hands. Eight new regional water councils will bring local leaders, customers and businesses together to se
items.bodyHtml:
Communities across England will get a bigger say over how water companies invest in their area under plans to put more power in local hands.

Eight new regional water councils will bring local leaders, customers and businesses together to set the priorities for their region, helping shape billions of pounds of investment in water and flood infrastructure.

Decisions about the water system are taken nationally, despite communities facing very different challenges. From Lake Windermere, where discharge of sewage has damaged local tourism, or in Cambridge, where drought and water shortages have stalled growth – local areas have not had enough influence over the decisions that directly affect them.

The new councils will change that, giving communities and local leaders a stronger voice over priorities including sewage and water quality, flooding, drought and future water supplies. Mayors will also receive new powers through the strengthened Water Bill to hold water companies to account for their performance.

The reforms are part of the Prime Minister’s drive to move power out of Westminster and give communities greater control over the services and investment that shape their lives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

I know how desperate people are for change when it comes to water. I share their frustration at seeing sewage and pollution blight our rivers, lakes, and seas, while decisions about their local areas are taken miles away.

That’s not right. So for the first time, local people will have a real say over what they need from their water company, whether that is cleaning up polluted rivers, building new reservoirs or protecting homes from floods.

That is what moving power closer to communities looks like. Making sure local voices are heard and local priorities come first.

Existing regional partnerships have already shown what can be achieved when decisions are shaped around local needs. Greater Manchester’s Integrated Water Management Plan has brought together planning, regulation and investment, with improved drainage helping support town-centre regeneration. In East Anglia, Water Resources East has brought partners together to tackle severe water scarcity, including the constraints it places on sustainable growth in Greater Cambridge.

The eight new regional water councils will build on that approach and embed it across England.

Local leaders have been asked to submit proposals on how they want to run the new bodies by the end of the year. Each council will then draw up a plan setting out the biggest pressures on its region’s water system, the choices that need to be made and the public and private investment that can help address them.

Environment Secretary, Dame Angela Eagle, said:

For decades, the water industry has failed to work for the people and places it was meant to serve.

I am determined to put the public at the heart of decision-making – shaping what their bills will be spent on, so they can see real differences happening in their communities.

I share the country’s desire to see change now, and that’s why we are creating a radical new water system that will put public interest first.

This comes after the Environment Secretary took the unprecedented step of setting clear expectations for the next Price Review, warning water companies they must provide better value for money for struggling households.

Government is pushing ahead with reforms to overhaul a system in which shareholders never lose and customers never win. Water companies are being held to higher account with new powers for automatic fines, and the introduction of criminal liability for water bosses who cover up or hide sewage spills.

Further details on the Government’s approach to the water industry will be set out in the 10-year plan for Britain, to be published later this year.

SUPPORTIVE QUOTES:

Tracy Brabin, Mayor of West Yorkshire, said:

The privatisation of water has been a disaster for our region, with household bills set to rise by over 40% after years of underinvestment in infrastructure to line the pockets of wealthy shareholders and executives.

I’ve long called for directly-elected Mayors to be able to hold water companies to account, influence their operations, and direct the money raised from fines to support those communities hit hardest by illegal sewage dumping.

Through this new regional water council, we will do everything we can to ensure that Yorkshire Water finally puts people above profit and helps us build a greener, more affordable region with cleaner rivers and lower bills.

Mayor of the East Midlands, Claire Ward said:

Water is fundamental to our communities, our environment, and our economy – and decisions about our water should reflect the needs of the people and places they affect. People rightly expect clean rivers, secure water supplies, and better protection from flooding – but feel unable to influence those things.

Giving Mayors and communities a stronger voice means we can push for cleaner rivers, greater resilience to flooding and drought, and the investment our region needs to grow. This is a positive step towards a water system that works better for local people.

Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig said:

For too long, water in this country has been managed in a fragmented, unaccountable way that provided shareholder profit over public good. These reforms are an important step forward, giving Mayors a stronger voice to shape investment around local priorities and hold water companies to account for delivering for our residents.

In Greater Manchester, we know first-hand the impact flooding and dry weather can have on our communities. We need a more joined-up approach that works with nature and responds to local needs. That’s why, through our Integrated Water Management Plan, we are showing what can be achieved when that approach is taken and partners work together.

Richard Benwell, chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said:

Regional control of water investment could be a victory for people and nature. England’s rivers, wetlands, and waterways are vital natural infrastructure, protecting communities from floods and droughts, supporting wildlife, and providing the clean water we all depend on. Greater regional control offers an opportunity to put people at the heart of decisions, hold polluters to account, and turn ambitious national goals into healthier rivers and real improvements on the ground.

To realise this potential, the new regional councils must have the powers and funding to deliver. They need to be able to invest in nature and curb pollution across agriculture, chemicals, and wastewater. The Prime Minister must also continue to show leadership, ensuring regional plans deliver the nationwide improvements that people and nature deserve.

Matthew Browne, Head of Public Affairs at The Wildlife Trusts, said:

Putting communities at the heart of water management could finally turn the tide on our polluted rivers. By giving local leaders wide-ranging powers and bringing together all those with a stake in the water system, the Government can place freshwater recovery in the hands of people able to take the radical, comprehensive action needed to fix our water.

This is good news for communities, nature and the economy. Water is critical national infrastructure, and healthy, well- functioning rivers mean thriving wildlife, water supplies for farming and new homes, fewer floods, and fantastic places for people to enjoy.

It is community campaigning that first sounded the alarm about increasing threats to rivers. It is community control that holds the key to bringing our waters back to health.

Mark Lloyd, CEO of The Rivers Trust, said:

We’ve long been calling for a regionwide systems planning approach to how our water is managed, and it’s encouraging to see the government recognise that this is needed in today’s announcement. We look forward to working with local leaders to shape what this looks like in practice, including strategic plans that integrate water management identifying solutions and funding across sectors, via the Catchment-Based Approach. This will help ensure we can deliver rivers fit for the future and a resilient water system that works for communities, and protects us from the economic damage of pollution, flooding, drought and biodiversity decline.
items.bodyText:
Communities across England will get a bigger say over how water companies invest in their area under plans to put more power in local hands.

Eight new regional water councils will bring local leaders, customers and businesses together to set the priorities for their region, helping shape billions of pounds of investment in water and flood infrastructure.

Decisions about the water system are taken nationally, despite communities facing very different challenges. From Lake Windermere, where discharge of sewage has damaged local tourism, or in Cambridge, where drought and water shortages have stalled growth – local areas have not had enough influence over the decisions that directly affect them.

The new councils will change that, giving communities and local leaders a stronger voice over priorities including sewage and water quality, flooding, drought and future water supplies. Mayors will also receive new powers through the strengthened Water Bill to hold water companies to account for their performance.

The reforms are part of the Prime Minister’s drive to move power out of Westminster and give communities greater control over the services and investment that shape their lives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:


  I know how desperate people are for change when it comes to water. I share their frustration at seeing sewage and pollution blight our rivers, lakes, and seas, while decisions about their local areas are taken miles away.

  That’s not right. So for the first time, local people will have a real say over what they need from their water company, whether that is cleaning up polluted rivers, building new reservoirs or protecting homes from floods.

  That is what moving power closer to communities looks like. Making sure local voices are heard and local priorities come first.


Existing regional partnerships have already shown what can be achieved when decisions are shaped around local needs. Greater Manchester’s Integrated Water Management Plan has brought together planning, regulation and investment, with improved drainage helping support town-centre regeneration. In East Anglia, Water Resources East has brought partners together to tackle severe water scarcity, including the constraints it places on sustainable growth in Greater Cambridge.

The eight new regional water councils will build on that approach and embed it across England.

Local leaders have been asked to submit proposals on how they want to run the new bodies by the end of the year. Each council will then draw up a plan setting out the biggest pressures on its region’s water system, the choices that need to be made and the public and private investment that can help address them.

Environment Secretary, Dame Angela Eagle, said:


  For decades, the water industry has failed to work for the people and places it was meant to serve.

  I am determined to put the public at the heart of decision-making – shaping what their bills will be spent on, so they can see real differences happening in their communities.

  I share the country’s desire to see change now, and that’s why we are creating a radical new water system that will put public interest first.


This comes after the Environment Secretary took the unprecedented step of setting clear expectations for the next Price Review, warning water companies they must provide better value for money for struggling households.

Government is pushing ahead with reforms to overhaul a system in which shareholders never lose and customers never win. Water companies are being held to higher account with new powers for automatic fines, and the introduction of criminal liability for water bosses who cover up or hide sewage spills.

Further details on the Government’s approach to the water industry will be set out in the 10-year plan for Britain, to be published later this year.

SUPPORTIVE QUOTES:

Tracy Brabin, Mayor of West Yorkshire, said:


  The privatisation of water has been a disaster for our region, with household bills set to rise by over 40% after years of underinvestment in infrastructure to line the pockets of wealthy shareholders and executives.

  I’ve long called for directly-elected Mayors to be able to hold water companies to account, influence their operations, and direct the money raised from fines to support those communities hit hardest by illegal sewage dumping.

  Through this new regional water council, we will do everything we can to ensure that Yorkshire Water finally puts people above profit and helps us build a greener, more affordable region with cleaner rivers and lower bills.


Mayor of the East Midlands, Claire Ward said:


  Water is fundamental to our communities, our environment, and our economy – and decisions about our water should reflect the needs of the people and places they affect. People rightly expect clean rivers, secure water supplies, and better protection from flooding – but feel unable to influence those things.

  Giving Mayors and communities a stronger voice means we can push for cleaner rivers, greater resilience to flooding and drought, and the investment our region needs to grow. This is a positive step towards a water system that works better for local people.


Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig said:


  For too long, water in this country has been managed in a fragmented, unaccountable way that provided shareholder profit over public good. These reforms are an important step forward, giving Mayors a stronger voice to shape investment around local priorities and hold water companies to account for delivering for our residents.

  In Greater Manchester, we know first-hand the impact flooding and dry weather can have on our communities. We need a more joined-up approach that works with nature and responds to local needs. That’s why, through our Integrated Water Management Plan, we are showing what can be achieved when that approach is taken and partners work together.


Richard Benwell, chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said:


  Regional control of water investment could be a victory for people and nature. England’s rivers, wetlands, and waterways are vital natural infrastructure, protecting communities from floods and droughts, supporting wildlife, and providing the clean water we all depend on. Greater regional control offers an opportunity to put people at the heart of decisions, hold polluters to account, and turn ambitious national goals into healthier rivers and real improvements on the ground.

  To realise this potential, the new regional councils must have the powers and funding to deliver. They need to be able to invest in nature and curb pollution across agriculture, chemicals, and wastewater. The Prime Minister must also continue to show leadership, ensuring regional plans deliver the nationwide improvements that people and nature deserve.


Matthew Browne, Head of Public Affairs at The Wildlife Trusts, said:


  Putting communities at the heart of water management could finally turn the tide on our polluted rivers. By giving local leaders wide-ranging powers and bringing together all those with a stake in the water system, the Government can place freshwater recovery in the hands of people able to take the radical, comprehensive action needed to fix our water.

We look forward to working with local leaders to shape what this looks like in practice, including strategic plans that integrate water management identifying solutions and funding across sectors, via the Catchment-Based Approach. items.title: Veteran support centre network to more than double across the UK
items.summary: Veteran support centre network to more than double as part of the £50m VALOUR system rollout £13.2m is being distributed to 21 organisations across the UK to give veterans and their families easier access to healthcare, jobs and housing Vet
items.bodyHtml:
• Veteran support centre network to more than double as part of the £50m VALOUR system rollout
  • £13.2m is being distributed to 21 organisations across the UK to give veterans and their families easier access to healthcare, jobs and housing
  • Veterans Minister visited site in Aldershot ahead of Remembrance Sunday to thank the armed forces community and those who support them

Minister for Veterans and People Calvin Bailey MBE MP visited Citizens Advice Rushmoor in Aldershot on Monday 2 November to meet staff and the local veterans they are supporting.  

Earlier this year, 14 organisations were awarded over £13m to launch the first wave of VALOUR-recognised centres. Citizens Advice Rushmoor is one of 21 organisations receiving a share of over £13.2m of funding to launch the second wave of centres by the beginning of 2027. 

VALOUR has been designed to help the UK’s estimated two million veterans get the support they need through VALOUR-recognised centres, a helpline service or on GOV.UK.  

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

It is a privilege to be able to honour our veterans, not just as we mark Remembrance Day, but year-round as we remember the service and the sacrifice of those who fought for the lives we live today.

I’m incredibly proud to see the VALOUR network grow to provide support to more veterans and their families - those who have given so much to protect communities across the country.

Minister for Veterans and People Calvin Bailey MBE MP said: 

Ahead of Remembrance Sunday, I’m pleased that we can pay tribute to the service and sacrifice of our armed forces community by giving veterans easier access to the support they need, regardless of where they are in the UK. 

I’ve heard wonderful stories of how centres like Citizens Advice here in Rushmoor are making a real difference to people’s lives. Joining the VALOUR system will help them support even more veterans and their families.

Calum Stewart, CEO of Citizens Advice Rushmoor, said: 

Becoming a VALOUR-recognised centre is a huge step for Citizens Advice Rushmoor and for the veterans we support in Aldershot - Home of the British Army - and beyond. No veteran should have to navigate support alone. We know that good advice can make a lasting difference, helping people understand their options, resolve problems, and move forward with confidence. 

Through our network of local Citizens Advice charities across the South East, we bring together trusted advice, local knowledge and strong community connections. As part of the VALOUR system, we’ll build on those strengths to help more veterans and their families access joined-up advice and support, getting the right help at the right time so they can live independent and stable lives.

VALOUR is overseen by a headquarters in the Office for Veterans’ Affairs (OVA) within the Ministry of Defence. It will bring together national oversight, regional coordination and local delivery to improve how services work together. 

VALOUR field officers are also working regionally to strengthen collaboration between partners such as councils, local public services and charities. 

The continued roll out of VALOUR demonstrates the government’s delivery of the 10-year Veterans Strategy, which aims to celebrate, contribute and support those who serve and have served. Funding for VALOUR is included in the Defence Investment Plan.

Twenty-one lead organisations are receiving £13,260,580 of development funding in round 2, with £26,516,357 million granted in total. They will join the first round of 14 organisations announced in March 2026, and are: 

  • The Poppy Factory 
  • Sir Oswald Stoll Foundation 
  • Age UK Waltham Forest 
  • Mid Suffolk Citizens Advice Bureau   
  • Stevenage Borough Council 
  • Defence Medical Welfare Service charity 
  • Veterans Support Northern Ireland 
  • Adferiad 
  • Monmouthshire County Council 
  • City of York Council 
  • Leeds City Council 
  • Herefordshire Veterans Support Centre   
  • The Veterans Contact Point 
  • Loughborough Wellbeing Centre 
  • CVS Lincolnshire 
  • Citizens Advice Rushmoor 
  • The Lantern Trust (Weymouth) 
  • Wiltshire Council 
  • Westmorland & Furness Council 
  • Dover District Council 
  • East Durham Veterans Trust – will receive additional funding in round 2 

Read more about VALOUR

items.title: Government backs local journalism with £6 million funding while careers campaign reaches thousands of youngsters
items.summary: The ‘Inspiring the Future’ campaign, which encourages children to consider careers in journalism, has reached more than 11,000 students and engaged with more than 100 schools This all forms part of the Government’s Local Media Action Plan,
items.bodyHtml:
• The ‘Inspiring the Future’ campaign, which encourages children to consider careers in journalism, has reached more than 11,000 students and engaged with more than 100 schools 
  • This all forms part of the Government’s Local Media Action Plan, backing the vital role of local media in communities across the country

Fifty organisations are set to benefit from the government’s £6 million Local News Fund, helping to ensure people can continue to benefit from trusted, high-quality local journalism.  

With audiences moving online and consuming their news through an increasingly diverse range of sources, the role of local journalism has never been more important, especially as the Government seeks to devolve power to a local level , given its integral role in holding power to account and tackling mis- and disinformation online.  

Central to the Government’s ‘Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan’, the Local News Fund aims to strengthen communities and social cohesion, rebuild social trust, and support local growth by supporting local journalism.  

The majority of funding has been awarded to local print and online news outlets and independent local TV and radio stations, who received grants of up to £125,000. The money will be used to invest in community outreach projects, digital tools, apps and new multimedia services that can help these organisations reach new and younger audiences while developing more sustainable sources of income. These grants have been evenly distributed across England and Wales, providing funding support for local journalism in every region.  

The remainder of the Fund has been awarded to seven organisations, including software developers and major industry players, to develop infrastructure that can benefit the sector as a whole, with grants of up to £275,000 awarded.  

Media Minister Ian Murray said: 

For decades our local media has remained among the most trusted sources of news. But as the media landscape has become more complex, many outlets have been forced to reduce their numbers or even close. I am determined not to leave local journalism to collapse. This government knows it is critical to communities and fosters a self-confident nation that everyone feels part of. 

Through the Local News Fund we are taking action to help newsrooms innovate and adapt their business models for the online world, while incentivising and encouraging the production of high-quality, trustworthy news that Britain’s towns and villages deserve and rely on.

Another key measure in the Local Media Action Plan is the ‘Inspiring the Future’ careers campaign, joint-funded by the News Media Association (NMA), which connects local media employers and journalists with schools to inspire the next generation of reporters. This initial six-month campaign focused on the North West, targeting schools in more deprived areas, with 79% having above national average free school meal eligibility, and the Government will seek to roll it out nationally subject to evaluation and funding. 

Theo Bamber, Chief Executive, News Media Association, said:  

Alongside DCMS and Education and Employers, we are very pleased to have supported the ‘Inspiring the Future’ pilot connecting local media professionals with the next generation of talent. 

As power is devolved out of Westminster, the role of local news media holding power to account will become even more important. This initiative will support that by helping young people understand our industry, the benefits of a career in local media, and the vital role it plays in local communities across the country.

This Journalism Matters Week, an annual campaign run by the NMA that showcases the industry as a key part of the UK’s national infrastructure, the National Committee for the Safety of Journalists will meet to agree on a refreshed National Action Plan, reaffirming this Government’s commitment to journalist safety and tackling obstacles to news gathering which is another pillar of the Local Media Action Plan. Bringing together representatives from government, journalism, policing, prosecution services and civil society, the aim of the National Action Plan is to set out how the safety of journalists can be protected in the UK. 

ENDS  

Notes to Editors: 

Quotes in support of the Local News Fund: 

Polly Curtis, Co-Chair of the Local News Fund Steering Board, said: 

This fund showed there is incredible talent and capacity across the country to revitalise local news when communities are so desperately in need of trusted sources of information. The solutions are out there and this fund could go even further in the future to help journalists across communities to become ever more sustainable. 

We want to thank everyone who applied and encourage applications to the next round in 2027. There are too many news deserts in this country and this fund is starting to make a difference.

Jeremy Clifford, Co-Chair of the Local News Fund Steering Board, said: 

We were delighted with the volume of bids that came in from publishers and tech developers for the local news fund which underlined the critical importance of this initiative in helping the industry to design and implement changes that will support sustainability. I would like to thank everyone who took the time to submit their ideas. 

However, the volume and quality of the bids presented a major headache for the Steering Board - how to make the limited funding reach as far as possible. I am confident the awards made by the DCMS will go a long way in helping to shape the future for so many publishers. My personal hope is that we will see a lot of collaboration and sharing of knowledge to benefit the wider news industry. 

Unfortunately, given the limited funds, it also meant we had to turn down many worthwhile and quality bids. I would urge the DCMS to source more funding in 2027 so those publishers who did submit bids can reapply and re-enter their plans - so many of which merit funding.

Laura Davison, NUJ general secretary, said:  

The NUJ warmly welcomes the government taking active steps to support local journalism. The union has long campaigned for government grants to preserve the sector so it is positive to see funding for a range of outlets to support jobs, greater local coverage and public interest journalism. We note that other projects focus on ‘responsible’ uses of AI in newsrooms, and the union will monitor the use and impact of these grants in consultation with members.  

While we’re excited to see what difference the funding makes, many of our members remain deeply worried about their livelihoods and the state of the industry. The level of interest in the Fund demonstrates just how much the sector has been crying out for support. We hope to see further government investment to really turn the tide.

Joanne Forbes, NCTJ chief executive, said:  

Local journalism matters enormously. It holds power to account and tells stories that would otherwise go untold. AI could make a real difference to newsrooms already struggling with limited resources, but we must protect the quality and trust that good journalism depends on. 

We’re grateful to DCMS and the Local News Fund steering board for backing this project. It will bring publishers and journalists together to develop practical guidance and training to help newsrooms make the most of AI, from the biggest to the  smallest.

On the Local News Fund: 

  • Applicants were assessed by a Local News Fund Steering Board, composed of independent industry experts, and were required to demonstrate an established track record of providing local news in England or Wales.  
  • The Local News Fund is competitive, with all bids assessed according to technical and strategic criteria set out in the Fund advert and application form. A technical assessment of bids was conducted by the Government Grants Managed Service, and a strategic assessment conducted by the Local News Fund Steering Board composed of independent industry experts to guide final decisions on awards by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. Bids were assessed according to factors including their overall quality, deliverability and likely impact over the short and long term. 
  • Bidders also had to meet eligibility criteria, by demonstrating a sustained track record in the provision of local journalism over at least the past 12 months, and by demonstrating that their content is editorially accountable. 
  • Next year, £1 million from the Fund will be dedicated to tackling local ‘news deserts’, areas that have no dedicated local print, online, TV or radio outlet, in collaboration with key community stakeholders and the Fund’s Steering Board. Up to a further £5 million will also be made available next year to continue supporting financial sustainability and innovation in the sector. 

On the Local News Fund Steering Board: 

  • The government appointed the members of a Local News Fund Steering Board on 15 June following a fair and open recruitment process. The purpose of the steering board is to play an advisory role in providing independent expertise and objective advice to the government in the decision-making process for distribution of funding under the Local News Fund. 
  • This includes a role in setting the bidding and eligibility criteria for the Local News Fund. In convening this board, the government aims to benefit from a wide range of experience of the local media sector and related industries. This will help to ensure value for money in the distribution of funding and that the best bids are selected for Local News Fund grants, for the benefit of local media and the communities that they serve. 
  • The steering board comprises eight members, including two co-chairs. The DCMS Senior Responsible Owner for the Fund also attends meetings. The Board may also agree to invite others to attend on an ad hoc basis to provide specialist knowledge if and when required. The membership is:

  • Polly Curtis (co-chair): Chief Executive at Demos - previous experience at the Guardian, Huffpost UK, Tortoise Media and PA Media

  • Agnes Gulyas: Professor of Media and Communications, Canterbury Christ Church University 
  • Jaldeep Katwala: Director, Sir Lenny Henry Centre for Media Diversity, Birmingham City University; - previously Network Manager for the Public Interest News Foundation and Non Executive Director of the Bristol Cable 
  • Owen Meredith: Managing Director of Public Policy, DMGT - previously CEO of the News Media Association 
  • Lorna Willis: CEO of Techskills - previously CEO at Archant Community Media

The ‘Inspiring the Future’ campaign, which encourages children to consider careers in journalism, has reached more than 11,000 students and engaged with more than 100 schools 
  This all forms part of the Government’s Local Media Action Plan, backing the vital role of local media in communities across the country


Fifty organisations are set to benefit from the government’s £6 million Local News Fund, helping to ensure people can continue to benefit from trusted, high-quality local journalism.  

With audiences moving online and consuming their news through an increasingly diverse range of sources, the role of local journalism has never been more important, especially as the Government seeks to devolve power to a local level , given its integral role in holding power to account and tackling mis- and disinformation online.  

Central to the Government’s ‘Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan’, the Local News Fund aims to strengthen communities and social cohesion, rebuild social trust, and support local growth by supporting local journalism.  

The majority of funding has been awarded to local print and online news outlets and independent local TV and radio stations, who received grants of up to £125,000. The money will be used to invest in community outreach projects, digital tools, apps and new multimedia services that can help these organisations reach new and younger audiences while developing more sustainable sources of income. These grants have been evenly distributed across England and Wales, providing funding support for local journalism in every region.  

The remainder of the Fund has been awarded to seven organisations, including software developers and major industry players, to develop infrastructure that can benefit the sector as a whole, with grants of up to £275,000 awarded.  

Media Minister Ian Murray said: 


  For decades our local media has remained among the most trusted sources of news. But as the media landscape has become more complex, many outlets have been forced to reduce their numbers or even close. I am determined not to leave local journalism to collapse. This government knows it is critical to communities and fosters a self-confident nation that everyone feels part of. 

  Through the Local News Fund we are taking action to help newsrooms innovate and adapt their business models for the online world, while incentivising and encouraging the production of high-quality, trustworthy news that Britain’s towns and villages deserve and rely on.


Another key measure in the Local Media Action Plan is the ‘Inspiring the Future’ careers campaign, joint-funded by the News Media Association (NMA), which connects local media employers and journalists with schools to inspire the next generation of reporters. This initial six-month campaign focused on the North West, targeting schools in more deprived areas, with 79% having above national average free school meal eligibility, and the Government will seek to roll it out nationally subject to evaluation and funding. 

Theo Bamber, Chief Executive, News Media Association, said:  


  Alongside DCMS and Education and Employers, we are very pleased to have supported the ‘Inspiring the Future’ pilot connecting local media professionals with the next generation of talent. 

  As power is devolved out of Westminster, the role of local news media holding power to account will become even more important. This initiative will support that by helping young people understand our industry, the benefits of a career in local media, and the vital role it plays in local communities across the country.


This Journalism Matters Week, an annual campaign run by the NMA that showcases the industry as a key part of the UK’s national infrastructure, the National Committee for the Safety of Journalists will meet to agree on a refreshed National Action Plan, reaffirming this Government’s commitment to journalist safety and tackling obstacles to news gathering which is another pillar of the Local Media Action Plan. Bringing together representatives from government, journalism, policing, prosecution services and civil society, the aim of the National Action Plan is to set out how the safety of journalists can be protected in the UK. 

ENDS  

Notes to Editors: 

Quotes in support of the Local News Fund: 

Polly Curtis, Co-Chair of the Local News Fund Steering Board, said: 


  This fund showed there is incredible talent and capacity across the country to revitalise local news when communities are so desperately in need of trusted sources of information. The solutions are out there and this fund could go even further in the future to help journalists across communities to become ever more sustainable. 

  We want to thank everyone who applied and encourage applications to the next round in 2027. There are too many news deserts in this country and this fund is starting to make a difference.


Jeremy Clifford, Co-Chair of the Local News Fund Steering Board, said: 


  We were delighted with the volume of bids that came in from publishers and tech developers for the local news fund which underlined the critical importance of this initiative in helping the industry to design and implement changes that will support sustainability. I would like to thank everyone who took the time to submit their ideas. 

  However, the volume and quality of the bids presented a major headache for the Steering Board - how to make the limited funding reach as far as possible. I am confident the awards made by the DCMS will go a long way in helping to shape the future for so many publishers. My personal hope is that we will see a lot of collaboration and sharing of knowledge to benefit the wider news industry. 

  Unfortunately, given the limited funds, it also meant we had to turn down many worthwhile and quality bids. I would urge the DCMS to source more funding in 2027 so those publishers who did submit bids can reapply and re-enter their plans - so many of which merit funding.


Laura Davison, NUJ general secretary, said:  


  The NUJ warmly welcomes the government taking active steps to support local journalism. The union has long campaigned for government grants to preserve the sector so it is positive to see funding for a range of outlets to support jobs, greater local coverage and public interest journalism. We note that other projects focus on ‘responsible’ uses of AI in newsrooms, and the union will monitor the use and impact of these grants in consultation with members.  

  While we’re excited to see what difference the funding makes, many of our members remain deeply worried about their livelihoods and the state of the industry. The level of interest in the Fund demonstrates just how much the sector has been crying out for support. We hope to see further government investment to really turn the tide.


Joanne Forbes, NCTJ chief executive, said:  


  Local journalism matters enormously. It holds power to account and tells stories that would otherwise go untold. AI could make a real difference to newsrooms already struggling with limited resources, but we must protect the quality and trust that good journalism depends on. 

  We’re grateful to DCMS and the Local News Fund steering board for backing this project. It will bring publishers and journalists together to develop practical guidance and training to help newsrooms make the most of AI, from the biggest to the  smallest.

On the Local News Fund: 


  Applicants were assessed by a Local News Fund Steering Board, composed of independent industry experts, and were required to demonstrate an established track record of providing local news in England or Wales.  
  The Local News Fund is competitive, with all bids assessed according to technical and strategic criteria set out in the Fund advert and application form. A technical assessment of bids was conducted by the Government Grants Managed Service, and a strategic assessment conducted by the Local News Fund Steering Board composed of independent industry experts to guide final decisions on awards by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. Bids were assessed according to factors including their overall quality, deliverability and likely impact over the short and long term. 
  Bidders also had to meet eligibility criteria, by demonstrating a sustained track record in the provision of local journalism over at least the past 12 months, and by demonstrating that their content is editorially accountable. 
  Next year, £1 million from the Fund will be dedicated to tackling local ‘news deserts’, areas that have no dedicated local print, online, TV or radio outlet, in collaboration with key community stakeholders and the Fund’s Steering Board. Up to a further £5 million will also be made available next year to continue supporting financial sustainability and innovation in the sector. 


On the Local News Fund Steering Board: 


  The government appointed the members of a Local News Fund Steering Board on 15 June following a fair and open recruitment process. The purpose of the steering board is to play an advisory role in providing independent expertise and objective advice to the government in the decision-making process for distribution of funding under the Local News Fund. 
  This includes a role in setting the bidding and eligibility criteria for the Local News Fund. In convening this board, the government aims to benefit from a wide range of experience of the local media sector and related industries. This will help to ensure value for money in the distribution of funding and that the best bids are selected for Local News Fund grants, for the benefit of local media and the communities that they serve. 
  The steering board comprises eight members, including two co-chairs. The DCMS Senior Responsible Owner for the Fund also attends meetings. The Board may also agree to invite others to attend on an ad hoc basis to provide specialist knowledge if and when required. The membership is:  
  Jeremy Clifford (co-chair): Executive Media Consultant, Chrysalis Transformations - previously at JPI Media and Archant 
  Polly Curtis (co-chair): Chief Executive at Demos - previous experience at the Guardian, Huffpost UK, Tortoise Media and PA Media 
  George Adelman: Managing Director and Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, FT Strategies 
  John Baron: editor and cofounder of the West Leeds Dispatch; Advisory Board Member of the Independent Community News Network 
  Agnes Gulyas: Professor of Media and Communications, Canterbury Christ Church University 
  Jaldeep Katwala: Director, Sir Lenny Henry Centre for Media Diversity, Birmingham City University; - previously Network Manager for the Public Interest News Foundation and Non Executive Director of the Bristol Cable 
  Owen Meredith: Managing Director of Public Policy, DMGT - previously CEO of the News Media Association 
  Lorna Willis: CEO of Techskills - previously CEO at Archant Community Media

items.title: 'First Dates' maître d's charity unveils new restaurant in Staffordshire women's prison
items.summary: The Right Course, a charity founded by Channel 4 ‘First Dates’ maître d’ Fred Sirieix, opens its first restaurant in a UK women’s prison. Backed by Hilton and the Government’s Hospitality Support Fund, it will train prisoners in hospitality
items.bodyHtml:
• The Right Course, a charity founded by Channel 4 ‘First Dates’ maître d’ Fred Sirieix, opens its first restaurant in a UK women’s prison.
  • Backed by Hilton and the Government’s Hospitality Support Fund, it will train prisoners in hospitality skills to build genuine pathways to employment.
  • Programme will also provide a new supply of trained staff for the hospitality sector, helping cut long running shortages and reducing reoffending by giving prisoners skills and employment opportunities.

Restaurants, pubs and hotels across the West Midlands could gain access to a new supply of hospitality trained staff thanks to the opening of a new training restaurant inside a women’s prison at HMP Drake Hall by charity The Right Course.

Founded by maître d’ Fred Sirieix, the new restaurant ‘Flavours Unlocked’ will provide industry-standard training, recognised qualifications and direct links with employment, giving participants a pathway into secure work once they leave prison, reducing reoffending and making our streets safer.

This includes through companies such as hotel group Hilton, which has contributed expert trainers and shared its practices to ensure participants are trained to the highest possible standard. The programme is also backed by funding from the Government’s £1.5m Hospitality Fund operating over 2026-27, with additional funding to support training from the Government’s new Hospitality Grant Scheme.

The opening was attended on Monday by Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden, as well as Sirieix and other prominent leaders helping turn around lives and hospitality businesses.

Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden said:

Hospitality is a vital part of Britain’s economy, but businesses need access to skilled, dedicated staff to succeed.

“The Right Course is a fantastic charity, improving the lives of its participants. Working with charities and employers, we are determined to unlock talent wherever it is found and allow people to build a better future for themselves, businesses and their communities.”

Catherine McKinnell, Minister for Prisons, Probation and Reducing Reoffending, said:

Prison must be a punishment, but it must also give offenders the tools to turn their backs on crime for good.

Education and employment are vital to that mission, and programmes like The Right Course show what can be achieved when prisons, charities and businesses work together to help offenders build better lives .

That means fewer people reoffending, fewer victims and safer streets.

Fred Sirieix, Founder and Trustee of The Right Course said:

By working in partnership with industry leaders like Hilton, and the prison regime, we are creating the right environment for our learners to turn their lives around, to gain the confidence, skills and aspirations needed to positively contribute to society.” 

I want our graduates to be the best so that our employer partners snap them up and see them as valued members of their team. It’s up to our new learners to seize this opportunity.

Stephen Cassidy, Senior Vice President, UK & Ireland, Hilton, said:

At Hilton, our mission is to create opportunities for all and break down barriers to employment.

Through our partnership with The Right Course, Flavours Unlocked is helping bring that commitment to life by giving women in custody practical hospitality training, industry skills and a clearer route into work. 

For our industry, it is also a powerful reminder that talent can be found in many different places, and that with the right support, hospitality can open the door to meaningful, long-term careers.

Hospitality is a vital UK industry, a cornerstone of all our lives. However, the sector faces numerous challenges that requires multiple approaches for it to thrive. The Right Course offers one practical way to provide the sector with a pipeline of trained and engaged staff ready to work, while giving people who have spent time in prison a second chance, cutting reoffending and helping them build transferrable skills such as communication, customer service and teamworking.

items.title: Major upgrades at Beacon Barracks now underway
items.summary: A ground-breaking ceremony has been held to mark the start of construction on £206m of new and improved infrastructure at Beacon Barracks, Stafford. The new infrastructure will support the Royal Engineers, Royal Military Police, Intelligenc
items.bodyHtml:
A ground-breaking ceremony has been held to mark the start of construction on £206m of new and improved infrastructure at Beacon Barracks, Stafford.

The new infrastructure will support the Royal Engineers, Royal Military Police, Intelligence Corps and Joint Military Command - Centre, directly contributing to their ability to carry out their roles. 

The project, which is being delivered for the Army under the Defence Estate Optimisation (DEO) Portfolio, will prepare the barracks for the relocation of the Royal Engineers Works Groups from Chetwynd Barracks in Chilwell, and 174 Provost Company and 262 Military Intelligence Section from Venning and Parsons Barracks in Telford, from 2029. 

The Defence Infrastructure Organisation (DIO) contracted Bovis to deliver the works, which include two new Single Living Accommodation blocks, each with 116 bedspaces. New workspaces will be built for the Royal Engineers, Intelligence Corps and Joint Military Command - Centre, and a new Police Station will be built for the Royal Military Police.  

New storage facilities will be built including a new armoury and several existing buildings will be refurbished to provide further offices, stores, garages, and training facilities. New-build designs include air source heat pumps, photovoltaic systems, rainwater recovery systems, efficient ventilation with heat recovery systems, and efficient lighting systems. 

Throughout construction, Bovis will deliver a social value programme, including creating pathways into construction careers with the team facilitating apprenticeships and work placements. 

Belinda Lunn, DEO Army Programme Director, and Major Davies, Officer Commanding Stafford Support Unit, ceremonially broke ground on the site of one of the new buildings on 29 October. 

Belinda Lunn, Defence Estate Optimisation – Army Programme Director, said: 

The start of the main construction phase at Beacon Barracks is a significant milestone in delivering modern, fit-for-purpose facilities for our people. This investment will enhance the day-to-day experience of personnel, strengthen operational effectiveness, and help ensure the Defence estate is used as efficiently as possible.

Warren Webster, DIO’s Major Programmes and Projects (Army) Director, said: 

It was a real pleasure to be at Beacon Barracks today, where I’ve witnessed first-hand the excellent collaboration between all of our partners.  

Our collective efforts are the foundation of successful delivery of this major investment in the site, allowing it to host additional personnel and directly contributing to Defence capability.

Major Davies, Officer Commanding Stafford Support Unit, said: 

This marks the start of the latest of a series of significant investments in Beacon Barracks over the last decade or so. We are looking forward to welcoming colleagues from the Royal Engineers, Royal Military Police, Intelligence Corps and Joint Military Command Centre and will work with our partners in DIO and Bovis to ensure the new and upgraded infrastructure being prepared for them meets their needs.

Andrew Mackay, Managing Director Public Sector, Bovis said:  

We are proud to be delivering these important upgrades to Beacon Barracks for the DIO. Through our longstanding relationship with the DIO, we understand the importance of providing modern, high-quality infrastructure and facilities that support our Armed Forces and their families. We look forward to progressing this project and delivering a lasting legacy for those who live and work at the barracks.

Once vacated, the Chetwynd Barracks, Venning Barracks and Parsons Barracks sites will be redeveloped. Nearly 1,300 new homes are planned at Chetwynd Barracks, the largest of the three sites.

Belinda Lunn, Defence Estate Optimisation – Army Programme Director, said: 


  The start of the main construction phase at Beacon Barracks is a significant milestone in delivering modern, fit-for-purpose facilities for our people. This investment will enhance the day-to-day experience of personnel, strengthen operational effectiveness, and help ensure the Defence estate is used as efficiently as possible.


Warren Webster, DIO’s Major Programmes and Projects (Army) Director, said: 


  It was a real pleasure to be at Beacon Barracks today, where I’ve witnessed first-hand the excellent collaboration between all of our partners.  

  Our collective efforts are the foundation of successful delivery of this major investment in the site, allowing it to host additional personnel and directly contributing to Defence capability.


Major Davies, Officer Commanding Stafford Support Unit, said: 


  This marks the start of the latest of a series of significant investments in Beacon Barracks over the last decade or so. We are looking forward to welcoming colleagues from the Royal Engineers, Royal Military Police, Intelligence Corps and Joint Military Command Centre and will work with our partners in DIO and Bovis to ensure the new and upgraded infrastructure being prepared for them meets their needs.


Andrew Mackay, Managing Director Public Sector, Bovis said:  


  We are proud to be delivering these important upgrades to Beacon Barracks for the DIO. Through our longstanding relationship with the DIO, we understand the importance of providing modern, high-quality infrastructure and facilities that support our Armed Forces and their families. We look forward to progressing this project and delivering a lasting legacy for those who live and work at the barracks.


Once vacated, the Chetwynd Barracks, Venning Barracks and Parsons Barracks sites will be redeveloped. Nearly 1,300 new homes are planned at Chetwynd Barracks, the largest of the three sites.

items.title: Lost stone rises up in Dorset's Valley of Stones Nature Reserve
items.summary: A mysterious 5-foot stone, hidden for generations, has been raised once more in one of England’s most extraordinary prehistoric landscapes. The rock, which has been named the Bride Stone, was brought back into view at the Valley of Stones N
items.bodyHtml:
A mysterious 5-foot stone, hidden for generations, has been raised once more in one of England’s most extraordinary prehistoric landscapes.

The rock, which has been named the Bride Stone, was brought back into view at the Valley of Stones National Nature Reserve (NNR), thanks to a joint effort by Natural England, community archaeology company Past Participate, and local volunteers.

The stone emerged during scrub clearance carried out as part of the management of the reserve. Standing apart from the scattered boulders that give the Valley of Stones its name, archaeological excavation by Past Participate suggests it once formed part of a Stone Age tomb.

Raising the sarsen stone (credit Catherine Roberts)

Rob Beard, reserve manager for Natural England, said:

I’m thrilled to have the Bride Stone standing over the valley. It’s a visual testament to all the similar monuments that have been lost. Its return adds another chapter to the story of a landscape where nature and human history have been intertwined for millennia.

The stone stands at the heart of a prehistoric landscape, surrounded by stone circles, standing stones, chambered tombs and barrows. It will, I hope, inspire people to visit the Valley of Stones National Nature Reserve and evoke the spirit of this special, secret landscape.

Dr Anne Teather, director of Past Participate, said:

The repositioning of this stone celebrates the exceptional discoveries that have been made recently in the Valley of Stones, and it will serve as a focal point for visitors to this area for decades to come. The Bride Stone represents a tangible reminder of the numerous ancient monuments that have been lost, dismantled or destroyed in this landscape.

The extraordinary scattering of large blocks of silicified sandstone, known as sarsen boulders, were shaped by Ice Age weathering. Some of these ancient stones are thought to have been used by people in Neolithic times to create monuments such as standing stones and stone circles.

National Nature Reserves protect England’s most important habitats, species, and geology, delivering nature recovery at a landscape scale. That’s why Natural England is delivering the King’s Series of National Nature Reserves, which will create or extend 25 NNRs by 2027, leaving a legacy for people and nature.

Background:

  • Photos are available from Natural England South and South West press office, which it shares with the Envrionemnt Agency:  communications_sw@environment-agency.gov.uk .
  • The work has been undertaken by Past Participate and Historic England, funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund and supported by Natural England, who manage the reserve.
  • In 2022, a rare 6,000-year-old polishing stone, or “polissoir,” was uncovered at this site. This sparked much of the research since.
  • The “Living Amongst the Sarsens” project is made possible with the National Lottery Heritage Fund. Thanks to National Lottery players, Past Participate has been able to examine the archaeological heritage of the Valley of Stones landscape. Past Participate is grateful to National Lottery players for their support.
  • For information about the site visit: Valley of Stones

Contact Natural England South and South West press office on 0800 028 2484 or email: communications_sw@environment-agency.gov.uk .
