items.title: New visitor levy powers to put money back into local communities
items.summary: Local leaders are a step closer to getting new powers to invest more in high streets, cultural sites and other attractions that make communities great places to live, work and visit. This Visitor Levy Bill, introduced in the House of Common
items.bodyHtml:
Local leaders are a step closer to getting new powers to invest more in high streets, cultural sites and other attractions that make communities great places to live, work and visit.

This Visitor Levy Bill, introduced in the House of Commons today, marks the most significant step in making fiscal devolution a reality, giving mayors and leaders who know their areas best the ability to introduce a small fee on overnight stays. Money raised through the levy will stay in the local area, giving communities investment in the places and services used by visitors and residents.

Mayors who choose to introduce a levy will be able to invest in what makes their regions special and improve the visitor experience from better high streets to public spaces – including public toilets and parks, cultural events and security and destination promotion. Money raised from visitors will stay in the area, helping attract more visitors, support local businesses and improve places for the people who live there too.

But the government will continue to protect lower cost family breaks by requiring the levy to be charged as a percentage rate of the cost of accommodation, rather than as a flat fee, meaning those choosing cheaper accommodation will pay less. Ten mayors have also committed that any levy introduced in their areas would be no higher than 5%, providing certainty for visitors and businesses while preserving local choice.

This piece of legislation builds on the significant commitment made at the Budget to drive good growth in every postcode, including through the government’s high streets strategy and wider plans to rewire the state, and shift power from Whitehall back to local communities.

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities, and Local Government Angela Rayner said:

Millions of people visit our wonderful towns and cities each year, and it’s right that our communities should be able to feel the benefit of that footfall.

Every pound raised through these levies will stay in the local area. Whether that’s better transport, thriving high streets, or more attractions that keep visitors coming back.

This is about giving mayors and local leaders the choice to invest back into what matters most to local people, while protecting lower-cost stays and making sure businesses have their say.

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester said:  

In Greater Manchester, we campaigned for an Overnight Visitor Levy to boost our region and give mayors the powers to raise additional funds through a modest levy on overnight stays. This would give us access to new funding that we can reinvest into our places to support our visitor economy, improve public services and drive good growth.  

In Manchester we pioneered a similar scheme in recent years which has been a resounding success. Our industry-led City Visitor Charge has shown that the model can work, generating millions of pounds that has been invested back into things like street cleaning and our work to attract major events, with widespread support from the hospitality sector.   

The Overnight Visitor Levy also represents a major moment for devolution and a further vote of confidence in the ability of mayors and local leaders to make decisions in the best interests of their places. It means we can attract more events, make our region more welcoming for tourists with cleaner streets and invest in long term projects like extending the tram network. 

The important thing now is that this is genuinely devolved. Any levy needs to work for our city region and be shaped with our councils, businesses and the local hospitality sector, with the money raised here being used for the benefit of people and businesses in Greater Manchester.

David Skaith, Mayor of York and North Yorkshire, said: 

We’re home to historic towns and cities, two of the UK’s best National Parks and a coastline brimming with character. 

There’s something for everyone, and we welcome more than 40 million visitors every year. That’s why an Overnight Visitor Levy will be a total gamechanger for our county. 

Investing in York and North Yorkshire’s cities, towns and villages to make them a better place to visit, and to live in, is at the heart of why I will be introducing a Levy in our county.

Steve Rotheram, Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, said:  

This is something I’ve been calling for over many years, so I’m really pleased the government is taking forward plans to give Mayors the power to introduce a visitor levy locally. 

Our visitor economy is already worth more than £6.8bn a year and supports more than 55,000 jobs across the Liverpool City Region. A modest levy on overnight stays could potentially raise up to £18m a year – money that would stay here and be reinvested directly into the events, culture, experiences and infrastructure that bring millions of visitors to our region. 

Visitor levy mechanisms are often used in many great cities across the globe to improve the visitor offer and attract even more people to enjoy the experience. It would give us more money to support the things that make our visitor economy such a success, while helping our businesses and communities to benefit from its continued growth. 

We’ve shown time and again that local people know what our area needs far better than someone sitting behind a desk in Whitehall. I look forward to working with government as these powers are developed to make sure we get a system that is fair, workable and delivers the greatest possible benefit for our region.  

Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said:  

After years of lobbying, I wholeheartedly welcome this Bill, which would give London greater freedom to raise and invest new funding locally.  

A modest levy could support our hugely successful visitor economy, creating benefits for Londoners, businesses and visitors alike, as well as helping to cement London’s reputation as one of the world’s leading destinations.

Claire Ward, Mayor of the East Midlands, said:  

We have so much to be proud of across the East Midlands. I want more people to discover our fantastic towns and cities, our attractions and everything else our region has to offer. And I want the communities that welcome them to share in the benefits. 

An Overnight Visitor Levy would give us the chance to put more money back into the places that make our region what it is. That means supporting our attractions and independent businesses and helping our high streets and town centres attract even more people. 

It’s important that local people and businesses are part of this conversation from the start. There will be full consultation before a levy is introduced, giving people the opportunity to help shape how it works and where the money raised could make the biggest difference. Those who know their communities best should have a real say in how they benefit.

Tracy Brabin, Mayor of West Yorkshire, said: 

Bradford’s year as UK City of Culture proved what we can achieve when we invest in our visitor economy, which is why I’m supportive of these powers to ask those who stay overnight to make a small contribution to support our great region. 

This could be invested in bringing more gigs, performances, art and sport to our world-recognised venues, making our streets cleaner and safer, introducing night buses, and opening up more creative careers for our young people. 

I’ll work closely with council leaders, businesses and our communities to ensure we get this right and build a brighter region that works for all.

Helen Godwin, Mayor of the West of England, said: 

Tens of millions of visitors spend billions of pounds in the West of England each year, brought here by amazing attractions like the Roman Baths, Clifton Suspension Bridge, Weston-super-Mare’s Grand Pier, and Bristol Zoo Project. And there’s much more on the way for our exciting region, particularly with the Aviva Arena opening in a few years’ time. 

The overnight visitor levy will allow us to invest more money raised here right back into the West, like other places already do around the world. That could well mean transport and tourism improvements, helping communities to see and feel a difference from devolution.

Kim McGuinness, Mayor of the North East, said:  

The North East has vibrant cities, stunning coast and countryside in Northumberland and Durham and a welcome that keeps people coming back. A levy here will mean we can compete with rival destinations which already raise money from visitors. 

We want to double the scale of our tourist economy and create thousands of new jobs as we do so. A small amount raised on each overnight stay means we can bring more major festivals to our region, support brilliant local events, improve the visitor experience and showcase the North East to the world.

Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, said:  

The Government’s commitment to fiscal devolution will be a gamechanger, giving Mayors more freedom to invest in the sectors we know will deliver the economic growth and jobs our regions need. More than 100 million people come to the West Midlands every year to enjoy our rich heritage, exciting entertainment venues and world-class sport and cultural events, and that supports 150,000 local jobs. I want our visitor economy to be able to keep raising its game with new and even more exciting reasons for people to keep coming here.

Oliver Coppard, Mayor of South Yorkshire, said: 

OVL is a big step in putting power in the right place, allowing people that know their communities best to take significant decisions about the future of that place. Whether we take the decision to implement the levy or not, we now - rightly - control that decision. That’s a radical step and one I’m pleased to see government taking in tandem with us as Mayors.

Karin Hindsbo, Interim Director of Tate said: 

These powers could be transformative for the UK’s cultural venues. Museums and galleries are at the heart of this country’s offer to tourists, attracting millions of people to British towns and cities every year. Overnight visitor levies should provide vital support for these cultural spaces and help them deliver the countless benefits they bring to local communities.

The appeal of a city is never simply its hotels, attractions or events; it lies in the combination of its cultural life, public realm, creativity, heritage and everyday experiences. A modest contribution from overnight visitors can help destinations reinvest in the very assets and experiences that underpin their appeal. The challenge – and the opportunity for the UK – is to ensure that this investment is strategic, transparent and benefits both visitors and the communities who live there.

Tourism makes an enormous contribution to York and North Yorkshire, supporting businesses, employment and communities across the region. Any future levy must therefore be carefully designed, with meaningful engagement across the tourism and hospitality sector, alongside residents and other stakeholders.

Historically we are a city which embraces visitors from the world over. We’ve already seen through the Accommodation Business Improvement District (ABID) model the benefits for the visitor economy by being able to invest in marketing and cultural activities.

The Bill sets out new details today on how the levy will work, including who will be protected, how decisions will be made locally and how the rules will be enforced. The levy will only apply to the first 28 consecutive days of a stay, as longer stays count as long-term accommodation.

Protections will ensure occasional hosts, such as people who only rent out a spare room from time to time, will only pay the levy if they earn above a set amount. Local leaders and mayors will also be able to adjust this threshold to reflect their local tourism market.

The new powers to introduce a levy will bring England in line with places like Germany, Italy, the United States, the Netherlands and Canada, and let communities make the most of the tens of million overnight stays in England every year. 

The government recognises the pressures facing hospitality businesses and has designed the levy so that decisions are taken locally, businesses must be consulted before a scheme is introduced and lower-cost stays face proportionately lower charges. Money raised will stay in the area and can be reinvested in the transport, high streets, public spaces, events and attractions that bring visitors in and support the local visitor economy.

Those wanting to introduce a levy will first need to publish a draft plan and an impact assessment setting out the expected impact on the local economy, businesses and visitors, alongside the proposed rate, threshold, exemptions and how the money will be spent. They will then be required to consult local people and businesses seek the necessary agreement within their Strategic Authority, consider their views before taking a final decision, publish the responses and issue final versions of both documents, so they are transparent and accountable.

Combined or Strategic Authority Members can suggest changes to the plan, which mayors will need to consider. In Foundation Strategic Authorities, a levy can only go ahead with unanimous support. Authorities with a levy will also need to publish an annual report on what they raise, what they spend and their future spending plans.

The government has today confirmed national exemptions for student accommodation, care homes, children’s homes, and school boarding houses. Mayors and local leaders will also be able to set additional limited local exemptions, like for camping pitches.  

Temporary accommodation, shelters and refuges will not be charged either, because they provide vital homes for vulnerable people rather than for visitors.

Hotels and other accommodation providers will be responsible for accounting for and paying the levy and the government will give them guidance on how to register, pay and report. Strategic authorities will also help providers get it right, and it will be up to local leaders on how they use their enforcement powers proportionately. These are standard tax powers, in line with those that apply to national self-assessed taxes.

All of this action builds on top of the measures announced at the Budget to back businesses, with all retail, hospitality and leisure properties seeing their business rates either frozen in real terms, reduced or cut to zero.

The cross-government high street strategy, Hope On the High Street, also sets out the approach to backing town centres and helping high streets thrive again. This includes establishing a ‘high streets first’ principle which will encourage public bodies to consider the wider benefits their estate decisions can bring to high streets and local growth.

For more information: 

  • The United Kingdom has invested less in its future than any other G7 country over the past three decades. Giving local leaders greater control over funding and investment decisions will help unlock opportunities that have too often been overlooked by a Whitehall-led approach. 
  • According to the latest Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the level of national taxes collected at the ‘sub-national level’ is far below the European Union average and is the lowest in the G7. In contrast, countries such as France, Japan, and the USA have much higher shares of local tax collection, enabling greater local investment. 
  • OECD research has also found that enhanced fiscal decentralisation is associated with higher economic growth – suggesting that doubling the share of tax or spending controlled by subnational governments is associated with an increase in national GDP per capita by 3% on average. 
  • VisitBritain) found that there were 40m inbound visits to the UK last year with the visitors spending a total of £35bn and staying for a total of 293 million nights in the UK.
  • There are 89.6 million overnight trips made by British residents, spending £27.3 billion and generating around 260 million overnight stays.

Local leaders are a step closer to getting new powers to invest more in high streets, cultural sites and other attractions that make communities great places to live, work and visit.

This Visitor Levy Bill, introduced in the House of Commons today, marks the most significant step in making fiscal devolution a reality, giving mayors and leaders who know their areas best the ability to introduce a small fee on overnight stays. Money raised through the levy will stay in the local area, giving communities investment in the places and services used by visitors and residents.

Mayors who choose to introduce a levy will be able to invest in what makes their regions special and improve the visitor experience from better high streets to public spaces – including public toilets and parks, cultural events and security and destination promotion. Money raised from visitors will stay in the area, helping attract more visitors, support local businesses and improve places for the people who live there too.

But the government will continue to protect lower cost family breaks by requiring the levy to be charged as a percentage rate of the cost of accommodation, rather than as a flat fee, meaning those choosing cheaper accommodation will pay less. Ten mayors have also committed that any levy introduced in their areas would be no higher than 5%, providing certainty for visitors and businesses while preserving local choice.

This piece of legislation builds on the significant commitment made at the Budget to drive good growth in every postcode, including through the government’s high streets strategy and wider plans to rewire the state, and shift power from Whitehall back to local communities.

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities, and Local Government Angela Rayner said:


  Millions of people visit our wonderful towns and cities each year, and it’s right that our communities should be able to feel the benefit of that footfall.

  Every pound raised through these levies will stay in the local area. Whether that’s better transport, thriving high streets, or more attractions that keep visitors coming back.

  This is about giving mayors and local leaders the choice to invest back into what matters most to local people, while protecting lower-cost stays and making sure businesses have their say.


Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester said:  


  In Greater Manchester, we campaigned for an Overnight Visitor Levy to boost our region and give mayors the powers to raise additional funds through a modest levy on overnight stays. This would give us access to new funding that we can reinvest into our places to support our visitor economy, improve public services and drive good growth.  

  In Manchester we pioneered a similar scheme in recent years which has been a resounding success. Our industry-led City Visitor Charge has shown that the model can work, generating millions of pounds that has been invested back into things like street cleaning and our work to attract major events, with widespread support from the hospitality sector.   

  The Overnight Visitor Levy also represents a major moment for devolution and a further vote of confidence in the ability of mayors and local leaders to make decisions in the best interests of their places. It means we can attract more events, make our region more welcoming for tourists with cleaner streets and invest in long term projects like extending the tram network. 

  The important thing now is that this is genuinely devolved. Any levy needs to work for our city region and be shaped with our councils, businesses and the local hospitality sector, with the money raised here being used for the benefit of people and businesses in Greater Manchester.


David Skaith, Mayor of York and North Yorkshire, said: 


  We’re home to historic towns and cities, two of the UK’s best National Parks and a coastline brimming with character. 

  There’s something for everyone, and we welcome more than 40 million visitors every year. That’s why an Overnight Visitor Levy will be a total gamechanger for our county. 

  Investing in York and North Yorkshire’s cities, towns and villages to make them a better place to visit, and to live in, is at the heart of why I will be introducing a Levy in our county.


Steve Rotheram, Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, said:  


  This is something I’ve been calling for over many years, so I’m really pleased the government is taking forward plans to give Mayors the power to introduce a visitor levy locally. 

  Our visitor economy is already worth more than £6.8bn a year and supports more than 55,000 jobs across the Liverpool City Region. A modest levy on overnight stays could potentially raise up to £18m a year – money that would stay here and be reinvested directly into the events, culture, experiences and infrastructure that bring millions of visitors to our region. 

  Visitor levy mechanisms are often used in many great cities across the globe to improve the visitor offer and attract even more people to enjoy the experience. It would give us more money to support the things that make our visitor economy such a success, while helping our businesses and communities to benefit from its continued growth. 

  We’ve shown time and again that local people know what our area needs far better than someone sitting behind a desk in Whitehall. I look forward to working with government as these powers are developed to make sure we get a system that is fair, workable and delivers the greatest possible benefit for our region.  


Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said:  


  After years of lobbying, I wholeheartedly welcome this Bill, which would give London greater freedom to raise and invest new funding locally.  

  A modest levy could support our hugely successful visitor economy, creating benefits for Londoners, businesses and visitors alike, as well as helping to cement London’s reputation as one of the world’s leading destinations.


Claire Ward, Mayor of the East Midlands, said:  


  We have so much to be proud of across the East Midlands. I want more people to discover our fantastic towns and cities, our attractions and everything else our region has to offer. And I want the communities that welcome them to share in the benefits. 

  An Overnight Visitor Levy would give us the chance to put more money back into the places that make our region what it is. That means supporting our attractions and independent businesses and helping our high streets and town centres attract even more people. 

  It’s important that local people and businesses are part of this conversation from the start. There will be full consultation before a levy is introduced, giving people the opportunity to help shape how it works and where the money raised could make the biggest difference. Those who know their communities best should have a real say in how they benefit.

  Bradford’s year as UK City of Culture proved what we can achieve when we invest in our visitor economy, which is why I’m supportive of these powers to ask those who stay overnight to make a small contribution to support our great region. 

  This could be invested in bringing more gigs, performances, art and sport to our world-recognised venues, making our streets cleaner and safer, introducing night buses, and opening up more creative careers for our young people. 

  I’ll work closely with council leaders, businesses and our communities to ensure we get this right and build a brighter region that works for all.

  Tens of millions of visitors spend billions of pounds in the West of England each year, brought here by amazing attractions like the Roman Baths, Clifton Suspension Bridge, Weston-super-Mare’s Grand Pier, and Bristol Zoo Project.   The overnight visitor levy will allow us to invest more money raised here right back into the West, like other places already do around the world. That could well mean transport and tourism improvements, helping communities to see and feel a difference from devolution.

items.title: Energy reforms to cut bills and put power back in people's hands
items.summary: Energy Independence Bill builds on the Budget by delivering a major overhaul of Britain’s energy system, putting affordability and public control at its heart New laws will underpin plans to scrap gas standing charges, protect household bil
items.bodyHtml:
• Energy Independence Bill builds on the Budget by delivering a major overhaul of Britain’s energy system, putting affordability and public control at its heart
  • New laws will underpin plans to scrap gas standing charges, protect household bill savings and crack down on rogue energy companies and landlords
  • Communities to get a greater stake in clean energy projects, alongside reforms to speed up grid connections 
  • Delivers on manifesto commitment to issue no new oil and gas licences to explore new fields in the North Sea

Families and businesses will benefit from a fairer energy system, cheaper bills and greater public control under landmark legislation introduced to Parliament today (Wednesday 4 November).

The Energy Independence Bill is a down payment on longer-term reforms that will fix Britain’s broken energy system, putting affordability at its heart, while unlocking barriers to deliver clean power.  

Building on last week’s Budget, the government will bring forward amendments to the Bill to support plans to scrap standing charges on household gas bills, ending the daily charge paid even when no gas is used.

The move will give around 23 million households greater control over their energy costs, with around 60% of gas account holders expected to save an average of £45 a year.

The Bill will also put the decision to shift 75% of domestic Renewables Obligation costs from energy bills to public spending on a lasting legal footing, protecting savings already delivered to households.

It follows last week’s Budget, which announced a £100 payment for up to 20 million households in England this winter, and further reforms to prevent unnecessary policy costs being added to energy bills.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: 

For too long, families have paid the price for an energy system that isn’t working for them. Bills are too high and events around the world can send costs soaring.  

That’s why we’ve taken immediate action to help people with energy bills, with £50 off the annual price cap and our new £100 energy payment for 20 million households. And this Bill will make the changes needed for the long-term: protecting people when energy companies let them down, giving communities a stake in the power produced on their doorstep, and building more cheap, green power here at home.  

Together, these changes will bring bills down for good, give families greater security and put Britain back in control of its energy future.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: 

Energy is an everyday essential. No one should have to worry about being ripped off by rogue companies or see bills driven up by price shocks thousands of miles away.

Today is a first downpayment on fixing a broken system, protecting consumers from unfair costs and putting the public back in control.

Through this Bill, we will build a clean energy future which people feel in their pockets, households and communities, ensuring support reaches those who need it most.

Other measures in the Bill include:

  • Stronger consumer protections: Giving Ofgem tougher powers to crack down on rogue energy companies and bosses, including unfair bonuses, while regulating energy brokers to tackle mis-selling and hidden commissions, expected to save businesses around £100 million a year
  • Warmer homes for renters: Giving local authorities stronger powers to tackle rogue landlords who fail to meet energy efficiency standards, including fines of up to £30,000, supporting plans to save households in upgraded rented homes around £210 a year by 2030
  • Making home upgrades easier: Establishing the Warm Homes Agency in law to help families access support to improve their homes and cut heating costs.
  • Putting power in local hands: Requiring developers to offer communities up to a 20% stake in new renewable projects, alongside mandatory community benefits so local people share in the rewards
  • Building a stronger grid: Establishing publicly owned Great British Grid in law through an upcoming amendment, alongside reforms to speed up electricity infrastructure and help homes and businesses connect faster

The Bill will also deliver on the government’s pragmatic approach to the North Sea, by ending new licences to explore new oil and gas fields while supporting continued production from existing licensed areas.

New Transitional Energy Certificates will enable further production in already explored areas, including through existing infrastructure. This could unlock around 60 million barrels of oil and support hundreds of jobs.

Oil and gas will remain part of Britain’s energy mix for decades to come. The government is committed to a fair transition, backed by the £2 billion Energy Wealth Fund and North Sea Jobs Service, supporting workers and investment in the industries of the future.

Together, these reforms mark the first step towards a more affordable, clean energy system, with stronger consumer protections, greater public control and communities sharing in the benefits of renewable and low carbon power.

Notes to editors

The Energy Independence Bill will update the laws governing consumer protection, support with bills, home upgrades and energy infrastructure. The Bill will: 

Deliver a fairer deal for consumers 

Strengthening Ofgem:

Energy markets have changed, but regulation has not always kept pace, leaving gaps in consumer protection. The Bill will strengthen Ofgem’s duties, remit and enforcement powers so it can act faster against wrongdoing and secure stronger redress when households and businesses are let down. 

Renewables Obligation costs:

Moving 75% of domestic Renewables Obligation costs to the Exchequer has already removed around £90 a year from average household bills. But the current powers need renewing every 6 months. The Bill will put this funding on an enduring legal footing for the period to March 2029, with powers to require suppliers to pass the savings on, including to customers on fixed deals. 

Energy brokers and price comparison services:

Hidden commissions, pressure selling and mis-sold contracts can leave consumers paying too much, with limited ways to challenge unfair treatment. The Bill will bring energy brokers and price comparison services under Ofgem regulation, with consistent standards and powers to order compensation, impose fines and ban rogue operators. The government estimates this could save businesses more than £100 million a year in costly mis-selling and hidden commissions. 

Charges on electricity exported to the grid:

Consumers currently face charges on electricity they store and return to the grid, while other charges discourage the use of surplus renewable power. The Bill will enable these charges to be removed, helping households and businesses benefit from batteries, electric vehicle-to-grid charging and cheaper electricity when there is an abundance of clean electricity generation. 

Better data for energy-support schemes:

Current data-sharing rules can make it harder to identify and support bill payers facing energy related challenges who fall outside the legal definition of fuel poverty. The Bill will widen those rules so future energy support can better reach eligible bill payers facing high bills, greater energy needs or hard-to-heat homes, while maintaining existing privacy safeguards. The bill will also expand government’s ability to provide future targeted support with energy bills for low-income and vulnerable households when required. 

Upgrade homes and empower communities 

Warm Homes Agency:

Families face a confusing mix of schemes and organisations when trying to insulate their homes or switch to clean heating. The Bill will enable existing schemes and functions to be transferred either to the Warm Homes Agency or to another body, giving consumers a trusted source of advice and support and helping deliver the Warm Homes Plan. 

Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards:

Weak enforcement can leave tenants paying to heat cold homes and inefficient business premises. The Bill will give local authorities stronger powers to enforce energy-efficiency standards across the domestic and non-domestic private rented sectors, including better compliance information and a maximum civil penalty of £30,000 for breaches of domestic regulations. The measure will support the move to EPC C from 1 October 2030 which is expected to reduce average energy bills in upgraded properties by £210 a year, while helping lift households out of fuel poverty.  

Schemes providing support with energy bills:

Existing powers place limits on the government’s ability to target support to households in need more effectively. The measure will ensure the government has the powers needed to intervene swiftly and effectively when required, without needing to rely on emergency legislation during an energy price shock. 

Smart meters and battery storage:

Government’s powers to drive the smart meter rollout expire before its planned completion and communications upgrade, while existing smart-appliance powers do not cover batteries. The Bill will extend smart-meter oversight powers to 2033 and allow government, if needed, to require batteries to have smart capabilities, helping consumers use and store electricity when it is cheaper. 

Community benefits:

Benefits for communities hosting energy projects are voluntary and vary between places. The Bill will allow government to introduce requirements on operators of new onshore wind and ground mount solar projects over 5 MW to enter legally binding benefit agreements with local community groups with minimum contribution levels and greater transparency. Communities will decide how benefits support local priorities.  

Community energy and shared ownership:

Communities do not always have a clear route to invest in and benefit directly from local clean-energy projects. The Bill will support shared ownership by amending existing primary powers to give local people greater opportunities to take a stake in the projects near them. 

Deliver homegrown clean energy we control 

Reformed National Pricing:

Electricity market rules were not designed for today’s growing renewable generation, and lengthy reform processes can leave investment and grid development poorly coordinated. The Bill will provide targeted powers to update market rules, network charging and trading arrangements, helping Britain use clean power more efficiently and reduce overall system costs. 

Land rights, consents and grid infrastructure:

Outdated consent and land-access processes can delay the grid upgrades needed to connect clean power, homes and businesses. The Bill will modernise permissions, access rights and processes for essential works, helping networks build faster while maintaining protections for landowners, communities and the environment. 

North Sea transition:

The Bill will end new licences, introduce Transitional Energy Certificates to support existing offshore fields throughout their lifetime, and update the North Sea Transition Authority’s objectives and powers to better equip the regulator in its role as a steward of the transition.  

Fracking:

The Bill will end new licences for onshore oil and gas fields in England, including licences that could be used for shale-gas fracking.

Rights for offshore renewable workers:

Some offshore renewable and low-carbon workers beyond UK territorial waters lack the employment protections available to offshore oil and gas workers. The Bill will enable these gaps to be closed, extending protections such as the minimum wage, protection against unfair dismissal and working-time rights, helping ensure clean energy jobs offer fair treatment and good working conditions.

See the Energy Independence Bill factsheets

items.title: CMA publishes decision in strategic review of market remedies
items.summary: Removal of 23 remedies reduces unnecessary burdens on businesses. The CMA is continuing to consider consultation responses for 2 remedies relating to retail banking and private motor insurance. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) ha
items.bodyHtml:
• Removal of 23 remedies reduces unnecessary burdens on businesses.  
  • The CMA is continuing to consider consultation responses for 2 remedies relating to retail banking and private motor insurance.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has today published its final decision on 31 market remedies to ensure they remain appropriate and focused on delivering benefits for consumers, businesses and the UK economy.

The review looked at 33 existing market remedies that the CMA identified may no longer be needed to deal with problems they were designed to fix, for reasons including being superseded by new laws and regulations.

Remedies play an important role in improving competition, but businesses need to dedicate resources to comply with them and the CMA or other bodies must monitor them  – so it is important to assess whether they are still needed and whether they are the best use of resource.

Following consultation on its provisional decision published in August, the CMA has confirmed its decision to remove 23 remedies, to remove 2 remedies in part and retain 6 remedies.

The CMA   is continuing to consider the consultation responses received on whether to partially remove 2 further remedies – the Retail Banking Market Investigation Order and the Private Motor Insurance Market Investigation Order – given the range of views received. An update on these  will be published later this month.    

The final decision forms part of the CMA’s commitment to ensuring that market remedies continue to address the competition concerns they were designed to address, while removing requirements where they are no longer needed.

More information can be found on the case page.

For media enquiries, contact the CMA press office.

items.title: Designers to get stronger and simpler protection in major reforms
items.summary: The government has today (4 November 2026) announced a major overhaul of the UK’s designs system. Reforms will make design protection and enforcement simpler for the country’s 80,000 design businesses. The UK’s design sector contributed clo
items.bodyHtml:
The government has today (4 November 2026) announced a major overhaul of the UK’s designs system. Reforms will make design protection and enforcement simpler for the country’s 80,000 design businesses.

The UK’s design sector contributed close to £137 billion to the economy in 2023 and supports more than 2 million jobs. But the current designs system has long been criticised as overly complex, placing a disproportionate burden on lone designers and microbusinesses. These have been estimated to make up 92% (PDF, 15.8 MB) of design businesses.

Following a consultation led by the Intellectual Property Office (IPO), which closed in November 2025, the government is today (4 November 2026) setting out a package of targeted reforms.

These include measures to:

  • stop competitors copying designs and blocking designers from selling their own products

  • give smaller design businesses a simpler, more affordable route to court when they believe their designs have been copied

  • reduce the administrative burden of registering designs, with more consistent processes and simpler registered and unregistered protections

  • clarify and modernise protection for designs involving animation, with new filing options for moving image files

Together, these measures will create a design system that is clearer, easier to use and better suited to modern design by being:

  • simpler to navigate

  • more resistant to misuse

  • more accessible - particularly for smaller firms and lone designers - when disputes arise

  • The reforms announced today (4 November 2026) are the government’s formal response to the consultation that closed in November 2025. They follow extensive engagement with designers, industry representative organisations and other stakeholders.

They will help ensure the UK’s design system remains fit for purpose in a fast-changing digital economy, laying the foundations for the decades ahead.

Changes will help smaller businesses safeguard their work and modernise design protection. They include the following.

Tackling anti-competitive design filings

The government intends to introduce legislation   to give the IPO new powers to consider whether a design is genuinely new before it is registered.

Some people exploit the design registration system to gain an unfair advantage over competitors. This can include:

  • registering designs created by someone else
  • copying a competitor’s product images or marketing materials
  • filing designs for generic or well-known products they had no hand in creating

These registrations are then used to block competitors by sending takedown notices to online marketplaces, dragging other businesses into costly legal disputes. Affected businesses reported spending between £10,000 and more than £50,000 to resolve these cases. The new powers will help protect designers from a serious threat that many — especially independent designers and small studios — cannot afford to challenge.

The IPO will also be able to consider whether a design application  has ‘individual character’ — in other words,  whether it creates a clearly different overall impression from anything already made public. This will help ensure protection is not granted to designs that are only trivially different from existing products.

The government will also consider bringing forward legislation to give the IPO clear powers to refuse bad-faith design applications. Before doing so, it will carry out further work to define bad faith in practice and identify the evidence needed to prove it. This will help ensure any specific new provision is clear, workable and proportionate.

Improving access to justice for small businesses

At present, registered design cases must go through the Patents Court or Intellectual Property Enterprise Court (IPEC) multi-track. This can put legal action beyond the reach of those who need it most. The government will take steps to allow registered design cases to be heard in the IPEC Small Claims Track for the first time.

The Small Claims Track is a simpler, lower-cost route through the courts for straightforward, lower-value disputes, with compensation claims capped at £10,000. This change would make access to justice easier and considerably more affordable for individual designers and small businesses.

In the coming months, the government will work with designers, legal professionals and business representative groups to consider how this change should be taken forward.

Giving designers more time to prepare for product launch

The government will introduce a new 30-month deferment period, bringing the UK into line with the EU and the international Hague systems. Designers will be able to apply for protection early and delay making their design public for up to 30 months.

This gives businesses more time to develop and launch products without alerting competitors too soon.

Modernising protection for digital and animated designs

The government will update the law to make clear that a design which includes animation, movement or transitions, can qualify for registered design protection. This will provide greater legal clarity for digital designers and businesses creating moving or interactive designs.

The IPO will also introduce new file format options  so animated designs can be filed as moving image files as part of the registration process. This better reflects how digital design work is created and presented.

This will give greater certainty and a simpler application process to designers working in:

  • digital product design
  • UX (user experience)
  • motion graphics and other moving formats

Improvements to unregistered design protections

The government will simplify the rules for unregistered design protection, which many designers find complex and difficult to navigate. Aligning the rules on what qualifies for protection and how long it lasts will make it easier for designers to understand what protects their work.

The government will also change the law so that supplementary unregistered design protection can apply when a design is disclosed anywhere in the world.

This removes a post-Brexit disadvantage: a UK designer launching at an international trade show or publishing work online globally will be able to have the same protection as one who first discloses their work in the UK.

Simplifying and modernising the design registration process

A series of practical changes will make the design registration process simpler and more streamlined. For example:

  • multiple objections will be set out in a single report rather than raised separately

  • response deadlines will be standardised

  • the registrar will have new powers to correct errors on the register

These changes will reduce the administrative burden on sole traders and microbusinesses, for whom registering and maintaining design protection can currently be time-consuming and complex.

Computer generated designs – ongoing work

The government will:

  • monitor AI use in the design industry

  • consider wider developments in AI and intellectual property

  • engage with international partners and industry stakeholders- recognising this is a fast-moving area

The existing legal framework for computer-generated designs will remain in place while this evidence base continues to develop.

A note on criminal sanctions

The Intellectual Property Act 2014 specifies that criminal sanctions can be made against anyone found to have intentionally copied a registered design without explicit consent from the design’s owner.

The call for evidence on criminal sanctions for unregistered design  infringement attracted strongly held views. However, the government concluded that there is insufficient robust evidence to demonstrate that introducing criminal offences for unregistered design infringement would be a balanced, proportionate and effective remedy.  

The government is therefore ruling out introducing these offences.

Minister responsible for Intellectual Property Chris McDonald said:

Britain’s designers are some of the best in the business, but small firms and independent designers too often struggle to reap their hard-earned rewards because of an outdated system.

Our reforms will make protecting their hard work simpler, so designers spend less time bogged down in admin and more time unleashing the creativity that drives them, and ultimately benefits us all through innovative products and services.

Adam Williams, CEO of the Intellectual Property Office, said:

Stronger, simpler and clearer design protection will help prevent the system being misused, remove unnecessary complexity and give designers a clearer and more accessible route to enforce their rights.

For small businesses and lone designers in particular, clearer rules and fewer barriers can make a real difference. By creating a system that works better from application through to enforcement and better reflects modern design practice, we will help give creators of all sizes greater confidence to invest in their ideas and turn them into successful products and enterprises.

Creative Industries Minister, Ian Murray said:

Britain’s designers shape everything from the clothes we wear to the places we live and work. But too many self-employed designers and small studios have had their work copied or been dragged into legal disputes, costing thousands of pounds, for simply protecting what they’ve created.

These reforms will make the system simpler, fairer and more affordable, so that smaller businesses can protect their ideas and focus on their growth.

Simon Wright, President of the Chartered Institute of Patent Attorneys (CIPA) said:

Our members advise designers and businesses of all sizes on protecting and enforcing their designs, so we see every day how much the system matters to those who rely on it. We welcome the Government’s measured proposals for reform and are particularly pleased to see that many of our recommendations have been taken on board. The planned changes have the potential to deliver practical improvements for designers and businesses, and we are eager to see the next steps.

We are grateful to the IPO for engaging so closely with the IP profession and other stakeholders throughout this process, and we look forward to continuing to work together as the reforms are implemented.

John Coldham, Chair of the Chartered Institute of Trade Mark Attorneys (CITMA) Designs & Copyright Working Group and Head of IP at Gowling WLG, said:

This design consultation has involved significant work, and the IPO has made significant effort to ensure the voices of all designers have been heard. The results are thoughtful and positive, reflecting the reality that design law has to suit a lot of different requirements. Even small design businesses operate across multiple platforms and countries, and need a design system that is simple whilst effectively protecting creativity cheaply. The retention of both UK design right and supplementary unregistered design, with plans to harmonise qualification, will come as a huge relief to designers. We look forward to working with government on the next steps of this vital work.

Kevin Scott, President of the IP Federation, said:

Innovative businesses need a designs framework that is clear, balanced and commercially workable. The IP Federation welcomes these reforms, which take a proportionate approach to improving the system and will help businesses invest in new products and technologies with greater confidence.

In particular, the IP Federation welcomes the confirmation that criminal sanctions for unregistered design infringement will not be introduced. This outcome aligns with its consultation response and supports a proportionate, civil enforcement-led system that maintains legal certainty and encourages innovation within a modernised designs regime. We are grateful to the IPO for engaging so closely with industry throughout this process, and we look forward to continuing to work together as the changes are taken forward.

Mat Hunter, Design Council CEO, said:

The Design Council welcomes the government’s plans to take forward changes that will make the UK’s design protection system clearer, more accessible and better suited to the needs of designers. For a sector that drives growth, innovation and progress towards a more sustainable economy, this is an important step forward. A more responsive IP framework will give them greater confidence to invest in new ideas and compete internationally.

These reforms recognise the changing nature of design and the need for a framework that keeps pace with innovation. We encourage the government to build on this progress and continue working with industry to ensure the UK’s design protection system remains fit for the future and supports designers of all disciplines and sizes.

Sarah Garry, Chief Executive of the British Brands Group, said:

Original design is central to how brands stand out and earn consumers’ trust. The British Brands Group welcomes the government’s reforms to the UK designs system, which will help make protection clearer and easier to use for businesses of all sizes. We are grateful to the IPO for engaging with our members throughout this process. We look forward to continuing to work together as changes are implemented and where stakeholder input is required.

Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, said:

Fashion is one of Britain’s greatest creative exports, and it thrives because of the talent and originality of its designers. We warmly welcome the government’s commitment to strengthening design protection, particularly its recognition that the breadth of unregistered design rights must be preserved, which is vital for fashion businesses.

A clearer, more modern system can help fashion designers of every size, from emerging names to established fashion houses, protect their work and invest with confidence in new creations. We are grateful to the government for listening to the sector, and we look forward to continuing to work together to ensure these changes deliver practical benefits for British fashion talent.

Chris Williamson, Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) President, said:

Good architecture is built on creativity and innovation. In a rapidly changing technological landscape, the government’s reforms to the UK designs framework will help to ensure that architects can better protect their work. We look forward to engaging with the IPO as the reforms are taken forward.

Helen Brocklebank, CEO of Walpole, said:

Walpole welcomes the significant work undertaken by the Intellectual Property Office to modernise the UK designs framework. These reforms are a positive step and provide a strong foundation for the future. There is more work to do, and we look forward to continuing to work constructively with the IPO to ensure the UK design system is effective, accessible and supportive of design-led businesses.

The government will introduce legislation, when parliamentary time allows, to implement those changes that require it.

As the creative economy continues to evolve, the IPO will continue to engage with industry bodies, design-led businesses and designers to help ensure the UK remains a leading place for them to innovate and grow.

  • The government’s full response to its Consultation on Changes to the design framework is published on GOV.UK.  The changes announced today (4 November 2026) are the government’s formal response to this consultation. It was led by the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) who sought views from designers, design businesses, representative organisations, legal professionals and any other interested parties. The consultation closed in November 2025 and received 90 responses.

  • Figures related to the UK’s design sector are set out in the Design Council’s Design Economy 2026 report. This report found that:

In 2023 the design economy contributed £136.7 billion in Gross Value Added (GVA) to the UK economy, 5.5% of total UK GVA.  It grew at almost twice the rate of the UK economy between 2019 and 2023.

In 2025 there were over 2.27 million people working in the design economy. Of these, 1.88 million were employed in design occupations.

Digital design is growing in importance. The total value of digital design in 2023 is £81 billion, an increase of 50% since 2019.

  • Design Council’s 2022 Design Economy Report ‘People, Places and Economic Value’ found that in 2020, 92% of all design businesses were micro-businesses.

  • The Intellectual Property Enterprise Court (IPEC) is a specialist court dealing with intellectual property disputes. Its Small Claims Track currently handles lower-value copyright, trade mark and unregistered design cases, with a financial limit of £10,000.

  • The Hague System is an international mechanism administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) that allows designers to protect their designs in multiple countries through a single application.

  • The Intellectual Property Office (IPO) is the official UK government body responsible for intellectual property rights including patents, designs, trade marks and copyright. More information is available at the IPO’s website.

items.title: New Ukrainian GCSE to help young people preserve their heritage
items.summary: Young people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will have the opportunity to study for a new Ukrainian GCSE, helping Ukrainians to preserve a vital connection to their language, culture and identity while opening pathways to future educ
items.bodyHtml:
Young people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will have the opportunity to study for a new Ukrainian GCSE, helping Ukrainians to preserve a vital connection to their language, culture and identity while opening pathways to future education and employment for all pupils.

The new qualification is part of the UK’s enduring support for the Ukrainian community and continued commitment to stand with Ukraine and its people.

While the qualification will be open to all, it marks a particularly significant milestone for Ukrainian children and young people living in the UK, who for the first time will have the opportunity to maintain proficiency in their home language and celebrate an important part of who they are, through our education system.

The qualification builds on the Government’s wider commitment to supporting Ukraine and Ukrainian families who have made their homes in the UK, while strengthening cultural and educational ties between the two countries.

The new GCSE comes after the government announced that the UK will give a further £10 billion of economic and military support in the largest ever package of financial backing for Ukraine.

Education Secretary, Lucy Powell, said:

As they build their lives here in the UK, it is right that Ukrainians and their children should have every opportunity to maintain that connection to their heritage and to be proud of who they are.

This new qualification is available to all pupils and will give them the chance to develop their language skills and celebrate Ukraine’s rich culture and history, while also opening pathways to future study and employment and strengthening our partnership with Ukraine.

Through that enduring partnership, we are building the lasting ties between our countries that will see the young minds of the future move forward together, and foster connections that transcend borders.

Minister for Europe, Lord Stewart Wood, said:

The introduction of a Ukrainian GCSE is a powerful symbol of the deep and enduring bonds between our two countries. It will give young Ukrainians in the UK the opportunity to celebrate their language and heritage, while gaining a qualification that recognises their skills.

Through our 100 Year Partnership, the UK and Ukraine are investing in the ties between our people that will last for generations.

Minister of Education and Science of Ukraine, Andrii Butenko, said:

Today marks an important milestone towards the introduction of a Ukrainian GCSE, long called for by the Ukrainian community in the UK.

British schools opened their doors to thousands of Ukrainian children following the start of Russia’s full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine, and we will always be grateful for that.

“We welcome the UK Government’s next step towards giving Ukrainian children a genuine choice in their education while respecting their identity.”

The announcement builds on both the UK-Ukraine 100-Year Partnership and the UK-Ukraine Schools Partnership, which fosters cross-cultural understanding and enhances English language skills while forging lasting links between school communities here and in Ukraine.

The programme has expanded to include more than 300 schools across both nations, supporting cultural exchange and connecting teachers and pupils through collaborative projects focused on reading for pleasure and shared learning.

In line with other modern foreign language GCSEs, the qualification will assess listening, speaking, reading and writing skills, while also recognising the cultural and historical contexts that shape the Ukrainian language.

The Ukrainian GCSE is expected to be available for first teaching in England, Wales and Northern Ireland from September 2028, with first assessments taking place in 2029.

AQA will now begin the next phase of development, bringing together language and subject experts to design a high-quality qualification that reflects the richness of Ukrainian language and culture, supporting learners while reflecting the needs and aspirations of the wider Ukrainian community.

AQA Chief Executive Officer, Colin Hughes

We’re pleased to be working with the Department for Education to develop the new GCSE in Ukrainian. The qualification will give young people – including those displaced by the war – an opportunity to gain formal recognition for their knowledge of Ukrainian, while contributing to greater understanding of the language and its culture in the UK. As an independent education charity, AQA’s role is to design and deliver high‑quality qualifications that meet learners’ needs and uphold rigorous academic standards.

The new GCSE comes as the Department for Education prepares to launch a consultation on the revitalised curriculum, one that retains strong academic foundations while broadening what a great education offers to give young people the capabilities and pathways to thrive in the real world.

As part of this, the language curriculum will now see changes that support more confident and purposeful language learning, to help pupils communicate effectively, engage with other cultures and develop a stronger foundation for further study.

items.title: Manchester company which took advantage of struggling businesses shut down
items.summary: Clark Sinclair Limited offered to arrange sales of financially distressed businesses for £1 and charged a fee. They misleadingly suggested directors could avoid scrutiny by selling their companies before liquidation. The company was wound u
items.bodyHtml:
• Clark Sinclair Limited offered to arrange sales of financially distressed businesses for £1 and charged a fee. 

  • They misleadingly suggested directors could avoid scrutiny by selling their companies before liquidation. 

  • The company was wound up by the High Court in Manchester on 29 October 2026.

A Manchester-registered company has been shut down following an Insolvency Service investigation which found they were providing misleading services to directors of companies in financial difficulty. 

Clark Sinclair Limited’s promotional emails suggested directors could avoid reputational damage by selling their companies before liquidation.  

The company offered to find buyers for companies with debts, telling clients that sales could be completed within days.  

The shares would be sold for £1, while Clark Sinclair charged brokering fees of between £2,500 and £6,800. 

Investigators identified £123,052 in customer payments, across two company accounts, and identified 51 companies which appeared to have changed ownership following payments to Clark Sinclair. 

The company also misrepresented the role of insolvency practitioners, incorrectly suggesting they sold company assets solely to pay their own fees. 

Clients were not warned that the various actions Clark Sinclair advised them to take could breach their duties as directors.  

Clark Sinclair’s registered sole director told investigators that they had never heard of the company, raising concerns that they were appointed without their knowledge or consent. 

Investigators were unable to identify who was behind the company.

Insolvency Service Chief Investigator, David Usher, said:

Clark Sinclair Limited took advantage of struggling businesses by offering directors a misleading route out of their company’s debts, charging thousands of pounds for the service. 

Selling a company does not prevent its former directors’ conduct from being investigated if it later enters liquidation.  

Clark Sinclair Limited not only deceived their customers but undermined the insolvency sector.

All enquiries concerning the affairs of this company should be made to the Official Receiver of the Public interest unit. Email PIU.OR@insolvency.gov.uk

Further information

  • Clark Sinclair Limited (company number 15324100) was incorporated on 3 December 2023. 

  • The company is registered at Initial Business Centre, Wilson Business Park, Manchester. 

  • The company was wound up the public interest under section 124A of the Insolvency Act 1986.

items.title: Small for-profit landlord fails to meet RSH's regulatory standards
items.summary: RSH found serious failings in Rentplus Homes Limited’s governance arrangements, with the landlord unable to demonstrate that its board has effectively responded to increasing risks, or that it has a robust business planning and risk managem
items.bodyHtml:
RSH found serious failings in Rentplus Homes Limited’s governance arrangements, with the landlord unable to demonstrate that its board has effectively responded to increasing risks, or that it has a robust business planning and risk management framework.

Arrangements with its unregistered parent company to provide support failed to operate in practice, negatively impacting on Rentplus Homes’ ability to protect its social homes.

Rentplus Homes is now facing significant liquidity pressures and is seeking to develop and implement plans to safeguard tenants’ homes from its viability risk.

RSH Chief Executive Jonathan Walters said: “Landlords must regularly assess and test their governance arrangements to make sure they are fit for purpose.

“But Rentplus Homes has failed to do this, which has had serious implications for its financial resilience and ongoing viability.

“Although Rentplus Homes is taking steps to manage emerging risks, it has not yet provided a credible route to resolve them at the pace we expect.

“We have serious concerns about this case, and are considering further regulatory intervention.”

Rentplus Homes was added to RSH’s gradings under review (GUR) list in August, following responsive engagement triggered by a self-referral to RSH in June 2026.

The self-referral concerned the administration of RPA1 Limited, a Rentplus group entity that owns approximately 68% of the homes managed by Rentplus Homes.

Following the publication of the regulatory judgement, Rentplus Homes has now been removed from the GUR list.

The full regulatory judgement can be found on RSH’s website.

ENDS

Notes for editors

  1. Rentplus Homes, based in Milton Keynes, is a small landlord as it owns fewer than 1,000 social homes. RSH does not issue grades to small landlords. However, where it considers there to be serious weaknesses or failings in a landlord’s delivery of the outcomes of our standards, it may publish or update a regulatory judgement to reflect this.
  2. Rentplus Homes Limited is not at the head of its group. It is a subsidiary organisation within a larger group of connected companies. The registered provider does not operate as a standalone entity in the group structure. It requires the ongoing support of related parties to fulfil its functions and meet its objectives. Today’s judgement concerns the registered provider only and does not represent an assessment of the non-registered entities within the group.
  3. According to the 2026 statistical data return Rentplus Homes manages 173 social homes. More recent management information records that the number of homes under management has increased to 283 homes. Rentplus Homes reported a turnover of £1.05m for year ended 31 December 2025 and employs no staff except for its non-executive directors.
  4. If RSH is investigating a landlord due to suspected serious failings, it may place them on the gradings under review list. This is likely to be where engagement is ongoing and RSH thinks it is appropriate to alert stakeholders to the fact that it has serious concerns about that landlord’s delivery of the standards outcomes, which it is investigating. More information about the gradings under review list and RSH’s approach is available on its How we approach regulatory judgements and gradings page.
  5. The regulatory standards page provides information about the economic and consumer standards that registered providers must meet.
  6. RSH promotes a viable, efficient and well-governed social housing sector able to deliver more and better social homes. It does this by setting standards and carrying out robust regulation focusing on driving improvement in social landlords, including local authorities, and ensuring that housing associations are well-governed, financially viable and offer value for money. It takes appropriate action if the outcomes of the standards are not being delivered.
  7. For media enquiries contact Vicky Moore vicky.moore@rsh.gov.uk or Christian Cosby christian.cosby@rsh.gov.uk. For general enquiries contact enquiries@rsh.gov.uk
