items.title: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029
items.summary: UK City of Culture 2029 winner will be announced in early 2027 Competition a key part of the government’s drive to boost pride and economic growth across the country Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have today been revealed a
items.bodyHtml:
• UK City of Culture 2029 winner will be announced in early 2027 
  • Competition a key part of the government’s drive to boost pride and economic growth across the country

Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have today been revealed as the four places shortlisted to be UK City of Culture 2029. 

These places are now in the running for the prestigious title that will unlock significant benefits for their local communities, such as increased investment, more access to cultural activities, and job creation. 

This competition supports a key part of the government’s drive to boost pride in every part of the country and ensure every town and city benefits from economic growth by devolving more power, funding and decision-making to local leaders alongside the pride in place programme. 

Each shortlisted place is now guaranteed to receive at least £125,000 to take forward elements of their bid, with one place ultimately going on to take the title and a prize fund of £10 million.  

The four locations were recommended by the UK City of Culture expert advisory panel, chaired by Sir Phil Redmond. The shortlist was whittled down from nine outstanding longlist applications which also included Inverness-Highland, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon. 

As part of their bids, places were asked to explain how they would use culture as a catalyst to transform their place and the lives of communities through boosting growth, opportunities and pride. 

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: 

Every place has a story worth telling of its own unique history, identity and contribution. It has been amazing to see this year’s bidders for UK City of Culture showcase what makes their community claim such a special place in our national story. Great culture is everywhere, but the opportunity to showcase it, to put it on display and to show how it is woven into our national story is not.

That is the beauty of the UK City of Culture competition, it is an undiluted celebration of what makes our largest towns and cities so brilliant.

Congratulations to Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham on making the shortlist. They are proud of their incredible culture, and they are right to be. I wish them the best of luck for the final stage of the competition.  

For all those places that have not made the shortlist, your journey does not end here. Their energy, enthusiasm and cultural contribution is seen and valued and the bids you have created will open up opportunities for years to come.

The UK City of Culture 2029 winner will be announced in early 2027. 

Previous winners Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford have shown the vast benefits of winning the prestigious title, which include attracting millions of pounds in additional investment to help boost regeneration, a year in the cultural spotlight with hundreds of events encouraging long-lasting participation in the arts, growth for local tourism and a lasting boost to community pride. 

Last year Bradford led a showstopping cultural programme of over 6,500 events - over 80% of which were free - that resulted in capital investment for more than 30 local cultural organisations. Bradford’s year in the spotlight also led to increased opportunities for local people to get involved with events, with over 88,000 residents taking part in key projects throughout the year. 87% of Bradford 2025 audiences also agreed that the event made them feel proud of their local area.  

There is also evidence that bidding to win UK City of Culture in its own right brings many benefits, including supporting a place to develop its cultural strategy and bring together key partners. 

Sir Phil Redmond, Chair of the UK City of Culture Expert Advisory Panel, said: 

Once again there is a hard choice ahead. The four places on the shortlist continue to demonstrate both the variety and strength of creative ambition across the UK. 

Each place represents a different view, or aspect, epitomising what culture is, the sum of all we do together, and while each approaches it differently, they all share the common aim of reminding the rest of the UK of who they are, where they are and why they are worth visiting. 

I look forward to doing that myself, along with the rest of the Advisory Panel in the near future.

The competition, delivered by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) in collaboration with the devolved governments in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, brings culture into the heart of communities and gives people an opportunity to get involved in everything the arts have to offer. 

The nine longlisted bidders received a £60,000 grant to strengthen their applications which were assessed. 

All bidding places, including those who were unsuccessful, will receive detailed feedback on their bids including areas for development. DCMS will also engage with them on how best they can maintain momentum and realise their cultural ambitions in the future. 

Welsh Secretary of State Stephen Kinnock, said:

Huge congratulations to Wrexham on being shortlisted for the City of Culture 2029!

Wales’s newest city has a huge amount to offer in heritage, culture and sport and I’d like to wish them every success with the next stage of their bid. Wrexham now has real chance to become Wales’s first City of Culture, bringing investment, more visitors and boosting pride in the community.

Councillor Lynn Williams MBE, Leader of Blackpool Council, said: 

Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of.

Being shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029 is a chance to celebrate everything that makes Blackpool what it is. Our music, dance, comedy and entertainment, the Ballroom, the Tower, the Opera House, the Grand Theatre; our bandstands, festivals, fireworks and Illuminations. It is in Rebellion, our community arts groups and theatres. It is in the traditions passed down through generations, but also in the new things that are shaping our culture today, from gaming and digital creativity to new music, art and performance. Blackpool has never been a town that stands still.

It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen. We have always been a town that entertains the country, and there is nowhere quite like Blackpool.

Councillor Jane Carr, Leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said:

I’d like to congratulate our fellow UK City of Culture 2029 shortlisted cities, Blackpool, Sheffield and Wrexham. This is a huge honour and a tribute to the hard work and vision of everyone who has helped to shape Milton Keynes’ bid. 

The last nine months have been nothing short of inspiring. Thousands of residents, organisations and the creative community came together to develop our bid. They all have a strength of belief in the creative and cultural future of our city, and we’re looking forward to sharing this momentum and spirit of optimism with the UK City of Culture judges. 

We’re now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond. Whoever is announced as the winner next year, we will enter our 60th year with our heads held high and know that – as our bid sets out – we’re just getting started.

Councillor Fran Belbin, Leader of Sheffield City Council, said:  

Being shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029 is fantastic news for Sheffield and a proud moment for everyone who has helped shape our bid.  

Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit. From our world-renowned music heritage and vibrant independent arts scene to our festivals, libraries, theatres, museums, galleries and grassroots creativity, culture is part of who we are.  

This recognition reflects the incredible talent, energy and ambition that exists across our city. We look forward to taking our bid to the next stage and continuing to showcase everything that makes Sheffield such a special place.

Joanna Knight OBE, Chair of the Wrecsam2029 bid, said:  

What an incredible moment for Wrexham! To be shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029 is fantastic news and something our whole community should be immensely proud of. 

We have such an extraordinary story to tell, and the ambition, creativity and passion to make 2029 something truly spectacular. The support we’ve had from people and organisations locally, nationally and internationally has been phenomenal, and there’s a real sense that something very special is happening here. 

Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean – not only for Wrexham, but for North Wales and the whole of Wales. The opportunities are enormous, and we’re determined to make the most of them. 

Wrexham is the right place and it’s the right time, and being shortlisted proves that others can see our potential too. Now we need everyone to get behind us, celebrate everything that makes this place so special and help us bring it home!

Notes to Editors: 

The expert advisory panel includes representatives from England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, bringing together a wide range of experience. 

To learn more about each shortlisted bid visit their websites: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham. 

Full list of longlisted bids: (*shortlisted place) 

  • Blackpool* 
  • Inverness-Highland 
  • Ipswich 
  • Middlesbrough 
  • Milton Keynes* 
  • Portsmouth 
  • Sheffield* 
  • Swindon 
  • Wrexham* 

The first-ever UK Town of Culture competition is also ongoing with fifteen shortlisted towns: Basildon, Birkenhead, Corby, Great Yarmouth, Grimsby, Ilfracombe, Isle of Bute, Leith, Lerwick, Pontypridd, Port Talbot, Rotherham, Sandown, Stockton Town Centre Ward and Strabane. The shortlisted places will now work to develop and finalise their full bids, which will explain how they would use culture to create transformational opportunities and better lives for people living in their local area ahead of a winner being announced next year.

Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have today been revealed as the four places shortlisted to be UK City of Culture 2029. 

These places are now in the running for the prestigious title that will unlock significant benefits for their local communities, such as increased investment, more access to cultural activities, and job creation. 

This competition supports a key part of the government’s drive to boost pride in every part of the country and ensure every town and city benefits from economic growth by devolving more power, funding and decision-making to local leaders alongside the pride in place programme. 

Each shortlisted place is now guaranteed to receive at least £125,000 to take forward elements of their bid, with one place ultimately going on to take the title and a prize fund of £10 million.  

The four locations were recommended by the UK City of Culture expert advisory panel, chaired by Sir Phil Redmond. The shortlist was whittled down from nine outstanding longlist applications which also included Inverness-Highland, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon. 

As part of their bids, places were asked to explain how they would use culture as a catalyst to transform their place and the lives of communities through boosting growth, opportunities and pride. 

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: 


  Every place has a story worth telling of its own unique history, identity and contribution. It has been amazing to see this year’s bidders for UK City of Culture showcase what makes their community claim such a special place in our national story. Great culture is everywhere, but the opportunity to showcase it, to put it on display and to show how it is woven into our national story is not.

  That is the beauty of the UK City of Culture competition, it is an undiluted celebration of what makes our largest towns and cities so brilliant.

  Congratulations to Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham on making the shortlist. They are proud of their incredible culture, and they are right to be. I wish them the best of luck for the final stage of the competition.  

  For all those places that have not made the shortlist, your journey does not end here. Their energy, enthusiasm and cultural contribution is seen and valued and the bids you have created will open up opportunities for years to come.


The UK City of Culture 2029 winner will be announced in early 2027. 

Previous winners Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford have shown the vast benefits of winning the prestigious title, which include attracting millions of pounds in additional investment to help boost regeneration, a year in the cultural spotlight with hundreds of events encouraging long-lasting participation in the arts, growth for local tourism and a lasting boost to community pride. 

Last year Bradford led a showstopping cultural programme of over 6,500 events - over 80% of which were free - that resulted in capital investment for more than 30 local cultural organisations. Bradford’s year in the spotlight also led to increased opportunities for local people to get involved with events, with over 88,000 residents taking part in key projects throughout the year. 87% of Bradford 2025 audiences also agreed that the event made them feel proud of their local area.  

There is also evidence that bidding to win UK City of Culture in its own right brings many benefits, including supporting a place to develop its cultural strategy and bring together key partners. 

Sir Phil Redmond, Chair of the UK City of Culture Expert Advisory Panel, said: 


  Once again there is a hard choice ahead. The four places on the shortlist continue to demonstrate both the variety and strength of creative ambition across the UK. 

  Each place represents a different view, or aspect, epitomising what culture is, the sum of all we do together, and while each approaches it differently, they all share the common aim of reminding the rest of the UK of who they are, where they are and why they are worth visiting. 

  I look forward to doing that myself, along with the rest of the Advisory Panel in the near future.


The competition, delivered by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) in collaboration with the devolved governments in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, brings culture into the heart of communities and gives people an opportunity to get involved in everything the arts have to offer. 

The nine longlisted bidders received a £60,000 grant to strengthen their applications which were assessed. 

All bidding places, including those who were unsuccessful, will receive detailed feedback on their bids including areas for development. DCMS will also engage with them on how best they can maintain momentum and realise their cultural ambitions in the future. 

Welsh Secretary of State Stephen Kinnock, said:


  Huge congratulations to Wrexham on being shortlisted for the City of Culture 2029!

  Wales’s newest city has a huge amount to offer in heritage, culture and sport and I’d like to wish them every success with the next stage of their bid. Wrexham now has real chance to become Wales’s first City of Culture, bringing investment, more visitors and boosting pride in the community.


Councillor Lynn Williams MBE, Leader of Blackpool Council, said: 


  Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of.

  Being shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029 is a chance to celebrate everything that makes Blackpool what it is. Our music, dance, comedy and entertainment, the Ballroom, the Tower, the Opera House, the Grand Theatre; our bandstands, festivals, fireworks and Illuminations. It is in Rebellion, our community arts groups and theatres. It is in the traditions passed down through generations, but also in the new things that are shaping our culture today, from gaming and digital creativity to new music, art and performance. Blackpool has never been a town that stands still.

  It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen. We have always been a town that entertains the country, and there is nowhere quite like Blackpool.


Councillor Jane Carr, Leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said:


  I’d like to congratulate our fellow UK City of Culture 2029 shortlisted cities, Blackpool, Sheffield and Wrexham. This is a huge honour and a tribute to the hard work and vision of everyone who has helped to shape Milton Keynes’ bid. 

  The last nine months have been nothing short of inspiring. Thousands of residents, organisations and the creative community came together to develop our bid. They all have a strength of belief in the creative and cultural future of our city, and we’re looking forward to sharing this momentum and spirit of optimism with the UK City of Culture judges. 

  We’re now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond. Whoever is announced as the winner next year, we will enter our 60th year with our heads held high and know that – as our bid sets out – we’re just getting started.


Councillor Fran Belbin, Leader of Sheffield City Council, said:  


  Being shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029 is fantastic news for Sheffield and a proud moment for everyone who has helped shape our bid.  

  Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit. From our world-renowned music heritage and vibrant independent arts scene to our festivals, libraries, theatres, museums, galleries and grassroots creativity, culture is part of who we are.  

  This recognition reflects the incredible talent, energy and ambition that exists across our city. We look forward to taking our bid to the next stage and continuing to showcase everything that makes Sheffield such a special place.


Joanna Knight OBE, Chair of the Wrecsam2029 bid, said:  


  What an incredible moment for Wrexham! To be shortlisted for UK City of Culture 2029 is fantastic news and something our whole community should be immensely proud of. 

  We have such an extraordinary story to tell, and the ambition, creativity and passion to make 2029 something truly spectacular. The support we’ve had from people and organisations locally, nationally and internationally has been phenomenal, and there’s a real sense that something very special is happening here. 

  Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean – not only for Wrexham, but for North Wales and the whole of Wales. The opportunities are enormous, and we’re determined to make the most of them. 

  Wrexham is the right place and it’s the right time, and being shortlisted proves that others can see our potential too. Now we need everyone to get behind us, celebrate everything that makes this place so special and help us bring it home!


Notes to Editors: 

The expert advisory panel includes representatives from England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, bringing together a wide range of experience. 

To learn more about each shortlisted bid visit their websites: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham. 

Full list of longlisted bids: (*shortlisted place) 


  Blackpool* 
  Inverness-Highland 
  Ipswich 
  Middlesbrough 
  Milton Keynes* 
  Portsmouth 
  Sheffield* 
  Swindon 
  Wrexham* 


The first-ever UK Town of Culture competition is also ongoing with fifteen shortlisted towns: Basildon, Birkenhead, Corby, Great Yarmouth, Grimsby, Ilfracombe, Isle of Bute, Leith, Lerwick, Pontypridd, Port Talbot, Rotherham, Sandown, Stockton Town Centre Ward and Strabane. The shortlisted places will now work to develop and finalise their full bids, which will explain how they would use culture to create transformational opportunities and better lives for people living in their local area ahead of a winner being announced next year.

items.title: Cowardly killers who dodge sentencing face tough new prison punishments
items.summary: Judges to get new powers to keep lock offenders in cells and restrict social visits Builds on reforms giving judges powers to order offenders into the dock to face justice Part of wider Government reforms to put victims first and ensure off
items.bodyHtml:
• Judges to get new powers to keep lock offenders in cells and restrict social visits
  • Builds on reforms giving judges powers to order offenders into the dock to face justice
  • Part of wider Government reforms to put victims first and ensure offenders are brought to justice

Killers who refuse to face their victims’ families at sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks on end under tough new rules announced today (22 October). 

The government has already changed the law so offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can face a fine or up to two years’ additional imprisonment for contempt of court. But for murderers already facing decades behind bars, this can offer little deterrent. 

The new powers will allow Crown Court judges to impose prison sanctions on offenders who refuse to attend sentencing, including restricting social visits for almost a month - ensuring even those facing decades behind bars have something more to lose.  

This means notorious killers including Thomas Cashman and Jordan McSweeney who refused to appear in court to hear their sentences could have faced additional judge-imposed punishments had these rules been in place at the time. 

Minister for Prisons, Probation and Reducing Reoffending Catherine McKinnell said:  

Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. 

Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences. 

We committed to change this and we’ve already strengthened the law so offenders can be ordered into court. Now we’re going further, giving judges tougher punishments for those who still refuse – from being confined to their cells for weeks to losing prison privileges and visits.

Under new rules laid before Parliament today, judges will be able to impose a range of sanctions, including: 

  • Loss of prison privileges for almost three months (84 days). 
  • Cellular confinement for up to three weeks (21 days). 
  • Loss of social visits for nearly a month (27 days). 
  • Restrictions on social visits to once every four weeks, for almost three months (84 days). 

The move builds on wider reforms which give judges the power to order offenders to attend sentencing and those who still refuse could now face additional prison sanctions. This is on top of the powers that allow judges to impose longer sentences.

The Victims’ Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said: 

Today’s announcement reflects the tireless efforts of victims’ families who refused to accept that offenders could simply opt out of facing justice.

Having worked with the families of Sabina Nessa, Zara Aleena and Jan Mustafa, I know how offenders’ refusal to attend sentencing hearings compounds trauma and robs families of one of the very few moments of accountability in the justice process. Their determined campaigning, alongside that of Olivia Pratt-Korbel’s family, helped ensure that this harm could no longer be ignored

It is now essential that these powers are used consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve.

Further information

  • The measures will come into effect next year, after the regulations have been through the usual parliamentary process.  
  • For offenders aged 18 to 20 held in Young Offender Institutions, judges will be able to remove privileges for up to 21 days or impose cellular confinement for up to 10 days. 
  • In line with the Government’s commitment to supporting children of prisoners, visits from prisoners’ children will be exempt, helping to maintain family ties where safe, appropriate and in the child’s best interests. 
  • The new sanctions can be imposed instead of, or in addition to, other penalties available to the court. 
  • The powers also cover offenders who attend sentencing but are removed from court for disruptive behaviour. 
  • No measure can guarantee prisoners attend their sentencing hearing, but these powers strengthen the consequences for offenders who refuse to comply with a court order and ensure they can be appropriately punished.

items.title: Record funding, record results: 7,000 miles of smoother journeys as government tackles potholes
items.summary: new reports show record spending on road maintenance, with councils spending over £800 million more than 2 years ago to help motorists avoid unnecessary repair bills nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing taking place this year, up 10% on l
items.bodyHtml:
• new reports show record spending on road maintenance, with councils spending over £800 million more than 2 years ago to help motorists avoid unnecessary repair bills
  • nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing taking place this year, up 10% on last year
  • government releases a further £220 million today to councils across England to go even further to repair potholes across the country

Nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing – the equivalent of travelling between London and Singapore – will be completed this year according to new figures published today (21 October 2026) as the government looks to give drivers more breathing space and help with the cost of living.

Figures from local councils shows over 10% more resurfacing than took place last year as data also shows that councils are starting to properly invest in their roads with £4.9 billion total being spent this year, £800 million more than before this government came to power.

The record figures show that the government’s £7.3 billion in funding for road maintenance is starting to deliver better roads for communities that have suffered from potholes, helping the average driver save up to nearly £600 pounds on costly repairs.

Following the publication of today’s data, the government has gone even further and unlocked £220 million in incentive-based funding to councils across England for meeting performance-based targets. Further funding will be released later in the year only if councils reach their performance targets, and can be withheld if they fail to reach them as part of the government’s efforts to hold councils to account.

Potholes continue to be a daily nuisance for drivers across the country, whether they’re travelling to work, the school run or a hospital appointment. But record funding and new measures to hold councils to account and make transport better, also shown in the recent announcement to tackle antisocial behaviour on transport, including £100 fines on buses and a crackdown on loud music on trains.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said:

For too long potholes have been a source of national embarrassment, forcing hard-working people to fork out for repairs and posing a danger to all road users. But today’s figures show that we are starting to turn a corner.

While we know there is much more to do, our record funding, combined with tough new rules holding councils to account, mean that drivers are making smoother journeys while giving people roads they can rely on.

The reports councils submitted to the government show that 94% of councils will complete preventative roadworks this year, stopping the same part of road being patched over and over again, and stamping out potholes before they have the chance to form in the first place.

It shows councils are doing more preventative works than last year, where only 76% did this work, showing that councils are changing behaviour as a result of clear direction from government, record funding and strict monitoring – meaning more money stays in the pocket of drivers.

Meanwhile additional figures released last week show local road conditions improved in the year ending March 2026, with less minor roads needing maintenance as a result of works last year.

Dan Joyce, Operations Director at Kwik Fit, said:

Kwik Fit teams across the country have been repairing damage from potholes all too often, with tyres, wheels and suspension components most frequently suffering from the impact. Potholes not only cause costly damage, they can also present a significant risk to road safety.

We welcome this increased investment, especially the additional focus on proactive maintenance as this helps prevent potholes before they become a danger to road users, or a drain on drivers’ wallets.

RAC head of policy Simon Williams said:

This data is encouraging. It’s good to see so many miles of road being resurfaced, but it’s also positive that the preventative maintenance message has got through as we’ve long argued that councils need to take steps to stop potholes appearing in the first place, and not just patch them up. Surface dressing, if done properly, is a very cost effective way of improving more roads for the long term.

The proof, of course, will be in whether drivers and other road users notice the difference. Getting the country’s roads up to a decent standard, and keeping them there, isn’t an overnight job. But at least we’re now on the right track.

Media enquiries 0300 7777 878

Switchboard 0300 330 3000

Potholes continue to be a daily nuisance for drivers across the country, whether they’re travelling to work, the school run or a hospital appointment. But record funding and new measures to hold councils to account and make transport better, also shown in the recent announcement to tackle antisocial behaviour on transport, including £100 fines on buses and a crackdown on loud music on trains.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said:


  For too long potholes have been a source of national embarrassment, forcing hard-working people to fork out for repairs and posing a danger to all road users. But today’s figures show that we are starting to turn a corner.

  While we know there is much more to do, our record funding, combined with tough new rules holding councils to account, mean that drivers are making smoother journeys while giving people roads they can rely on.


The reports councils submitted to the government show that 94% of councils will complete preventative roadworks this year, stopping the same part of road being patched over and over again, and stamping out potholes before they have the chance to form in the first place.

It shows councils are doing more preventative works than last year, where only 76% did this work, showing that councils are changing behaviour as a result of clear direction from government, record funding and strict monitoring – meaning more money stays in the pocket of drivers.

Meanwhile additional figures released last week show local road conditions improved in the year ending March 2026, with less minor roads needing maintenance as a result of works last year.

Dan Joyce, Operations Director at Kwik Fit, said:


  Kwik Fit teams across the country have been repairing damage from potholes all too often, with tyres, wheels and suspension components most frequently suffering from the impact. Potholes not only cause costly damage, they can also present a significant risk to road safety.

  We welcome this increased investment, especially the additional focus on proactive maintenance as this helps prevent potholes before they become a danger to road users, or a drain on drivers’ wallets.


RAC head of policy Simon Williams said:


  This data is encouraging. It’s good to see so many miles of road being resurfaced, but it’s also positive that the preventative maintenance message has got through as we’ve long argued that councils need to take steps to stop potholes appearing in the first place, and not just patch them up. Surface dressing, if done properly, is a very cost effective way of improving more roads for the long term.

  The proof, of course, will be in whether drivers and other road users notice the difference. Getting the country’s roads up to a decent standard, and keeping them there, isn’t an overnight job. But at least we’re now on the right track.

items.title: World-first taskforce to protect communities from climate change
items.summary: Government holds a world-first Climate and Nature Security Taskforce meeting to better prepare for the impacts of climate change and nature loss Leading experts from across security, military, academia and industry join forces to assess ris
items.bodyHtml:
• Government holds a world-first Climate and Nature Security Taskforce meeting to better prepare for the impacts of climate change and nature loss
  • Leading experts from across security, military, academia and industry join forces to assess risks and find solutions to the climate and nature threats to national security   
  • Following the UK’s hottest summer on record, and the world bracing for the impacts of a super El Niño, government takes action to protect communities and families

Communities across the UK will be better protected against the growing threats of climate change, as the world’s first Climate and Nature Security Taskforce met for the first time this week.

The taskforce will make independent recommendations to help shape government’s approach to tackling national and international climate security challenges, and to help ensure Britain can best prepare itself for the climate crisis.

The Minister for Climate Transition, Katie White, will chair the inaugural meeting, alongside Baroness Fiona Twycross. The taskforce brings together experts from across the fields of climate, nature and security to assess the UK’s readiness for security challenges created by climate change and nature loss – including General Richard Nugee, Comfort Ero, President of the International Crisis Group and Rosie Hails, Director of Science for the National Trust.  

The taskforce will establish the most significant climate and nature security risks facing the UK and define a clear vision for a more climate- and nature-secure UK.  This comes as the UK has experienced a series of extreme weather events over the past year, including record-breaking heatwaves, severe drought conditions, wildfires and rising flood risks.

Minister for Climate Transition, Katie White, said: 

This summer, we saw homes destroyed, families evacuated and huge stretches of our British countryside scorched by wildfires. Climate change isn’t some distant problem to worry about tomorrow, it’s happening right now. 

National security starts at home, protecting the people and places we love. That’s why our new taskforce brings together some of Britain’s best minds, from military leaders to climate scientists and security experts, to get ahead of these threats, take greater control of our future and make Britain stronger, safer and ready for whatever comes next.

General Richard Nugee said: 

The ministerial taskforce is a significant step forward. It offers the opportunity for real change to be proposed and delivered to ensure that this country is more resilient to the shocks from nature loss and climate change that are likely to occur in the future.

Erin Sikorsky, Director at the Centre for Climate Risks and Security, said: 

This summer’s heatwaves and wildfires made clear that climate change is already a security problem. The question now is how to prepare, prevent, and adapt going forward. I commend the UK government for taking that question seriously, and I’m honoured to join the taskforce to identify recommendations for the climate resilience and security investments the UK and its partners need.

The impacts of climate change stretch to almost every corner of Britain’s way of life – from migration to energy systems, supply chains and financial stability – and this taskforce will boost the UK’s preparedness for these security challenges. 

The taskforce – formally titled the National Security and Resilience Risks of a Changing Climate and Nature Loss Taskforce – has a clear set of objectives: 

  • identify key gaps and help prioritise the most significant climate- and nature-related risks to UK national and international security and resilience, ensuring existing evidence is translated into clear, actionable policy priorities
  • review and challenge work on security and resilience in response to global climate change impacts and nature loss and make recommendations to improve the UK’s preparedness and response to these threats
  • identify and recommend opportunities and areas of focus in addressing climate and nature-related security risks, including where the UK can strengthen resilience, secure advantage and shape outcomes internationally
  • support the development of an actionable UK approach to climate and nature security by clearly defining gaps and opportunities and providing recommendations to enhance preparedness, resilience and international influence

Notes to editors

The Climate and Nature Security Taskforce is made up of expert members from across military, security, government, and academia.

Membership

Full list of members:   

  • Tim Benton, Professor Emeritus, University of Leeds; formerly Research Director 
  • Nick Bridge, Associate Fellow, Environment and Society Centre, Chatham House 
  • Edd Denbee, Senior Manager, Bank of England 
  • Duncan Depledge, Senior Lecturer in Geopolitics and Security, Loughborough University 
  • Comfort Ero, President and CEO, International Crisis Group 
  • Bassam Fattouh, Director, Oxford Institute for Energy Studies 
  • Rosie Hails, Director of Science and Nature, National Trust 
  • Olivia Lazard, Planetary Fellow, Berggruen Institute 
  • General Richard Nugee, Former Non-Executive Director for Climate Change and Sustainability, MOD 
  • David Obura, Chair, Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services 
  • Nathalie Pettorelli, Professor, Institute of Zoology, ZSL 
  • Suzanne Raine, Master, Selwyn College, University of Cambridge 
  • Nicola Ranger, Executive Director of Earth Capital Nexus and Professor in Practice, LSE 
  • Erin Sikorsky, Director, Center for Climate and Security 
  • Maarten Van Aalst, Director General, Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute 
  • Janani Vivekananda, Director of Climate Diplomacy and Security Programme, adelphi global

Terms of reference

Background:

Climate change and nature loss are globally escalating threats, driving instability, resource insecurity and economic shocks that directly affect UK security and resilience. These risks are becoming more systemic and severe as the planet continues to warm against a backdrop of ongoing energy volatility and growing global fragility. 

This taskforce will help close the gap between ambition and delivery, providing independent challenge to shape a more resilient, integrated approach. It will strengthen accountability, improve our international leadership and enhance UK preparedness for systemic risks, while also identifying opportunities for UK advantage. 

Objectives of the taskforce: 

  1. Identify key gaps and prioritise the most significant climate- and nature-related risks to UK national and international security and resilience, ensuring existing evidence is translated into clear, actionable policy priorities. 
  2. Review, input and challenge UK government work on security and resilience in response to global climate change impacts and nature loss and make recommendations to improve the UK’s preparedness and response to these threats. 
  3. Identify and recommend opportunities and areas of strategic focus for government in addressing climate and nature-related security risks, including where the UK can strengthen resilience, secure advantage and shape outcomes internationally. 
  4. Support the development of an actionable UK approach to climate and nature security by clearly defining gaps and opportunities and providing recommendations to enhance preparedness, resilience and international influence. 

Deliverables: 

Up to 2 meetings in 2026 chaired by the Minister for Climate Transition, Katie White, and Cabinet Office Parliamentary Under Secretary, Baroness Twycross. One in person and one virtual. 

Assessment of key gaps in the UK government response to the risks posed by climate change and nature loss, assurance of the government’s strategic approach in relation to these threats and recommendations for further work.

items.title: “Generational moment” as government acts on landmark antisemitism review
items.summary: A government commissioned independent review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has been published today and has found that antisemitism is a significant and growing challenge for the education sector, with Jewish pupils, students an
items.bodyHtml:
A government commissioned independent review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has been published today and has found that antisemitism is a significant and growing challenge for the education sector, with Jewish pupils, students and staff experiencing antisemitic abuse, harassment and discrimination in schools and colleges.

The review, which was led by Sir David Bell, has been described as a ‘generational moment’ by the Education Secretary as it found that three in five Jewish pupils aged 16-19 had experienced or witnessed antisemitism. It also found that antisemitism has evolved and though it has ancient roots, it has taken contemporary forms, including when linked to the Middle East, which has made it ‘unacceptably casual’.

The independent review makes clear that in order for contemporary antisemitism to be rooted out in schools and colleges, so Jewish pupils and staff can feel safe, teachers and school leaders need clearer guidance and a more consistent approach across the education system.

The government has today accepted all 27 recommendations made in the report, recognising that antisemitism is a distinct form of racism and hatred that requires a clear and sustained response, as its modern manifestations are pervasive and pernicious. 

Government will now take forward a wide-ranging package of measures, including dedicated antisemitism training for education leaders, strengthened safeguarding and political impartiality guidance, improved reporting of antisemitic incidents and enhanced support for schools and colleges managing complex cases.

An implementation group bringing together key stakeholders has been established to drive delivery of the recommendations, while Sir David Bell has been commissioned to undertake a one-year review of progress to ensure momentum is maintained and commitments are implemented. The group will support delivery across the education sector, help share expertise and best practice, and monitor progress against the review’s recommendations.

Education Secretary, Lucy Powell said:

Every child and every teacher should be able to go to school or college free from fear. Sir David Bell’s review shows we are a long way from that. Antisemitism is an ancient evil, and today it remains as pernicious as ever.

We have a duty to teach this generation and the next what antisemitism is, why it’s wrong and what happens when it takes hold. That goes for every school and college, whether or not they have Jewish staff and students. It’s part of teaching our young people the British values of tolerance, acceptance and respect.

Implementation is now my priority. I will make sure schools and colleges are better equipped to spot, challenge and prevent antisemitism wherever it happens.

Independent Reviewer, Sir David Bell said:

In leading this review, I have been seized of the urgency in tackling antisemitism in schools and colleges. Its modern manifestations are having a pernicious impact in too many places, so it is vital that my recommendations are acted upon and acted upon quickly.

Our schools and colleges play a vital role in educating the next generation of Britons. They are at the centre of our efforts to tackle antisemitism amongst the young. So, I call upon everyone with an interest in our nation’s future to redouble their efforts to ensure that our education system is safe for everyone, including our fellow Jewish citizens of whatever age.

Alongside practical support for leaders and staff, the response makes clear government will strengthen the treatment of antisemitism as a safeguarding issue - given antisemitic abuse, harassment and discrimination can have a significant impact on the safety, wellbeing and participation of Jewish children and young people.

The response also includes guidance to help schools navigate difficult issues relating to political impartiality and discussions about Israel and the Middle East, ensuring antisemitism is identified and challenged wherever it occurs.

Schools and colleges will also be encouraged to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, while new guidance and resources will help education professionals recognise and respond to antisemitism with confidence.

The reforms are designed to ensure education professionals are better equipped to understand how antisemitism manifests today, challenge antisemitic behaviour confidently and support pupils through difficult and sensitive discussions.

The government will strengthen the tools available to schools and colleges to prevent incidents from escalating and ensure concerns are addressed consistently and effectively.

By helping young people challenge prejudice, navigate difficult debates and develop respect for those from different backgrounds and faiths, we will build a stronger, more confident and more united Britain.

This work sits alongside the government’s broader efforts to tackle extremism, address rising hatred and heal divisions in society. By ensuring antisemitism is recognised, understood and challenged effectively, schools and colleges can play a vital role in creating communities where everyone feels they belong and where our shared values are upheld.

Notes to editors:

  • The Government’s response includes action to:
    • encourage all schools and colleges to adopt the IHRA working definition of antisemitism.
    • introduce dedicated antisemitism training for leaders and safeguarding staff;
    • strengthen key guidance, including Keeping Children Safe in Education and guidance on political impartiality.
    • develop further resources to help staff identify and challenge antisemitism;
    • improve reporting and recording of antisemitic incidents.
    • provide enhanced support and advice for schools, colleges and local authorities dealing with complex cases.
    • support better understanding of Jewish life, identity and contemporary antisemitism across the education system.
    • strengthen support for schools and colleges discussing controversial issues and sensitive geopolitical events in a balanced, informed and impartial way.
  • The implementation group includes:
    • Jonathan Frisher - Student
    • Ms Michele Phillips - Assistant Director at Someone Else’s Eyes
    • Rabbi David Meyer OBE - CEO PaJeS (Partnerships for Jewish schools)
    • Noni Csogor - Senior research and Policy Manager, Sixth Form Colleges Association
    • Mark Rusling - Head of Training, Antisemitism Policy Trust
    • Ruben Persey - Vice President Campaigns, Union of Jewish Students
    • Natalie Highfield, Senior Policy & Equalities Advisor at NAHT, the school leadership union
    • Jeff Greenidge, Director for Diversity & Governance, Association of Colleges

items.title: Major boost for young people in Telford as Youth Hub opens to support them towards work
items.summary: New Youth Hub open Monday to Saturday in Telford Shopping Centre, offering employment support to young people in the area. CV advice, skills training, mental health support, housing advice, and careers guidance will be offered under one roo
items.bodyHtml:
• New Youth Hub open Monday to Saturday in Telford Shopping Centre, offering employment support to young people in the area.  

  • CV advice, skills training, mental health support, housing advice, and careers guidance will be offered under one roof to make getting the right support easier. 

  • Telford is latest in a national network of Youth Hubs created as part of Government’s  £2.5 billion investment in youth employment  

Young people in Telford are set to benefit from expanded employment support through the area’s first Youth Hub, as the government continues to deliver opportunity directly into the heart of the community. 

Youth Hubs are located in an expanding number of locations across the country such as libraries and community centres, offering a range of support to help young people move closer to employment.  

In Telford, the Youth Hub will be based in Telford Shopping Centre and will be open Monday to Friday for young people seeking support.  

It will follow the model of other Youth Hubs, which bring together Jobcentre Plus, local authority services, employers and training providers under one roof to provide vital help to get young people aged 16 to 24 the skills to get into work.  

Youth Hubs are a key part of the Government’s £2.5 billion youth employment support package. Over the next three years, the Government is expanding its network of Youth Hubs to over 360 local areas across Great Britain, with the aim that a young person is no more than one hour away from a Youth Hub by public transport. 

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: 

This new Youth Hub marks a major step forward for young people in Telford, delivering real support and opportunity right here in the community. 

We are determined to bring opportunity to every corner of the country because no matter where you grow up, you deserve the chance to earn, to learn and to get on in life. 

The Telford Youth Hub will be based at Telford College Skills Shop. Unit 103 Telford Shopping Centre, TF3 4AE. 

It will work with local partners including Telford College, Telford & Wrekin Council, Landau and CVS Telford and Wrekin to help young people overcome barriers to work and move into employment.  

Alongside supporting young people, the Telford College Skills Shop helps local businesses by equipping job seekers with qualifications and training they need to be workplace ready, including through its Retail and Hospitality Academy, which supports Telford Centre businesses train and upskill their workforce.

Executive Director of Partnerships and Employer Engagement at Telford College, Sarah Davies said: 

We’re proud to be delivering this project in Telford in partnership with DWP, Telford & Wrekin Council and Landau. Previously, many young people who needed this specialist support have had to travel to Shrewsbury to get it.  

Now it’s right here on their doorstep, with employment support, training, mentoring and wellbeing help all under one roof. That makes a real difference because an extra bus journey can be one more barrier between them and the help they need. 

The hub sits within the new Telford College Skills Shop, our initiative to bring skills and workforce development opportunities into the heart of the town centre, helping retailers and hospitality businesses train their teams and find the talent they need.

It will work with local partners including Telford College, Telford & Wrekin Council, Landau and CVS Telford and Wrekin to help young people overcome barriers to work and move into employment.  

Alongside supporting young people, the Telford College Skills Shop helps local businesses by equipping job seekers with qualifications and training they need to be workplace ready, including through its Retail and Hospitality Academy, which supports Telford Centre businesses train and upskill their workforce.

Additional Information 

  • Youth Hubs support young people aged 16–24. 

  • The programme brings together national and local partners to deliver integrated employment support. 

  • Further Youth Hubs will continue to roll out across Great Britain as part of the Government’s Youth Guarantee. 

Councillor Shirley Reynolds, Telford & Wrekin Council’s Cabinet Member for Children, Young People, Education, Employment and Skills, said: 

We’re thrilled to see the launch of the new youth hub which expands the support which is available for young people across Telford and Wrekin. 

Working with our partners, the hub will complement Telford Job Box, a free service at Southwater One in central Telford which offers a dedicated space where young people can receive tailored support and helps residents,       including young people, to access employment, training, and education opportunities. 

This runs alongside our Telford and Wrekin Skills Strategy and our Stay Near, Go Far campaign, where we’re continuing to broaden opportunities and raise awareness of the wide range of skills, learning, and employment support available to help people stay local and succeed. 

It will also further enhance our existing youth offer, which provides advice and information on activities, support and wellbeing, reinforcing our commitment to ensuring every young person in Telford and Wrekin feels valued, supported and empowered to thrive.

items.summary: The Prime Minister spoke to the Prime Minister of Poland Donald Tusk this morning. The two leaders began by condemning the continuation of aggressive Russian attacks on Ukraine. NATO Allies needed to continue to apply pressure on Russia and
items.bodyHtml:
The Prime Minister spoke to the Prime Minister of Poland Donald Tusk this morning.  

The two leaders began by condemning the continuation of aggressive Russian attacks on Ukraine. NATO Allies needed to continue to apply pressure on Russia and step up support for Ukraine through the winter, the leaders agreed.  

The two leaders discussed the value of a stronger UK-EU relationship to both sides, as the Prime Minister looked ahead to the upcoming UK-EU summit. The Prime Minister outlined the challenges posed by Made in Europe and set out his ambitions for a closer trading partnership with the EU to deliver growth in every postcode. 

The two leaders looking forward to speaking again soon.

items.title: Jailed Birmingham accountant ordered to repay more than £300,000 after targeting Covid support schemes
items.summary: Fraudster Zeeshan Ashraf has been handed a confiscation order of more than £300,000 Ashraf was jailed for three years and eight months last year after admitting five counts of fraud The 46-year-old defrauded the Eat Out to Help Out, Bounce
items.bodyHtml:
• Fraudster Zeeshan Ashraf has been handed a confiscation order of more than £300,000 

  • Ashraf was jailed for three years and eight months last year after admitting five counts of fraud 

  • The 46-year-old defrauded the Eat Out to Help Out, Bounce Back Loan, and Covid Job Retention schemes

A Birmingham accountant who defrauded Eat Out to Help Out and other Covid support schemes has been ordered to repay more than £300,000. 

Zeeshan Ashraf was handed a confiscation order of £307,690 at Birmingham Crown Court on Tuesday 13 October. 

Ashraf was jailed for three years and eight months at the same court in February 2025 after defrauding the Eat Out to Help Out, Bounce Back Loan, and Covid Job Retention schemes. 

The 46-year-old fraudulently obtained £268,102 between April 2020 and April 2021 and attempted to claim a further £52,733. 

Ashraf, of Glaisdale Road, Birmingham, has been given three months to pay the confiscation order. If he fails to do so, he could face a further two-and-a-half years in prison and would still owe the full amount. 

Alexander Grierson, Head of Asset Recovery at the Insolvency Service, said: 

Zeeshan Ashraf stole hundreds of thousands of pounds from schemes designed to support businesses during the pandemic. 

He has served time in prison for his crimes and has now been ordered to pay back more than £300,000.

This should send a clear message to fraudsters: a conviction and prison sentence do not necessarily mark the end of enforcement action. We will pursue the proceeds of crime wherever we can.

Ashraf used his accountancy company, A-Z Certified Accountants Limited, to secure three £50,000 Bounce Back Loans from separate banks in 2020. Businesses were only entitled to a single loan.

Ashraf claimed the company had turnovers between £215,000 and £244,000 when it was actually just £8,000, allowing him to obtain the maximum £50,000 available through each loan application. 

He claimed the loans would be used to support his business during the pandemic. However, he spent the £150,000 he secured on lifestyle purposes, property investments and the repayment of personal loans. 

Ashraf also fraudulently received £91,174 through the Covid Job Retention Scheme after making multiple false or unauthorised applications to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) on behalf of his business clients. 

Further fraudulent claims for £38,082 under the scheme were unsuccessful. 

He also stole £26,928 from the Eat Out to Help Out Scheme by submitting numerous claims on behalf of hospitality companies which either did not exist or did not operate in the restaurant trade. 

Ashraf unsuccessfully attempted to claim a further £14,651 through Eat Out to Help Out. 

The £307,690 confiscation order includes the money Ashraf fraudulently obtained plus an uplift reflecting changes in the value of money since 2020. The amount would have been even higher had Ashraf not previously repaid around £33,000 of the Bounce Back Loans. 

The original criminal investigations were carried out by HMRC and investigators who are now part of the Insolvency Service. The confiscation proceedings were conducted jointly by HMRC and the Insolvency Service, with the case prosecuted by the Crown Prosecution Service.

Further information 

  • Zeeshan Ashraf is of Glaisdale Road, Birmingham. His date of birth is 5 July 1980 

  • A-Z Certified Accountants Limited (company number 07546636) 

  • Directors can find information about their obligations and responsibilities at the Insolvency Service’s Director Information Hub 

  • Further information about the work of the Insolvency Service, and how to complain about financial misconduct.

items.title: Faster clinical trials bring cutting-edge treatments to patients
items.summary: Government hits ambitious target to speed up clinical trials with delivery times slashed by 35% UK life sciences sector boosted by faster, more competitive clinical trials which close the gap between research and treatment Patients benefit
items.bodyHtml:
• Government hits ambitious target to speed up clinical trials with delivery times slashed by 35%
  • UK life sciences sector boosted by faster, more competitive clinical trials which close the gap between research and treatment
  • Patients benefit from quicker access to treatments for cancer, heart disease and other serious conditions

NHS patients will receive potentially lifesaving treatments faster, as new clinical research delivery data released today (21 October 2026) shows the government has hit its ambitious clinical trials target. 

Trials for conditions ranging from cancer to heart disease were set up quicker, meaning patients could receive treatments sooner - easing pressure on the NHS and marking a boost for the UK’s life sciences sector.

The BEATRIX study, which offers pregnant women a government-backed vaccine against group B streptococcus to help prevent infant deaths and stillbirths, is one example of research becoming reality in less than 150 days.

The average set-up time for commercial trials in the UK dropped to 100 days in the 3 months to March this year, down from 153 in the same period last year. All of the 24 commercial trials during those months were set up within 150 days, exceeding the 95% of commercial trials set up within 150 days goal set out in the Life Sciences Sector Plan last year.

It comes after the Prime Minister set out 4 steps to give people living with brain cancer a faster route from research to treatment last week, following his meeting with Archie Goodburn and the Health and Social Care Secretary.

The progress is yet another milestone in the UK’s life sciences growth, with more than £3 billion in new public-private investment attracted through the first year of the plan.

Health Innovation Minister James Frith said:

For patients and their families, a clinical trial can offer hope of a treatment that once seemed unimaginable.

That’s why meeting this target is so important. It means more patients will get the cutting-edge care they need sooner.

This is part of our mission to get new treatments to patients faster and make the UK a global leader in medical research.

The data today shows that 100% of studies receiving combined Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and research ethics committee approval in September 2026 did so within 60 days.

Trials included the CHILL study, where the first participant was screened just 113 days after the study entered set-up. Meanwhile, Moderna’s Nova 301 study recruited 2,500 volunteers in just 9 weeks.

Faster set-up of clinical trials will help more patients to access a trial relevant to them, which is why today’s data also marks a crucial milestone for cancer patients.

The Prime Minister and Secretary of State for Health and Social Care last week set out in their meeting with Archie Goodburn their commitment to closing the translation gap between the lab and treatments that benefit patients in the clinic for rare cancers.

A new cancer trials accelerator will make the NHS the first-choice partner for cancer clinical trials, building on the success of the Cancer Vaccine Launch Pad and Vaccine Innovation Pathway.

Professor Lucy Chappell, National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Chief Executive Officer and Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) Chief Scientific Adviser, said:

Clinical trials change lives. Faster study set-up means patients can gain access to promising new treatments sooner, giving more people the opportunity to benefit from the latest advances in areas such as cancer, vaccines and rare diseases.

Through our Industry Hub, a one-stop shop for sponsors looking to run research in the UK, and our UK-wide network of commercial research delivery centres, NIHR is making it much easier to bring world-leading trials to the UK.

By continuing to push for the UK to remain one of the best places in the world to do clinical research, we’re driving life-changing innovation for patients and the public. We’re also attracting investment, creating skilled jobs and delivering growth that benefits communities across the country.

Through the NIHR Industry Hub, commercial research delivery centres and wider research infrastructure, sponsors have a clearer route into the system and access to the expertise, sites and delivery capability needed to run studies across the NHS.  

The reforms are designed to make the UK a faster, more efficient and more predictable place to run commercial clinical research. Faster set-up is one part of that story: the wider goal is stronger recruitment, reliable whole-study delivery and greater confidence among global sponsors choosing where to place research. 

Steve Bates OBE, Executive Chair of the Office for Life Sciences (OLS), said:

This government has set a clear ambition for Britain to become the world’s leading innovation nation, underpinned by an innovation-led, research-driven economy. Commercial clinical trials are central to that ambition, bringing investment and growth to communities across the country while also giving patients earlier access to potentially life-changing treatments.

Today’s announcement shows the significant progress made by the NIHR, the NHS and partners across the research system to reduce trial set-up times and deliver upon the commitments in the Life Sciences Sector Plan.

We must now build on this progress. Global competition for life sciences investment and clinical trials is intense, and sustained delivery will be essential if the UK is to increase the number of patients participating in commercial trials and ensure that people can benefit from research regardless of where they live.

Lawrence Tallon, MHRA Chief Executive, said:

A faster, more predictable clinical trials system is essential to helping patients access innovative treatments sooner and making the UK a more attractive destination for global life sciences investment.

Our new Strategy to 2030 sets out our ambition to deliver health and prosperity through scientific excellence. By working in partnership across the UK research ecosystem and internationally, we want to help create a clinical research environment that is faster, more agile and globally competitive - delivering real benefits for patients, researchers and the life sciences sector.

More trials in the UK also create wider benefits for communities through jobs, investment and stronger local economies.

The UK government is also driving a wider transformation of the clinical trials landscape, spanning regulation, costing and contracting, study set-up, delivery capacity and recruitment. 

This includes investment through the Voluntary Scheme for Branded Medicine Pricing, Access and Growth (VPAG) investment programme to strengthen research delivery capacity and capability, alongside a clearer national route for industry through the NIHR Industry Hub and commercial research delivery centres.

Better research delivery strengthens the UK’s offer to sponsors, supports investment, skills and research capability, and creates more opportunities for patients to take part in transformative studies.

It comes as part of the government’s push to make the UK a life sciences superpower, including with the new Health Data Research Service (HDRS), a flagship commitment of the government’s 10 Year Health Plan and Life Sciences Sector Plan.

Backed by up to £600 million from government and the Wellcome Trust, HDRS will bring NHS and research data from across the UK into a single, secure system for approved research. Scientists will be able to identify eligible patients and recruit participants more quickly.

Britain has some of the world’s most powerful health data, but it is fragmented across different systems and organisations. Joining it up will help researchers understand how diseases develop, find suitable participants and translate discoveries into treatments.

Further stakeholder comments

Richard Torbett, Chief Executive of the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry (ABPI), said:

These figures demonstrate welcome progress in accelerating trial set-up, and we applaud the hard work that has gone into this across government, the NHS, regulators and the research community.

With international competition intensifying, it’s vital that gains in first-site set-up are replicated across every subsequent site and, most importantly, translate into more patients taking part in trials. The ambition to double recruitment, and then double it again, is the right one. Achieving it will take a concerted effort to reverse consecutive years of declining recruitment, and we look forward to working with the government to deliver on these shared goals.

Phillippa Brown, Head of Development Operations at GSK, said:

It’s encouraging to see the continued positive results in clinical trial set-up times, establishing a more predictable foundation for research.

To truly unlock the UK’s potential as a leader in clinical trials, we need sustained action to provide the resources and financial incentives for NHS sites to recruit more patients to clinical trials, while also harnessing the potential of health data and improving NHS access to innovation.

We stand ready to support this work, which will create the necessary infrastructure to enable sustainable life sciences growth and ultimately will deliver innovation to patients faster.

A Vertex Global Clinical Operations spokesperson said:

Our organisation has been regularly partnering with the Industry Hub since its launch early in 2026. The early signs are encouraging; we can see the potential in accelerating UK clinical research set-up and delivery, offering predictability for sponsors to determine study activation times.

Access points for sponsors are streamlined via our assigned key account manager and project manager. We have started to see the impact: a recent study saw site activation times of 112 days versus planned 120, under the government target.

Jonathan Brotherton, Chief Executive of University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust and Chair of the Shelford Group, said:

Faster trial set-up is good for patients, for the NHS and for the life sciences industry.

We are proud of the contribution the ten Shelford Group trusts are making, both in establishing clinical trials within the 150-day target and delivering more than a third of the UK’s Global and European research firsts.

Shelford Group trusts have made progress by working together to strengthen and harmonise our study set-up approaches - adopting shared tools that get trials set up more quickly.

We know there is more to do to improve the delivery of complex clinical trials and ensure that patients can benefit from research opportunities as quickly as possible and we’re committed to this.

Professor Frankie Swords, National Medical Director, NHS England and DHSC, said: 

A strong and thriving clinical research environment is good for everyone - patients of today, patients of tomorrow and of course our staff too. 

Making studies quicker and easier to set up gives research teams a better platform to recruit and deliver trials and creates more opportunities for people to take part in innovative research. 

Our ambition is to make research more routinely available right across the NHS, including in neighbourhood services and primary care, so that more people can benefit closer to home.

items.bodyHtml:
• Local government playbook written to support Prime Minister’s aim to take power out of Whitehall. 
  • Launched today, the playbook is a practical guide which local leaders can use to design and deliver better public services.
  • The Playbook launch is marked by an anniversary event in Sheffield celebrating the success of the Test, Learn and Grow programme.

Local leaders supported to drive change in their communities and improve public services with the launch of a new playbook to support decentralisation.

Upon taking office, the Prime Minister promised a clear break from centralisation, pledging to shift power away from Westminster and return decision-making to the people and communities where they live and work.

Launched today, the Playbook has been developed by the Test, Learn and Grow programme to help central and local government design public services to better meet the needs of local communities.

The programme works directly with local partners to design and deliver better public services. For example, Test, Learn and Grow supported Liverpool City Council to take a data-led, strategic approach to temporary accommodation for people experiencing homelessness. Improving the use and quality of data led to nightly temporary accommodation costs dropping by 30%, saving £6 million.

Cabinet Office Minister, Sally Jameson MP, said:

The Prime Minister promised to take power away from Westminster and return decision making to communities.

We know local leaders are best placed to integrate public services and respond to the needs of their residents, which is why we must empower them to set the policies that work for their areas.

That is why I am so pleased to announce this Playbook that will help places adopt regionalised ways of working and further kickstart the biggest transition of power out of Whitehall.

Cllr Fran Belbin, Leader of Sheffield City Council, said:

There is so much good work that takes place across the city every single day to help and support children from less advantaged backgrounds to help them achieve everything they want to.

We are delighted that so much of this work has been able to be showcased on a national platform through the Test, Learn & Grow pilot projects over the past 12 months. We look forward to this continuing over the next year and showing the country the fantastic work taking place right here.

To mark the launch of the Playbook, Minister Sally Jameson delivered a keynote address at the Sheffield event, highlighting examples of the programme’s work at the Sheffield event, highlighting examples of the programme’s work.

The Playbook enables central, regional, and local government teams to adopt a similar test and learn approach. By starting small, adapting quickly, sharing learning and working directly with places as equal partners, it aims to improve public services from the ground up.

Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) is a three-year UK public service reform programme testing new ways of designing and delivering public services that are closer to the people using them. It sits at the heart of the Government’s ambition to rewire the state: so that local leaders and services closest to the problem can join up and design solutions for and specific to the needs of the communities they serve. 

Launched in 2025 across ten local authority partners, the programme is tackling six core policy challenges - from improving employment outcomes for young people to reducing violence against women and girls.

The publication of the Playbook will be marked by a ‘Test, Learn and Grow’ one-year-on celebration event in Sheffield, hosted jointly by the Cabinet Office, Sheffield City Council and South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority.

Notes to editors:

  • The ‘Test, Learn and Grow’ Playbook will also be officially launched as a live guidance resource on GOV.UK, with regular updates as the programme learns more.

items.title: Consultation opens on Fornax permit draft decision
items.summary: The company wants to operate an energy from waste plant at Merchant Park, Newton Aycliffe in County Durham. Under the permit Fornax has applied for, the site would be able to accept clinical, commercial and industrial hazardous waste for in
items.bodyHtml:
The company wants to operate an energy from waste plant at Merchant Park, Newton Aycliffe in County Durham.

Under the permit Fornax has applied for, the site would be able to accept clinical, commercial and industrial hazardous waste for incineration in a high temperature thermal treatment facility.

After reviewing comments and evidence from a previous public consultation last summer, the Environment Agency is ‘minded to’ issue the permit.

This means after exploring the issues and concerns that have been raised, it can’t find any reason to refuse the application but is yet to make a final decision.

The draft permit document and draft decision document can be found at the Environment Agency’s consultation website.

Consultation open until 1 December

The draft decision document explains the Environment Agency’s decision-making and outlines how it has considered the comments from the previous consultation.

The draft permit outlines the conditions the operator would need to meet if the permit is granted.

The consultation will be open until 1 December 2026.

The information in the link also explains what the Environment Agency can and can’t take into account when deciding on the application.

Gary Wallace, Area Environment Manager in the North East, said:

We recognise the increased local interest around this proposed facility and have carefully considered all the information and consultation comments.

We will only grant the permit if we are satisfied the application meets all legal requirements and provides a high level of protection to the environment and human health.

It’s important the public have the opportunity to read the draft documents and provide comments. We’ll then make our final decision once we’ve reviewed consultation responses.

The Environment Agency assesses applications for environmental permits under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 (EPR).

Its role is to assess the application and decide if it meets all requirements under relevant environmental legislation, including ensuring that the proposed plant would not cause any significant pollution of the environment or harm to human health.

People can respond to the consultation directly on the website or alternatively by email to pscpublicresponse@environment-agency.gov.uk

Further background

Consultation responses

  • Responses to the consultation can be made electronically.
  • Information on the website explains how people can view the consultation documents and how they can provide comments. It also explains what the Environment Agency can and can’t take into account when deciding on the application.
  • Anyone wishing to comment on the proposals is urged to read the documentation online before responding directly on the website or by email to pscpublicresponse@environment-agency.gov.uk 
  • Those unable to view the documents or make representation via the consultation website or by email should contact the Environment Agency on 03708 506 506.

Environmental permits 

  • Environmental permits set out strict legal conditions by which an operator must comply in order to protect people and the environment. Should an environmental permit be issued, the Environment Agency has responsibility for enforcing its conditions.
  • The Environment Agency’s powers include enforcement notices, suspension and revocation of permits, fines and ultimately criminal sanctions, including prosecution.
  • The Environment Agency may only refuse a permit if it does not meet one or more of the legal requirements under environmental legislation, including if it will have a significant impact on the environment or harm human health. If all the requirements are met, we are legally required to issue a permit
