items.title: Drivers to save up to £300 when installing EV chargers at home, as government slashes unnecessary red tape
items.summary: People can now save up to £300 on charging at home without a driveway from today (21 October 2026) as the government has slashed red tape to make it cheaper, easier and quicker to install. Drivers will no longer need planning permission to
items.bodyHtml:
People can now save up to £300 on charging at home without a driveway from today (21 October 2026) as the government has slashed red tape to make it cheaper, easier and quicker to install.

Drivers will no longer need planning permission to install cross-pavement chargers which run under pavements from people’s homes to their cars. This will save drivers up to £300 on installation and open up home charging for as little as 2p per mile. This is all part of the government’s bid to deliver ‘everyday fixes’ that help people with the cost of living.

It comes as September 2026 saw another record-breaking month for UK electric car sales – up 36% in a year, with nearly 100,000 electric cars sold in a single month alone. Sales have been boosted by the government’s Electric Car Grant (ECG), which has now helped over 190,000 drivers save up to £3,750 off a new electric vehicle (EV).

Buses and Local Transport Minister Simon Lightwood said:

We’re saving drivers up to £300 off the cost of installing home charging by cutting unnecessary red tape.

The EV transition is in full swing – sales are up 36% on last year and over 190,000 have saved thousands making the switch in the last year alone.

Cross-pavement charging means residents without off-street parking can plug into cheaper domestic electricity prices, helping them access savings of up to £1,750 on running costs.

By slashing unnecessary red tape for these home chargers, the government is speeding up installations, putting money back in drivers’ pockets and revving up the transition to electric.

Changes to permitted development rights also mean it will be quicker and cheaper for charge point operators to install larger, higher-powered public EV charging hubs.

Vicky Edmonds, CEO of EVA England, said:

This might look like a small planning change, but for someone without a driveway, it could make the difference between being able to afford an electric car and ruling one out altogether. Removing the need for planning permission for cross-pavement charging is a really welcome and meaningful step towards a fairer transition.

Our research found that 60% of petrol and diesel drivers without off-street parking would never consider an EV. Being able to connect a car parked on the street to cheaper home electricity could help change that. It’s now up to local authorities and landlords to make these solutions easier to access in practice.

Dickson Abegunde, Director of Strategic Partnerships at Zoopla, said:

For buyers considering an electric vehicle, access to charging can be an important factor when choosing a home. Zoopla was proud to be the first property website to help buyers discover nearby on-street chargers and search for homes with EV charging facilities.

The government’s decision to remove planning permission requirements for qualifying cross pavement charging solutions is another welcome step towards making EV ownership more accessible, particularly for households without off-street parking.

Alongside this, the government has launched 2 consultations to make home charging easier and ensure new buildings are equipped with chargers, so people can plug in with ease.

Tenants and leaseholders could get a clearer, quicker, and more consistent route to installing a charge point, thanks to clear guidance for landlords on how to handle the process. The government is also considering mandatory requirements for landlords and freeholders to make it harder to refuse renters’ applications.

Building regulations could also be updated to ensure that charge points are installed in new and refurbished covered car parks.

Consultations on other changes to home charging

Respond to government consultations by 16 December 2026:

  • amending the building regulations: electric vehicle charging infrastructure

  • expanding electric vehicle charging access for tenants and leaseholders

Roads media enquiries

Media enquiries 0300 7777 878

Switchboard 0300 330 3000

items.title: Domestic abusers face eviction as survivors gain housing rights
items.summary: For the first time, domestic abuse survivors will be protected in social housing law without having to flee, helping them keep their tenancy and stay safely in their home while the perpetrator is made to leave. A new measure tabled for the
items.bodyHtml:
For the first time, domestic abuse survivors will be protected in social housing law without having to flee, helping them keep their tenancy and stay safely in their home while the perpetrator is made to leave.

A new measure tabled for the Social Housing Bill today (Tuesday 20 October) will stop survivors having to prove abuse again where a protection order is already in place. The proposals strengthen reforms in the Bill that will protect joint tenancies from abusive partners, helping end the choice between staying in danger and losing a home and support network.

Council tenants will also get stronger support to take charge of repairs, maintenance and communal services through a simpler Right to Manage, giving residents a clearer route to demand better when services fail.

Together, the reforms will put tenants first, raise standards and protect social homes, alongside the biggest investment in new social and affordable housing in a generation.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said:

No survivor should have to choose between staying with their abuser or losing their home, community and support network. We are changing the law so the perpetrator, not the survivor, can be made to leave.

Abusers will no longer be able to use a shared home as a weapon of control. Survivors will get the certainty of knowing their tenancy and their social home are protected.

We are also putting power back in tenants’ hands so they can demand better when services fail, while protecting the social homes communities need for generations to come.

New laws will help keep more social homes in the hands of communities, giving councils and housing associations twice as long to consider buying them before they leave the sector, alongside better information to help them make that decision.

Recognising that affordable homes can be particularly difficult to replace in rural communities, councils will have more control over protecting eligible areas from the Right to Buy, with the wider package of reforms expected to keep an additional 18,000 homes in the social sector over the next decade.

Alongside our £442 million investment to tackle rough sleeping, the Bill will also help tackle homelessness earlier by requiring councils and public services to identify people at risk and work together before they lose their home, while housing associations will be required to offer suitable homes to households referred by councils unless there is good reason not to. Veterans will also face fewer barriers to getting help, with plans to ensure they can seek homelessness support from any council in England regardless of local connection rules.

Kate Henderson, Chief Executive of the National Housing Federation, said:

Housing associations strongly support the government’s objectives in the Social Housing Bill to safeguard our social homes for future generations, tackle homelessness and to strengthen protections for survivors of domestic abuse.

No one should be forced to lose their home to escape abuse. We strongly welcome new powers to protect survivors’ ability to remain safely in their homes and reduce their risk of homelessness.

With almost 180,000 children growing up in temporary accommodation, we need councils, housing associations, mayors and the government all working together to end the housing crisis. Housing associations are committed to tackling homelessness in all its forms, as well as other damaging consequences of our broken housing system, such as overcrowding. We will continue to work with government to ensure these proposals deliver on our shared objectives, while strengthening our partnerships with councils to help more families access safe, secure and affordable homes.

Rachael Williamson, Executive Director of Policy, Communications and External Affairs, Chartered Institute of Housing, said:

We welcome these measures, particularly the strengthened protections for domestic abuse survivors, which reflect the importance of ensuring people are not forced to choose between their safety and their home. CIH has worked closely with government and sector partners throughout the development of the Bill to make the case for stronger protections for tenants, earlier action to prevent homelessness and measures that support the long-term future of social housing. We will continue to do so as the Bill progresses.

Alongside long-term investment in social and affordable housing, these reforms have the potential to improve outcomes for residents, strengthen communities and help ensure social housing continues to meet the needs of current and future generations.

Also confirmed today, from April 2027 Tenant Management Organisations that manage council housing will be brought under Freedom of Information rules. This means residents will be able to request information about services such as repairs, estate management, and rent collection, improving transparency and making these organisations more open and accountable.

Backed by £39 billion investment in council, social and affordable housing, the biggest in a generation, the measures will help protect the homes communities rely on while building the new homes they need.

Additional Information:

  • The Social Housing Bill was introduced to Parliament on 14 May 2026. The amendments will be tabled as the Bill progresses through its Commons stages. These include:
  • Extending the notification period for social housing disposals from 4 to 8 weeks;
  • Including additional property information in the notification for social housing disposals to include type of rent the home was previously let at;
  • Allowing councils to designate eligible rural areas themselves against specified criteria in order to exempt them from the Right to Buy. Currently councils are required to apply formally to Government for designation, and this will reduce bureaucracy;
  • Bolstering the discretionary possession grounds within the Bill’s domestic abuse tenancy reforms, streamlining the process for victims by ensuring the existence of a relevant protective order is sufficient for the court to consider to take action;
  • Modernising the social housing Right to Manage framework, including clearer and more proportionate governance requirements, stronger information-sharing requirements and new safeguards where serious failures put residents at risk
  • Introducing a new statutory ‘Duty to Collaborate’, requiring key public bodies to take proactive steps to identify households at risk of homelessness and take coordinated action to prevent homelessness or address it sooner;
  • Introducing a new statutory ‘Duty to Offer’, which will require a private registered provider to offer suitable accommodation to a homeless household referred to them by a local housing authority, unless they have a good reason not to do so; and
  • Providing a power for the Secretary of State to set out circumstances where local connection referrals must not apply, which the government intends to use for armed forces veterans.
  • This is backed by the government’s £39bn investment in social and affordable housing, the biggest in a generation
  • The social housing Right to Manage allows local authority tenants to take responsibility for managing housing services through a Tenant Management Organisation. It is separate from the Right to Manage available to qualifying leaseholders. This comes as new strengthened measures will be introduced to submit Freedom of Information requests to Tenant Management Organisations.

For the first time, domestic abuse survivors will be protected in social housing law without having to flee, helping them keep their tenancy and stay safely in their home while the perpetrator is made to leave.

The proposals strengthen reforms in the Bill that will protect joint tenancies from abusive partners, helping end the choice between staying in danger and losing a home and support network.

Council tenants will also get stronger support to take charge of repairs, maintenance and communal services through a simpler Right to Manage, giving residents a clearer route to demand better when services fail.

Together, the reforms will put tenants first, raise standards and protect social homes, alongside the biggest investment in new social and affordable housing in a generation.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said:


  No survivor should have to choose between staying with their abuser or losing their home, community and support network. We are changing the law so the perpetrator, not the survivor, can be made to leave.

  Abusers will no longer be able to use a shared home as a weapon of control. Survivors will get the certainty of knowing their tenancy and their social home are protected.

  We are also putting power back in tenants’ hands so they can demand better when services fail, while protecting the social homes communities need for generations to come.


New laws will help keep more social homes in the hands of communities, giving councils and housing associations twice as long to consider buying them before they leave the sector, alongside better information to help them make that decision.

Recognising that affordable homes can be particularly difficult to replace in rural communities, councils will have more control over protecting eligible areas from the Right to Buy, with the wider package of reforms expected to keep an additional 18,000 homes in the social sector over the next decade.

Alongside our £442 million investment to tackle rough sleeping, the Bill will also help tackle homelessness earlier by requiring councils and public services to identify people at risk and work together before they lose their home, while housing associations will be required to offer suitable homes to households referred by councils unless there is good reason not to. Veterans will also face fewer barriers to getting help, with plans to ensure they can seek homelessness support from any council in England regardless of local connection rules.

Kate Henderson, Chief Executive of the National Housing Federation, said:


  Housing associations strongly support the government’s objectives in the Social Housing Bill to safeguard our social homes for future generations, tackle homelessness and to strengthen protections for survivors of domestic abuse.

  No one should be forced to lose their home to escape abuse. We strongly welcome new powers to protect survivors’ ability to remain safely in their homes and reduce their risk of homelessness.

Backed by £39 billion investment in council, social and affordable housing, the biggest in a generation, the measures will help protect the homes communities rely on while building the new homes they need.

items.title: Domestic abuser who suffocated former partner now jailed after sentence increased
items.summary: Aiden Ford, 40, of Hanham, Bristol, had his suspended sentence of three years increased to an immediate sentence of four years and three months’ imprisonment after the Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP, referred his case to the Court of
items.bodyHtml:
Aiden Ford, 40, of Hanham, Bristol, had his suspended sentence of three years increased to an immediate sentence of four years and three months’ imprisonment after the Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP, referred his case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme. 

The court heard that Ford and the victim began a relationship in September 2024. Between February and August 2025, Ford subjected her to a campaign of repeated violent assaults and coercive and controlling behaviour including trapping her in his home, making threats to her life, and relentlessly contacting her after she tried to end the relationship. 

On one occasion, Ford forced the victim into his car and drove to a secluded area, where he restrained her in the passenger seat. The victim feared for her life as Ford violently assaulted her and suffocated her with his forearm. 

After the victim reported the abuse, the offender persistently pressured and ultimately persuaded the victim to withdraw her statements to the police.  

The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves KC MP said: 

Aiden Ford subjected his victim to a sustained and terrifying campaign of violence and coercive control, leaving her genuinely fearing for her life. 

There is no excuse, and no place for domestic abuse in our society. Tackling violence against women and girls is my number one priority, and I welcome the Court of Appeal’s decision to overturn Ford’s suspended sentence and increase his sentence following my referral.

On 11 June 2026, at Cardiff Crown Court, Aiden Ford was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment suspended for three years for one count of controlling and coercive behaviour, one count of suffocation, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of perverting the course of justice.  

On 20 October 2026, at the Court of Appeal, his sentence was increased to four years and three months’ imprisonment.

items.title: Water company bosses update National Drought Group on resilience
items.summary: Water company chief executives were called before the National Drought Group yesterday to update on the actions they are taking to protect customer supplies after government instructed daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels. Bosses
items.bodyHtml:
Water company chief executives were called before the National Drought Group yesterday to update on the actions they are taking to protect customer supplies after government instructed daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels.

Bosses set out measures being taken to protect customer supplies after severe drought was declared in parts of England last week, including sending less water from reservoirs into local rivers and reducing water pressure, where appropriate, overnight.  

Water companies are also speeding up leak detection and working to transfer water from elsewhere in the network to support the lowest reservoirs. These steps come after the government told water companies and the Environment Agency to put public supplies first. 

Water Minister Emma Hardy, who chaired yesterday’s meeting, said:   

Having instructed water companies to carry out daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels, while improving water quality checks, it’s right that the National Drought Group has now heard directly from water company bosses on the action they’re taking. 

It’s encouraging that these efforts are starting to ease the pressure on public supplies, but water companies must continue to step up their efforts, and we will keep holding them to account. 

While customer water supplies will not be interrupted, declaring a severe drought allowed us to ensure proactive steps are taken to safeguard water.

Although water companies remain responsible for maintaining public water supplies, we can all help by thinking about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks.

The National Drought Group heard that while the first half of October has been dry, wet weather is also expected to spread in later this week which could help water resources. The Environment Agency has said at least 120% of average rainfall is needed over the next six months for the country to be considered out of drought by the start of spring. 

The expert group – which includes the Met Office, Government, regulators, water companies, the National Farmers’ Union, the Canal & River Trust, anglers, hydrologists, and conservation experts – has again urged people to use water wisely in the coming weeks and months to protect supplies and the environment.   

Last week, the Government declared severe drought in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. The South East and South West have experienced their driest April to September in over a century, impacting reservoir levels in that area – particularly Ardingly in West Sussex and Wimbleball in Somerset.  

While customer supplies are uninterrupted, declaring severe drought allowed additional proactive steps to be taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs. Since then,   enhanced engagement has started with Local Resilience Forums in the severe drought areas to coordinate risk assessment and preparedness across local communities. 

The National Drought Group have been meeting regularly since August to coordinate the response to this year’s unprecedented dry weather and hold organisations to account for their actions.

The Environment Agency has stressed the need for drought plans to be translated into timely action, including quickly fixing leaks, communicating with customers about using water wisely, and submitting early applications to the government where restrictions on non-essential business use may be needed. 

  • The Environment Agency has granted drought permits to South West Water and South East Water to reduce the amount of water released from its reservoirs into local rivers. (Wimbleball into the River Exe and Ardingly into the River Ouse) 

  • Temporary pumps have also been put in place to help move water around the area supplied by South West Water’s Stithians reservoir in Cornwall, and Wessex Water is preparing applications for seven further drought permits, which the Environment Agency will prioritise on receipt. 

  • Applications for non-essential use bans by South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water are under consideration by the Environment Secretary. 

  • Fish rescue plans are being put in place in case reservoir levels fall further and action is needed to protect wildlife. 

Environment Agency Chief Executive Philip Duffy said:

The rain is welcome, but the drought is far from over. It will bring some welcome respite for farmers and the environment, but we need sustained rainfall to refill depleted reservoirs and help rivers and wildlife recover.

Water companies must act now to secure public water supplies and reduce pressure on our rivers and wildlife. The public can help too. Small changes in how we use water can make a real difference. Every drop counts.

Met Office Business Manager, John Loynd, said:

September and the first half of October continued the pattern of below-average rainfall across many parts of England, adding to existing drought pressures in some areas.

While more unsettled conditions are now affecting parts of the UK and bringing spells of rain and strong winds, it remains too early to say whether this will deliver the widespread, sustained rainfall needed to make a significant difference to the drought situation.

The Met Office will continue to work closely with the Environment Agency and water companies to monitor conditions and provide the latest forecasts and climate information.

CEO of Waterwise, Nicci Russell, said:

Water is scarce in England - and we all need to make sure we waste less, at home and at work.  

There are more of us than ever before, we’re using on average more than we used to, and the climate emergency means the water isn’t always available when we need it. Nothing happens without water.

items.title: Armed Forces, NHS and allies test UK battlefield injury response
items.summary: The Armed Forces, NHS and international partners conduct UK medical resilience exercise. Lessons from the war in Ukraine have been used to strengthen UK frontline care, medical resilience and innovation. The exercise demonstrates the Strate
items.bodyHtml:
• The Armed Forces, NHS and international partners conduct UK medical resilience exercise.
  • Lessons from the war in Ukraine have been used to strengthen UK frontline care, medical resilience and innovation.
  • The exercise demonstrates the Strategic Defence Review’s whole-of-society approach to national security.

The Armed Forces and the NHS took part in a joint exercise last week to strengthen the UK’s ability to treat Armed Forces personnel injured during conflict.

The wargame, led by Defence Medical Command, explored how the Armed Forces, the NHS and healthcare providers would work together to support military patients returning to the UK from a range of future operational scenarios.

Participants assessed plans for civilian health services to treat military patients returning to the UK after receiving life-saving care overseas at the point of injury and after potentially travelling vast distances.

Defence Minister Lord Coaker said:

Keeping people safe takes more than one organisation—it takes all of us working together. This exercise brought Defence, the NHS and our allies around the same table to put that partnership into practice.

By testing our plans now, we are building the trusted relationships and readiness needed to protect our country and care for those who serve.

Participants assessed plans for civilian health services to treat military patients returning to the UK.

They also explored medical lessons from Ukraine, including challenges for increasing hospital capacity, maintaining civilian access to health care, large-scale rehabilitation, likely injuries requiring treatment, and mental health care support.

The exercise is part of an ongoing UK and international programme to ensure medical preparedness keeps pace with the changing character of warfare.

Surgeon General Major General Phil Carter, said:

Wargames like this are a vital part planning the Operational Patient Care Pathway, helping ensure Defence, NHS, our health services, and our allies can manage returning casualties while continuing to care for civilian patients.

The war in Ukraine reinforces the need to keep learning, adapting and innovating. By regularly exercising together, we strengthen our readiness and national resilience.

Dr Mike Prentice, National Director for NHS Resilience, said:

The NHS has a vital role to play in the UK’s preparedness for future conflict. By working closely with the Ministry of Defence, we are putting our plans to the test, identifying potential challenges and strengthening the partnerships we would rely on in a crisis.

Preparing together now means we can ensure the NHS is ready to care for military personnel returning home, while continuing to meet the needs of the public - whatever the circumstances.

Part of routine preparedness planning, the exercise supports the Strategic Defence Review’s emphasis on resilience, readiness and a whole-of-society approach to national security.

Defence Medical Command is investing in life-saving innovations, including dried blood products to more easily restore blood supplies on the battlefield, and tranexamic acid autoinjector pens which cause clotting to reduce blood loss at the point of injury, as well as modern field hospital equipment and enhanced equipment to care for casualties.

Defence Medical Command is also learning lessons from the conflict in Ukraine including techniques to protect field hospitals, equipment and medical personnel from attack, advanced trauma training, stronger supply chains and the development of new technologies such as portable ultrasound equipment and uncrewed evacuation systems.

Lessons from the wargame will inform future planning across the Armed Forces and civilian health services, with further exercises scheduled in the coming months.

The Wargame was attended by military and civilian health providers from around the UK and the US and Canada.

Notes to editors:

Imagery of the event can be found here: 2026.10.15 RAMP Wargame - Defence Imagery

The Armed Forces, NHS and international partners conduct UK medical resilience exercise.
  Lessons from the war in Ukraine have been used to strengthen UK frontline care, medical resilience and innovation.
  The exercise demonstrates the Strategic Defence Review’s whole-of-society approach to national security.


The Armed Forces and the NHS took part in a joint exercise last week to strengthen the UK’s ability to treat Armed Forces personnel injured during conflict.

The wargame, led by Defence Medical Command, explored how the Armed Forces, the NHS and healthcare providers would work together to support military patients returning to the UK from a range of future operational scenarios.

Participants assessed plans for civilian health services to treat military patients returning to the UK after receiving life-saving care overseas at the point of injury and after potentially travelling vast distances.

Defence Minister Lord Coaker said:


  Keeping people safe takes more than one organisation—it takes all of us working together. This exercise brought Defence, the NHS and our allies around the same table to put that partnership into practice.

  By testing our plans now, we are building the trusted relationships and readiness needed to protect our country and care for those who serve.



Participants assessed plans for civilian health services to treat military patients returning to the UK.

They also explored medical lessons from Ukraine, including challenges for increasing hospital capacity, maintaining civilian access to health care, large-scale rehabilitation, likely injuries requiring treatment, and mental health care support.

The exercise is part of an ongoing UK and international programme to ensure medical preparedness keeps pace with the changing character of warfare.

Surgeon General Major General Phil Carter, said:


  Wargames like this are a vital part planning the Operational Patient Care Pathway, helping ensure Defence, NHS, our health services, and our allies can manage returning casualties while continuing to care for civilian patients.

  The war in Ukraine reinforces the need to keep learning, adapting and innovating. By regularly exercising together, we strengthen our readiness and national resilience.


Dr Mike Prentice, National Director for NHS Resilience, said:


  The NHS has a vital role to play in the UK’s preparedness for future conflict. By working closely with the Ministry of Defence, we are putting our plans to the test, identifying potential challenges and strengthening the partnerships we would rely on in a crisis.

  Preparing together now means we can ensure the NHS is ready to care for military personnel returning home, while continuing to meet the needs of the public - whatever the circumstances.


Part of routine preparedness planning, the exercise supports the Strategic Defence Review’s emphasis on resilience, readiness and a whole-of-society approach to national security.

Defence Medical Command is investing in life-saving innovations, including dried blood products to more easily restore blood supplies on the battlefield, and tranexamic acid autoinjector pens which cause clotting to reduce blood loss at the point of injury, as well as modern field hospital equipment and enhanced equipment to care for casualties.

Defence Medical Command is also learning lessons from the conflict in Ukraine including techniques to protect field hospitals, equipment and medical personnel from attack, advanced trauma training, stronger supply chains and the development of new technologies such as portable ultrasound equipment and uncrewed evacuation systems.

Lessons from the wargame will inform future planning across the Armed Forces and civilian health services, with further exercises scheduled in the coming months.


The Wargame was attended by military and civilian health providers from around the UK and the US and Canada.

items.title: British businesses secure £330 million of African infrastructure contracts
items.summary: Project deals announced as government backs closer trade ties with fast-growing West and Central African markets UK Export Finance increases its exposure capacity across West and Central Africa by £1.7 billion, creating more opportunity for
items.bodyHtml:
• Project deals announced as government backs closer trade ties with fast-growing West and Central African markets
  • UK Export Finance increases its exposure capacity across West and Central Africa by £1.7 billion, creating more opportunity for British exporters

British businesses are set to secure more than £330 million of export contracts to help deliver nine major infrastructure projects across Guinea and Benin.

The contracts will see UK companies supplying goods and services for projects spanning education, clean water, electricity transmission and government infrastructure, supporting jobs and growth at home while delivering vital infrastructure overseas.

The deals are being supported by £1.1 billion in financing and guarantees from UK Export Finance (UKEF), the government’s export credit agency.

They are being announced as the fifth UK-West and Central Francophone Africa Trade and Investment Forum (WCAF) opens today in Conakry, Guinea, bringing together British businesses and potential partners from across the region.

UKEF is also increasing its exposure capacity across the region by £1.7 billion, giving it greater capacity to support future projects involving British exporters.

Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said:

These deals are a major win for UK businesses, helping them secure new contracts in fast-growing markets and driving jobs and growth across the United Kingdom.

By backing projects like these, UK Export Finance is helping British firms win work overseas, creating opportunities for communities here at home while strengthening our trade partnerships across West and Central Africa.

Tim Reid, CEO of UK Export Finance, said:

British businesses have won a huge number of contracts to support key infrastructure projects across the region in recent years, driving job creation in the UK while helping our partners in francophone Africa build the infrastructure they need.

This is part of the reason we hold the WCAF, we’ve seen many deals signed over the years, and it highlights how UKEF can make a real difference around the world while driving growth in every postcode of the UK.

UKEF is providing finance worth £75 million to support a large-scale education infrastructure programme delivering new primary and secondary schools across four regions, improving access to education for thousands of children through modern classrooms, sanitation and related facilities, with the contract won by Planet One.

A further £91 million will back the Guinea Regional Water Project, a multi-region programme expanding access to clean, potable water through new treatment and distribution infrastructure, delivered by UK-headquartered Aqua Africa, which has previously secured UKEF-backed financing for water infrastructure in the region.

UKEF is also providing £129 million towards the La Cotiere Conakry Transmission project in Guinea, part of a wider electricity network programme to improve power distribution around the country’s coastal region, with the contract secured by Elecnor and expected to create UK supply-chain opportunities in transmission equipment, grid technology and engineering services.

In Benin, UKEF is providing finance of £82 million which will help fund a new government administrative complex, consolidating public services within a modern urban development, with the contract awarded to ACC UK Group Ltd and opportunities for UK firms to contribute design, engineering, security systems and specialist building services.

WCAF V, hosted by UKEF in partnership with DMA Invest and the Guinean government, will take place until 21 October 2026.

Atam Sandhu, CEO of DMA Invest, added:

WCAF is about turning relationships into results. Over five editions, our ambition at DMA has remained clear: to bring governments, businesses and financiers together to help move priority projects from discussion towards delivery. We extend our sincere thanks to the Government and people of Guinea for hosting WCAF V in Conakry, and for the leadership, commitment and hospitality that have brought this growing partnership together.

items.title: Operational update 20 October – UK military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
items.summary: The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, given escalating Houthi attacks in the region. The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical n
items.bodyHtml:
The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, given escalating Houthi attacks in the region. 

The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets. These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis. The UK will provide an RAF A400M to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia, alongside UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers. 

This support builds on the UK’s existing defensive military contribution to Saudi Arabia, including the deployment of air defence equipment to protect against missiles and drone attacks. It also includes an extension of air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi defensive air operations including to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen that threaten the Saudi and Yemeni people. 

The Houthis’ attempts to destabilise the region and undermine the security and stability of the Middle East are unacceptable. This reckless behaviour deepens Yemen’s already devastating humanitarian crisis, and it is in the UK’s national economic and security interest that they do not succeed. 

Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK - driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen. 

We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on civilian targets like King Khalid International Airport and are clear that Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:

The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region. 

That’s why today I have approved further UK military support. RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks.
items.bodyText:
The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, given escalating Houthi attacks in the region. 

The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets. These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis. The UK will provide an RAF A400M to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia, alongside UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers. 

This support builds on the UK’s existing defensive military contribution to Saudi Arabia, including the deployment of air defence equipment to protect against missiles and drone attacks. It also includes an extension of air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi defensive air operations including to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen that threaten the Saudi and Yemeni people. 

The Houthis’ attempts to destabilise the region and undermine the security and stability of the Middle East are unacceptable. This reckless behaviour deepens Yemen’s already devastating humanitarian crisis, and it is in the UK’s national economic and security interest that they do not succeed. 

Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK - driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen. 

We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on civilian targets like King Khalid International Airport and are clear that Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:


  The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region. 

  That’s why today I have approved further UK military support. RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks.

items.title: CMA outlines proposals to unlock contactless technology on Apple iPhone
items.summary: Apple’s fees and rules are blocking UK fintechs and other businesses from innovating and growing. Proposals expected to result in substantially lower access fees, helping make it commercially viable for more businesses to innovate and compe
items.bodyHtml:
• Apple’s fees and rules are blocking UK fintechs and other businesses from innovating and growing. 

  • Proposals expected to result in substantially lower access fees, helping make it commercially viable for more businesses to innovate and compete. 

  • Proposals would require Apple to grant access through the main contactless technology standards used internationally and give businesses more choice. 

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is consulting on proposals to transform how UK businesses build digital products and services on Apple’s iPhone.  

The UK is one of the world’s leading fintech hubs, with the sector generating around £214 billion in turnover and supporting more than 360,000 jobs. Fintechs are a UK success story, but Apple’s fees and access rules for key mobile contactless technology, known as near field communication (NFC), risk blocking their ability to innovate and grow. 

The CMA has heard concerns from businesses in the UK that Apple’s current NFC access arrangements may not be commercially viable, that fees, and other terms may be onerous, and that different technical approaches across jurisdictions and platforms can make it harder to scale and compete effectively. 

Contactless services in the UK 

Contactless technology is already central to everyday life in the UK. People increasingly use their phones to pay, travel, access buildings and hold important credentials. The increasing importance of this technology is clear from changes in contactless payments, currently the most popular use of this technology, which now represents 39% of all payments compared to just 3% of transactions a decade ago. Meanwhile, more than 60% of adults currently use a digital wallet, with Apple Wallet being the most popular choice in the UK. 

However, unlike in the EU, not a single firm has launched a wallet-type product to compete with Apple’s in the UK. Just six months after Apple agreed to provide NFC access for payments in the EU, Vipps launched the first alternative payment app, followed by PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA. 

The CMA wants to ensure that businesses in the UK with great ideas have a genuine opportunity to compete with existing wallets and develop the technologies and services of the future. Better access to the technology underpinning these services could help UK businesses develop a wide range of new products, such as account-to-account payments, digital IDs, travel passes and digital keys. 

What the CMA is proposing 

For businesses to compete effectively, access to the technology needs to work both technically and commercially. The CMA’s proposals therefore address two barriers: giving businesses access to the technologies they need and ensuring that access is available on terms which allow viable business models to develop. 

Giving businesses a choice of technology: The CMA proposals would require Apple to provide access through the main contactless technology standards used internationally. Evidence seen by the CMA suggests that neither technology raises inherent security concerns and that access to both standards would support the widest range of innovative use cases and enable UK firms to roll out payment services that are already offered in the EU. 

Making access commercially viable: Even where technical access is available, high fees can prevent businesses from developing viable products and competing effectively. Pricing is therefore a key part of ensuring that businesses have effective access to contactless technology. The CMA is not proposing to set the price and terms of contactless functionality access. Instead, it has proposed principles for how this should be determined, with the expectation that charges would be substantially lower than Apple’s current fees while still fairly rewarding Apple for providing access.  

These proposals are consistent with the CMA’s proportionate approach to intervention and principles set out in digital markets legislation. The measures would help UK fintechs and other businesses seize the potential of this technology, which makes everyday experiences faster and more seamless. It will not only improve people’s lives now by offering more choice, but create the conditions for a new generation of contactless products and services to be developed in the future.  

This could include:   

  • digital wallets and payment services 

  • digital IDs and age-verification tools 

  • digital car, hotel and workplace keys 

  • tickets and travel passes 

  • loyalty and rewards services 

 Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA, said: 

These proposals open the door to more innovation, more choice and economic growth, including in the UK’s important fintech sector.

We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple’s contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.  

By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services here - from payment apps and digital IDs to travel passes and digital keys.

David Geale, PSR Managing Director and Executive Director for Consumers, Payments and Competition at the FCA, said: 

We welcome steps the CMA has taken to boost competition and innovation. Improved access and substantially lower fees should create greater competition and more choice for consumers and businesses.  

Opening up this technology will also support the expansion of open banking, enabling more people to make payments directly from their bank accounts.” 

The consultation will close on Tuesday 17 November 2026, and a final decision will be made after responses have been assessed. Visit the case page to find out more about the consultation and submit a response.  

Notes to editors 

  1. The CMA is consulting on a proposed conduct requirement under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024. The consultation follows the CMA’s designation of Apple as having Strategic Market Status in relation to its mobile platform. 

  2. UK Finance (2026) estimates that contactless payments – whether made using a physical card or a mobile device – rose by 2% to 19.2 billion in 2025, representing 39% of all payments. A decade ago, contactless made up just 3% of transactions.   

  3. The Data City (2025) estimates that the fintech sector employs 362,651 people across 3,348 companies and generates a combined turnover of £213.6 billion from 3,583 businesses.   

  4. Which? (2026) found that 62% of UK adults currently use a digital wallet, with Apple Wallet (50%) being the most popular. 

  5. The two main contactless technology standards used internationally are known as secure element (SE), which stores information on-device and host-based card emulation (HCE), which stores data off-device. Both HCE and SE are established technologies, not developed by Apple, and used across mobile ecosystems to enable a range of contactless services. Apple currently only offers SE in the UK, and the proposals mean that it would be required to offer both HCE and SE.

items.title: Serious offenders detained in hospital will no longer receive benefits
items.summary: Serious offenders detained for treatment under a Hospital Order will no longer receive taxpayer-funded benefits worth hundreds of pounds a month. Change ends “double provision,” whereby offenders have their living costs met by the NHS while
items.bodyHtml:
• Serious offenders detained for treatment under a Hospital Order will no longer receive taxpayer-funded benefits worth hundreds of pounds a month.
  • Change ends “double provision,” whereby offenders have their living costs met by the NHS while also claiming benefits at the taxpayer’s expense.
  • Follows direct engagement with victims’ families who campaigned to close the loophole and a range of experts.

Under the current system, an offender can be paid over £800 a month in Universal Credit – amounting to thousands in taxpayer cash over several years. The proposed change is expected to save tens of millions of pounds each year.

As part of ongoing action to put fairness back at the heart of the welfare system, this intervention will stop hundreds of offenders receiving benefits from early next year – those already in hospital and future cases. 

Those transferred to mental health hospitals from prison are already banned from claiming. The regulations laid today will extend this to mental health hospital patients that are guilty of a dozen serious offences – focusing on violent and sexual offences.

The move will end the so-called “double provision” where people detained under a hospital order can receive benefits despite already having their bed and board fully funded by the taxpayer through the NHS.

Families of victims in high-profile cases - including the loved ones of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche and the victims of the Nottingham attacks, Grace O’Malley-Kumar, Barnaby Webber, and Ian Coates - have bravely highlighted the loophole which sees offenders continuing to receive benefit payments.

The change comes after extensive engagement between the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions and a range of experts and victims directly affected. 

Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, Pat McFadden said:

We said we’d act to tackle this gross unfairness and we’re delivering on that promise.

For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it.

The decision to remove benefits from serious offenders will not affect people currently detained under the Mental Health Act 1983, who have not committed any offence. 

Anyone detained under a hospital order for any reason will continue to receive appropriate mental health support. 

The regulations deliver on the promise made earlier this year to close the loophole, marking the latest step in reforming the welfare system to put fairness at its core, while ensuring it works for the people who need it most.

Emma Webber, Mother of Barnaby Webber said: 

This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do. It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers’ money.

A hospital bed does not erase the egregious crimes committed, nor the destruction they have caused. Closing this loophole finally delivers some basic accountability that victims deserve.

Leon Westcarr, Uncle of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche said: 

The loss of my niece can never be undone, but I am encouraged that this long-standing injustice has been recognised and addressed. I am grateful to the Secretary of State for listening, investigating the issue, and taking bold action to ensure that those responsible for the most serious crimes do not benefit from their actions. This is an important step towards fairness for victims and their families.

Linda Westcarr, Mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche said: 

I believe it is right that the Government reviews benefit entitlement for those who have committed the most serious offences, particularly where public money, funded by taxpayers, is involved. For many victims’ families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society. In my view, this is not simply a question of policy; it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised.

I recognise that a hospital order is a mental health disposal rather than a prison sentence, and that each case must be considered carefully. However, the seriousness of the offence and the lasting consequences for victims and their families must remain central to these decisions.

For families like mine, the consequences of losing a loved one are devastating and lifelong. Kennedi’s life was taken, her child is growing up without a mother, and our family continues to live with the trauma of her death.

I welcome this announcement as a step towards addressing these concerns and achieving a greater sense of fairness for victims’ families. I hope the Government will provide clarity on how and when the proposed changes will be implemented.

Kennedi mattered. Her life mattered. The voices of victims’ families must be heard, and their suffering must never be overlooked when decisions are made about the consequences of serious crime.

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, father of Grace O’Malley Kumar said: 

Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness. Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount. On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits.

On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated. We are grateful to the Secretary of State Pat McFadden for taking action and listening to our campaign which always been about what is good for the country.

Julian Hendy, from the Hundred Families said: 

This is a very welcome move and something we’ve been campaigning on for nearly a decade. 

Paying thousands of pounds of state benefits to mentally disordered offenders on hospital orders who have committed the most serious of crimes cannot be justified. It is unjust and morally wrong. 

Dangerous offenders should not be rewarded for their crimes, particularly when they have no costs and when victims’ families have to struggle so hard to get appropriate care and support.

That’s why we’re very grateful the government has taken action to close this dangerous loophole, which will surely help keep patients, their families, and the public safe.

Additional Information:

  • The Regulations will apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983 and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995

  • The offences under scope for England and Wales (not including the Scots Law equivalents) are:

  • Manslaughter (whether voluntary or involuntary)
  • Attempted murder
  • Wounding (etc) with intent to cause grievous bodily harm (GBH)
  • Rape
  • Assault by penetration
  • Causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent (aggravated – with penetration)
  • Rape of a child under 13
  • Sexual assault of a child under 13 (aggravated – with penetration)
  • Causing or inciting a child under 13 to engage in sexual activity (aggravated – with penetration)
  • Sexual activity with a child
  • Familial sexual offences (sexual activity with a child family member) (offender 18 or over)

  • Familial sexual offences (inciting a child family member to engage in sexual activity) (offender 18 or over)

  • Murder is not included because a Hospital Order is not an available disposal for the offence of murder which attracts a mandatory life sentence.
  • The affirmative regulations will be laid in Parliament on 20 October and remain subject to parliamentary approval.
  • Without these regulations, an offender on Universal Credit, in a single household, aged over 25 and receiving the LCWRA rate, could receive over £800 a month. 
  • The change is expected affect some 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future.
  • Removal of these benefits will save in the low tens of millions of pounds each year with full financial impacts to be published as part of the 2026 budget.
  • Individuals in scope will no longer be entitled to either Universal Credit, Pension Credit, State Pension and Employment and Support Allowance while they remain detained in hospital. 
  • The NHS will continue to provide appropriate mental health support.
  • The policy follows engagement with clinicians, victims’ groups, mental health experts and the devolved governments and the decision to remove benefits from serious offenders will not affect anyone currently detained under the Mental Health Act 1983, who has not committed an offence.
  • The change applies only to those convicted of a serious offence as defined in the regulations; it does not affect anyone on remand, unfit to plead, awaiting trial or those convicted of offences that are not detailed in the prescribed list.
  • While the change only comes into effect early next year, it will apply to both existing and future cases from the point that the regulations come into force, regardless of when their conviction was made.

items.title: Full steam ahead: new station for Bradford
items.summary: new station at Bradford Interchange to bring passengers more reliable services, better connections and faster journeys as Northern Powerhouse Rail moves one step closer Bradford Council says delivering the new station alongside the proposed
items.bodyHtml:
• new station at Bradford Interchange to bring passengers more reliable services, better connections and faster journeys as Northern Powerhouse Rail moves one step closer
  • Bradford Council says delivering the new station alongside the proposed West Yorkshire Mass Transit network will unlock thousands of jobs and homes, and more than £1 billion in economic benefits
  • new station will transform the city’s connections with some of the North’s largest cities, including Leeds, Manchester and York

Passengers across Yorkshire are set to benefit from major station improvements, as the government has today (20 October 2026) confirmed a new station at Bradford Interchange.

Bradford’s connections with some of the North’s largest cities, including Leeds, Manchester and York, will be transformed as passengers will be able to benefit from more frequent trains, improved journey times and reliability.

The Bradford Interchange site unlocks the potential to regenerate Bradford’s Southern Gateway, and in tandem with the proposed West Yorkshire Mass Transit, would support thousands of new homes, jobs and up to £1 billion in economic benefits.

The announcement marks a major milestone in the delivery of Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) and the government’s mission to drive growth in every postcode.

The station will also become part of Great British Railways (GBR), the new publicly owned railway that will bring track and train together, helping deliver a more reliable, efficient and passenger-focused railway.

The Prime Minister is driving change to give control back to local communities by empowering Mayors to shape transport to serve the communities they know best, and that is why the location decision was made with the Mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin.

NPR will deliver a turn-up-and-go railway for passengers from Bradford, meaning multiple trains an hour will run frequently enough between major cities across the North that passengers won’t need to check a timetable before going to the station.

Transport Secretary, Heidi Alexander, said:

Today marks an important milestone for Bradford with a brand-new station that will transform how people travel across the North.

By bringing Northern Powerhouse Rail into the heart of the city, we are unlocking the huge potential Bradford offers – improving connections, supporting economic growth and setting the foundations for new homes, jobs and opportunities across the region.

The new GBR station will be delivered in the 2030s and replace the outdated 1970s station, providing the modern transport hub that Bradford deserves. The city will be at the heart of the NPR network, transforming its connections with some of the North’s largest cities including Leeds, Manchester and York, creating opportunities for investment, regeneration and economic growth.

Bradford’s new city centre station is a key part of the government’s Northern Growth Strategy, which, with Northern Powerhouse Rail, is electrifying and upgrading routes between Leeds, Bradford, Sheffield and York, improving journey times and reliability across the region.

Tracy Brabin, Mayor of West Yorkshire, said:

Today is an exciting and important milestone for Bradford, with an ironclad commitment to a new station in the city centre.

Bradford has so much untapped potential, and faster, more frequent trains to Leeds and Manchester, and the transformation of the city centre through Bradford City Village, will help to finally unleash it.

Together with investment for northern powerhouse rail, a mass transit system for West Yorkshire and our brand-new Weaver Network, we are working in lockstep with the government to deliver a better-connected region.

Henri Murison MBE, Chief Executive of Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said:

The decision to build Bradford’s new station at the interchange in the city centre is a long-term commitment to the city and the wider North.

By unlocking the regeneration of the Southern Gateway, we will see homes and jobs for this city which otherwise would not be built or come here. Working with the council and Mayor Tracy Brabin and her team, I will be doing everything I can to push on and move forward with ambitious plans that enable future phases of Northern Powerhouse Rail. This network will better connect the young people in the city with opportunities in Manchester and Liverpool as well as Sheffield.

Bradford and the North’s next phase of growth will be built by business. Confidence is already building here, and this will help build it further.

Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, said:

This government is doing things differently. We are backing local leaders and investing in the infrastructure that people need. This is how we create good jobs where people live and growth that supports a high street you can be proud of. That is how we build a stronger future for cities like Bradford, boost West Yorkshire, and deliver our plan for growth in every part of the country.

Media enquiries 0300 7777878

Switchboard 0300 330 3000

items.title: PM puts the brakes on rip-off parking charges and car scams
items.summary: Drivers will get new rights to challenge unfair private parking charges under new rules announced today. This includes a guaranteed 5 minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends, and the right to have c
items.bodyHtml:
Drivers will get new rights to challenge unfair private parking charges under new rules announced today. This includes a guaranteed 5 minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends, and the right to have charges cancelled on appeal for issues they can’t control. 

Under the new Private Parking Code of Practice laid in Parliament today (20 October), charges will be scrapped on appeal for honest mistakes, like stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations like a medical emergency, breakdown or broken ticket machine. 

For smaller slip-ups, like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle’s registration or forgetting to confirm it in the machine when parking, drivers will face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal. 

The Code also freezes the maximum parking charge at £100. Operators who don’t comply risk losing access to DVLA data, meaning that even if they issue a charge, it will be far more difficult to identify the registered owner to pursue payment. 

In addition, unscrupulous second-hand car dealers who wind back odometers to disguise a vehicle’s true mileage will also face tougher action. Known as car clocking, fraudulently selling a clocked car is already illegal, but adding it to the official list of banned practices will make it easier for enforcers to crack down, protecting buyers and backing honest businesses. 

These changes are the latest measures in the Prime Minister’s series of everyday fixes, tackling the frustrations that cost people time and money to give families more room to breathe. 

Today’s action follows moves to stop unfair airline charges, tackle subscription traps, rogue traders, and rip-off school uniform costs. 

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: 

Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat. 

These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. 

We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off. 

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said:  

Parking should be straightforward, not another everyday hassle. These changes mean drivers get a fairer deal, protected time to park and leave without fear of being unfairly charged, and confidence that private parking providers are held to a higher standard.  

It’s yet another step forward in this government’s plan to take the stress out of everyday life and ease the pressure on people’s pockets.

Minister for Consumer Action, Kate Dearden, said: 

Nobody works hard for their money just to be deceived by a dodgy trader, and this is exactly the kind of everyday rip-off this government is going after. 

By making it easier to take action against car clocking, we are protecting consumers’ hard-earned money and supporting businesses that play by the rules.

The government has also promised today to go further still, by consulting as soon as possible next year on private parking debt recovery fees, including on whether to cut an existing £70 cap or scrap the fees altogether. 

Data shows just under 17 million private parking charges were issued in the UK last year. In 2025, the government set out proposals to improve standards by consulting on a new Private Parking Code of Practice. 

Today’s response sets out the measures being brought in to protect motorists. Parliament will now have time to scrutinise the new Code, before ministers press ahead to bring it into force as soon as possible. 

This Code brings in, for the first time, a fully independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board, and requires operators to share more information with government, giving drivers stronger protections than ever before. 

Since taking office, the government has also launched a review of airport drop-off charges, cut VAT on electricity bills this winter, frozen fuel duty and rail fares, and raised the Minimum Wage, as it continues to take action to ease the cost of living. 

For more information:

Private Parking Code of Practice 

  • The code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales.  

  • Motorists will have their parking charge cancelled where they can provide evidence that one of the scenarios set out in the Appeals Charter applies to them. 

  • Operators will have to report data on the charges they issue and how appeals are handled, to help raise standards across the industry. This will be scrutinised by a new independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board, giving drivers confidence that the Code is working as intended. The process to set the board up will commence once the code comes into force.  

  • The changes follow a public consultation that ran from July to September 2025 and received 4,526 responses from the public and industry. Motorists were clear that they wanted fairer appeals, and independent oversight of the private parking industry. 

  • The government intends to consult further on the remaining CMA recommendations post-publication of the Code. 

Car clocking 

  • The change applies to businesses selling cars to consumers. Car clocking will be added to the banned practices list (Schedule 20) under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024.

items.title: Readout of the Civil Society Council: 15 October 2026
items.summary: On Thursday 15 October, the Civil Society Council met at the King’s Trust in Manchester. The Prime Minister opened by recognising the vital contribution that civil society organisations make in our communities. He reflected that “if you sta
items.bodyHtml:
On Thursday 15 October, the Civil Society Council met at the King’s Trust in Manchester.  

The Prime Minister opened by recognising the vital contribution that civil society organisations make in our communities. He reflected that “if you start where people live, with organisations they trust, all kinds of things are possible”. He argued for a whole-government, whole-society approach to supporting people as they grow up and to tackle youth unemployment as part of the 10-year plan to be published later this year. 

The PM reflected on the power of partnership with civil society and the importance of coming together to deliver better outcomes. He reiterated the need “to face the same way and pull in the same direction. It’s about empowering people and places to find their own solutions and trusting them to do so.” He drew on the experience of Covid, and the particular contribution of faith communities during that time.   

The PM then spoke about Live Well in Greater Manchester where a joined-up, person-centred approach, with civil society as an equal partner, meant people could access the support they need. In this, he reflected that “civil society in all its many iterations is absolutely critical to the success of our country.” In response, the Council proposed a deep dive into the principles of Live Well and other community-led models. This will be taken forward by a coalition of partners with DHSC’s sponsorship, learning from and informing wider work on the transition to neighbourhood health.  

Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy MP reflected that as civil society organisations are dealing with the realities of peoples live everyday across the country, they should be a respected and trusted partner of government at every level, with a critical role to play as devolution is accelerated.   

Sally Jameson MP, Minister for the No10 North Devolution strategy, then joined a session on rewiring the state. Minister Jameson set out more details of the Government’s vision for devolution and public service reform, and invited Council Members’ reflections on the structures, capability and incentives needed to shift power closer to communities.  

Finally, Vicky Foxcroft MP, Minister for Civil Society and Youth, joined Council Members to discuss opportunities for young people. This focused particularly on how government and civil society can work together in giving young people the confidence, skills and support they need as they transition into the world of work.   

The Council Chair, Kate Lee, closed the discussion by thanking Council Members for their contributions. She reflected on progress since the last Council Meeting – across civil service capability building, embedding public participation, changes to procurement processes and work underway on volunteering rates – and agreed actions to be taken forward ahead of the next meeting.

items.title: MHRA authorises plozasiran (Redemplo) for adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome
items.summary: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has today, 19 October 2026, authorised plozasiran (Redemplo) to reduce triglyceride levels in adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS), alongside a low-fat diet. FCS
items.bodyHtml:
The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has today, 19 October 2026, authorised plozasiran (Redemplo) to reduce triglyceride levels in adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS), alongside a low-fat diet.  

FCS is a rare condition that causes abnormally high levels of fats called triglycerides in the blood. This can lead to inflammation of the pancreas, known as pancreatitis, causing severe abdominal pain.  

Plozasiran blocks the production of apolipoprotein C3, a protein made in the liver that slows the breakdown of fats. Reducing production of this protein helps lower triglyceride levels in the blood.  

The medicine is administered as a 25 mg injection under the skin once every three months. Patients or their caregivers can give the injection after receiving training.  

Julian Beach, Executive Director, Operations, said:  

“This authorisation provides an additional treatment option for adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome, a rare condition that can cause serious and painful complications.  

“Clinical trial data showed that plozasiran substantially reduced triglyceride levels when used alongside a controlled diet.  

“As with all medicines, we will continue to monitor the safety of plozasiran closely.”  

The authorisation is supported by a main study involving 75 adults with FCS. All participants followed a controlled diet, with 50 receiving plozasiran and 25 receiving placebo.  

After 10 months, participants receiving plozasiran had a median reduction in triglyceride levels of around 80%, compared with 17% among those receiving placebo. The study also recorded fewer episodes of acute pancreatitis in participants receiving plozasiran.  

The most common side effect reported with plozasiran is hyperglycaemia (raised blood sugar), which may affect more than one in 10 people. Other common side effects, which may affect up to one in 10 people, include headache, nausea and reactions at the injection site.  

Anyone who suspects they are experiencing a side effect should speak to their doctor, pharmacist or nurse and report it directly through the Yellow Card scheme at https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk or via the MHRA Yellow Card app.  

Notes to editors  

  • The marketing authorisation was granted on 19 October 2026 to Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals Ireland Limited.  

  • It was approved through the International Recognition Procedure (IRP), Route B, with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) as the reference regulator.   

  • More information can be found in the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) and Patient Information Leaflet (PIL), which will be published on the MHRA Products website in due course.  

  • The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is responsible for regulating all medicines and medical devices in the UK by ensuring they work and are acceptably safe. All our work is underpinned by robust and fact-based judgements to ensure that the benefits justify any risks.  

  • The MHRA is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care.  

  • For media enquiries, please contact newscentre@mhra.gov.uk, or call 020 3080 7651.

The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has today, 19 October 2026, authorised plozasiran (Redemplo) to reduce triglyceride levels in adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS), alongside a low-fat diet.  

FCS is a rare condition that causes abnormally high levels of fats called triglycerides in the blood. This can lead to inflammation of the pancreas, known as pancreatitis, causing severe abdominal pain.  

Plozasiran blocks the production of apolipoprotein C3, a protein made in the liver that slows the breakdown of fats. Reducing production of this protein helps lower triglyceride levels in the blood.  

The medicine is administered as a 25 mg injection under the skin once every three months. Patients or their caregivers can give the injection after receiving training.  

Julian Beach, Executive Director, Operations, said:  

“This authorisation provides an additional treatment option for adults with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome, a rare condition that can cause serious and painful complications.  

“Clinical trial data showed that plozasiran substantially reduced triglyceride levels when used alongside a controlled diet.  

“As with all medicines, we will continue to monitor the safety of plozasiran closely.”  

The authorisation is supported by a main study involving 75 adults with FCS. All participants followed a controlled diet, with 50 receiving plozasiran and 25 receiving placebo.  

After 10 months, participants receiving plozasiran had a median reduction in triglyceride levels of around 80%, compared with 17% among those receiving placebo. The study also recorded fewer episodes of acute pancreatitis in participants receiving plozasiran.  

The most common side effect reported with plozasiran is hyperglycaemia (raised blood sugar), which may affect more than one in 10 people. Other common side effects, which may affect up to one in 10 people, include headache, nausea and reactions at the injection site.  

Anyone who suspects they are experiencing a side effect should speak to their doctor, pharmacist or nurse and report it directly through the Yellow Card scheme at https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk or via the MHRA Yellow Card app.  

Notes to editors  


  
    The marketing authorisation was granted on 19 October 2026 to Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals Ireland Limited.  
  
  
    It was approved through the International Recognition Procedure (IRP), Route B, with the European Medicines Agency (EMA) as the reference regulator.   
  
  
    More information can be found in the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) and Patient Information Leaflet (PIL), which will be published on the MHRA Products website in due course.  
  
  
    The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is responsible for regulating all medicines and medical devices in the UK by ensuring they work and are acceptably safe. All our work is underpinned by robust and fact-based judgements to ensure that the benefits justify any risks.  
  
  
    The MHRA is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care.
